way from the Persian gulf. bound for
New York. when the accident happened.

track of the Hamburg American steamers
running from Europe to st. Thomas.


The Wheeling. owing to her small size
and scant coal supply, was unable to
tow the big liner, which had already
broken all Of her large hawsers in the
effort to take q tow from a British
steamer the I'd instant When the Wheel
ing parted company with her the Che
ruskia was making good weather. She
had four weeks provisions and the
Wheeling supplied some extra food.


The Navy Department has reported the
facts to the Hamburg-American steam

not look for them until the latter part

get cool, and the big ducks will not ap-

and wild goose season. Wild celery and

chfevous small boys, who came near

a crowded New York Central passenger
train late yesterday.

south of Yonkers, when the engineer
and fireman noticed the lads standing
on either side of the track. AS the
locomotive whizzed past a number of
small rocks were hurled at the flying
train.

open cab window and struck Frank
Burrows. the engineer, on the head,
near the temple. He toppled over un-
conscious.


Charles Gildersleeve, the fireman,
heard the rock fall and rushed across
the cab and seized the throttle, bring
ing the train to stop just before it
reached semaphore, which indicated
an open switch few rods ahead


Burrows soon regained conscious
ness, and. despite his injury, would
not leave his post until he had COM
pleted his trip.

CHICAGO, June THE wheat market was
a very irregular affair. Early market was
oversold at a lower level than last night be-
cause Of improving weather and lower corn
market, then advanced sharply enough to strip
the market Of its local short interest, then
broke to lower level than before. Near the
close a prominent local elevator concern abb
sorbed all the floating offers of September and
caused a quick rally. The July delivery was
more highty than the deferred months. Some
nervousness was expressed over the possibility
of a squeeze in that future in event the pres
ent liberal local stocks were shipped out The
weather forecast is for showery and warmer
weather northwest, ideal condition. The
shows an enormous increase, 10 per cent, in
acreage seeded to wheat in the three north
western Canadian provinces


Corn opened weak and lower and showed a
dragging tendency, without much further de-
cline since. Shorts who covered yesterday
were resellers today, mostly larger local pro-
fe- ional spectators. Fine and much warmer
weather in the belt was the chief incentive.
There was but little shipping demand, which
neutralzed the effect OF lack of noteworthy
offerings from the interior. Farmers now
generally busy plowing, and are averse to
selling prices now established. Cash corn was
about 1sc lower than yesterday. The weather
is better and the market will not stand up
up Ter improved weather at present.


Oats followed corn. Early prices were high
est There was some covering by local shorts,
which was responsible for top figures early,
but there was country selling on the advance.
Fine crop prospects were against present
values.

terests, but eased off from the top because of

when the Western Union Telegraph
company established two lines to Jack
sonville.

orange crop, which will not yield more
than 20 per cent.

quesa and swept to sea. The six men
aboard perished.

Frasch is ashore in three fathoms of
water at Crocker's reef, northeast of

having rescued six men from the

adrift in the gulf.

quicksand at Marquesas. The schooner
Vivian was swept to sea and lost.

night from Twin Cities, Wis, where
they landed Tuesday afternoon, having
been in the air twenty-one hours.

his right arm being lacerated when
caught between the rigging of the bal
loon and the basket


While over Lake Michigan Tuesday
morning the men had a narrow es-
cape from being precipitated into the
water. They were 5000 feet high when
they struck the cool air over the lake.
This cooled the oxygen gas, causing it
to condense rapidly.


In ten minutes they dropped more
than 5000 feet. From that time until
they landed about five hours later
their lives were in jeopardy.


They tossed out bag after bag Of
ballast until they established their
equilibrium about forty-five feet above
the water by trailing their guide rope.

by, but rancnnouses for distant were

LONG BEACH, Aug. 23.-Lightning
struck a high tension Pacific Electric
wire a short distance from the supply
station at Fifth street and American
avenue, about 2:35 o'clock this after
noon, putting all the machinery in the
supply station out of business, running
a transformer and damaging a big gen.
orator worth $4,000. For an hour all
local cars and the Los Angeles bound
cars this side of Dominguez junction
stood stock still. Hurried repairs were
made to avoid continued interruption
of traffic, but for some time the run
ming of the cars was only spasmodic.
The lightning caused a wild flash and
a terrific roar In the station. The work
men fled from the building. There was
no damage from fire. None was injured
It was stated that the lightning drove
back into the machinery all the cleo
triclty going out over the wires, and
this caused the trouble. There was
continuous rumbling of thunder this
afternoon, and a sprinkle of rain fell
in the northwest and the eastern parts
of town.

jaws of their captors. The boys and

VICTORIA, B. c., Aug. 5.-Brief
messages received from Juneau, Skag-
way and Cordova says there was no
panic when the Princess May struck
the reef north of Sentinel island this
morning, but the women and children
suffered much from cold in the small
boats, the majority having left the
sinking ship scantily clad.


Captain Mcleod and his officers took
the situation coolly and managed to
get all the passengers and the crew
away from the sinking steamer before
she foundered The boats hugged the
shore until daylight, when landings
were made.


In the meantime steamers were sent
from Juneau, where the distress signals
were received from several sources.
The steamship Victoria picked up the
call at sea, and it was also heard by
the United States naval station at Cor
doVa. The ships boats bearing the
survivors will reach Juneau late to-
night.


All the mail, including gold from the
Yukon sent as registered mail, was
landed on Sentinel island.


CAPTAINS REPORT


A message received tonight from
Captain Mcleod says the liner ran
ashore at 2 o'clock this morning on a
reef at the north end of Sentinel island.
The vessel began to sink Immediately.
and wireless messages were sent by
Operator Keller asking for assistance,
until water flooding into the engine
room rendered the apparatus useless.
The passengers and crew were all
saved and landed on Sentinel island.
When the landing was completed Pilot
John Richardson was sent with a
boats crew to Juneau, where he ar
rived tonight.


The steamer probably will be saved.
Wrecking apparatus will be sent north
at once to begin salvage operations,
The foreh Id and engine room are filled
with water but the vessel is not sub
merged

agent of the Canadian Pacific says the
companys steamer Princess Ena,
which was on the way up Lynn canal,

After a record breaking trip twice
across the continent on an Indian
motorcycle volney E. Davis reached
San Francisco yesterday. His journey
consumed more than four months and
a total distance of 10.400 miles.


Davis, former vice president of the
Motorcycle club, left here for New
York June 10. BY easy stages he
travelled through Arizona, New Mexico,
Texas. Oklahoma. Kansas. Missouri,
Illinois, Indiana, Ohio. Pennsylvania
and New York


JohniSorenson. who challenged Davis
to I0eke his ride, accompanied him
as far as Dallas, Tex Through the
Yuma desert they encountered sand
storms and terrific heat 1t became
necessary to moisten their mouths
every few minutes from the canteens.
Many miles the plucky riders bumped
railroad ties, while Davis, in taking a
short cut across the shore of Salton
sea, punctured his tires.


Desert conditions extended to Texas.
Here heavy rains converted the soil
into impossible black mud. Davis
went to Chicago alone. When he got
there he had ridden over rough sur
face for 1900 miles.


June 20 Davis entered New York,
having made the longest continuous
journey of any motorcycle rider. His
motor did not skip a stroke in the
whole trip.


The return home was made easier
by favorable weather. Instead of GO
ing back through the desert, he fol-
lowed the Union Pacific. Davis set
out from New York September 6. He
finished in good physical condition.

strong Inducements to persuade him
to undertake a similar trip. Misera Bile
roads, frequently no road at all, the

SAN BERNARDINO, May 15.-When
Joe Harris, known to the police of the
country as "Sheeny joe" and George
Fitzwilliams, pickpockets, alighted from
a Salt Lake passenger train in San Ber-
nardino they met an old friend who
knew them years ago in Chicago.


Though the meeting was cordial it
was far from what the two light
fingered individuals had anticipated,
and on the next train that left the city
the two men stood on the rear platform
waving farewell to Policeman Jack
Stuart.


Years ago while a member of the
Chicago police force Stuart arrested
Harris. Both men were we'll known to
him, and as they stepped from the train
yesterday they were instantly recog-
nized.


Stepping up to the new arrivals,
Stuart said: Are you gentlemen look
ing for rooms?" When informed that
they We're. he said: "Well, fellows, l
am afraid there won't be any room here
for you this week. There are going to
be lot of people here" When he told
them their names and cited some of
their past history Harris recognized
him.


Until the next train departed the
three men walked arm in arm about
the city.

PASADENA, May 16-Missem and
Ketchum are among the names given
to the police in the gambling raid at
545 South Raymond avenue made early
Saturday evening and reported by the
police late that night. The person at
whose place the poker game was be-
ing run, and who is charged with con-
Quoting the same, gave his name as
James Lee and he deposited $25 cash
bail to insure his appearance in court
this morning. Others gave their names
as Jack Johnson, George Lucas, Henry
Nichols, George Missem and John
Ketchum, and each deposited $40 cash
bail. It is thought that all the names
are fictitious and that the players are
Pasadena business men.

The fad for metal beds is passing, ac-
cording to a writer in Suburban Life
for April, who says: I'VE are told that
metal beds are more sanitary, and so
they probably are, especially for hospi-
tails, where the simplest white painted
frames are used. But the fashion for
brass beds ran into such hideous
shapes and such tawdry elaboration
that the pendulum has swung the other
way now, and the wooden beds have
come into vogue again. Properly hand
led, they should be as easy to care for
as the brass bed, and they are far pref
tier. However, there is no doubt that
good metal bed can be bought for
much smaller price than good wooden
one. Choose the simplest-the hospital
cot with no ornaments at all, or the all
brass bed; the white beds with brass
cups and vases do not wear so well,
the brass ornaments coming off and
denting easily"

New York, Feb. T.-Col Robert NJ.
Thompson and others interested in the
United States Naval Academy have
bought the noted picture THE Fight Be-
tween the Kearsarge and the Alabama"
painted by the late Alfred c. Rowland
and have presented it TO the institution at
Annapolis.


The canvas depicts priests, peasants.
and gendarmes on the shore near Cher
bOurg. France, where on June 10, 1854,
was fought the desperate battle between
the two vessels.


The artist represents spectators spell
bound as they watch the old Kearsarge,
which represented the Union. and the
Confederate Alabama maneuvering for
position and working their deadly guns.
A brisk breeze lifts the white bonnets of
the peasant women and blows the gown
of the venerable priest who had dismiss
ed his parishioners at the sounds of the
conflict The embattlAd craft are seen
emerging from the smoke of their own
guns.

and the Petrol have been in Atlantic
waters.

SAN JOSE, April Julius Dusoevoir
had narrow escape from death this
afternoon at 4 o'clock when he fell
from his monoplane in its first success
full fight on the Linda Vista golf links.
His fall was broken by piano wire
supports running underneath the aero
plane and he escaped with a broken
finger. The aeroplane was. badly
wrecked, the three supporting wheels,
planes and propellers being crushed
when the. runaway airship hit the
ground.


The accident was witnessed by sew
eral hundred people. Dusoevoir's en-
gine clearly showed it's power when he
turned it loose. The aeroplane ran
swiftly along the ground and then
gradually ascended.


For a hundred feet or so the machine
skinned along, the wheels clearing the
ground fully 10 feet. Suddenly the
aviator plunged backward from his
seat and would have been dashed
against the ground but for the wires
running from the framework under
meath the planes. Here he was held
as the craft dashed along for so more
feet without guiding hand.


Then it dropped suddenly and people
f1ocked to the rescue of the aviator
caught in the wreck. Dusoevoir was
unable to offer an explanation for his
fall

Files and horses are intimately asso-
ciated. The latter provide the ferment
material In which flies deposit eggs for
their Matching. When winged they repay
with ingratitude. pursue and torture the
animals that provided their nursery.
Owners OF horses try to protect them
from the flies with nets aud blankets.
They short-sightedly attack the effect
and leave the cause untouched.


Many accidents are due to these fly
prosecutions OF horses. They make the
more nervous ones frantic. They break
away to escape them. The flies deposit
their eggs on their hair and the horses
acquire the bolts"


If horse owners pay attention to the
cause they will have less reason to look
after the effect. A sprinkling OF manure
with kerosene destroys egg and maggot.
Kerosene costs less than fly nets and
blankets or repairs OF runaway break
age.

after three good bit" her sister answered.

Mother will for him, reach home"

Editor Herald: To the banks of a
rushing stream came, day by day, a
vast and mournful throng, beset by
sickness, sorrow and fear. For all
must ford the stream daily. Save only
a wealthy and privileged few, who
were exempt. And there was no bridge.
The small and weak were beaten down
by the raging waters; while security
there was none for even the stalwart
and strong; snags and pitfalls often
drew them down and they were seen
no more. ,,,


And the stream was named THE
Economic Problem" or as others
called it, "The Distribution Difficulty"
And the cry went up, growing ever
more exigent: who will solve the
problem? Who will bridge the diff
culty?"


Boats of charity and petty reforms
there were, but as these were mostly
fndiVidualistic eXpedients and often
sank in midstream, the peoples plight
was sad indeed.


There were some called Socialists
who brought plans to bridge the
stream. But the priests cried "Sacri-
lege! Would you defeat the will Of
God?" And the lawyers said "Uncon-
stitutional." Still others called states
men were instructed by certain "in-
terests" to shout "Lawandorder!" at
the top of their voices, while all Of
them, as representatives of the priv
ileged few, decried the Socialists, say
ing: "They disagree among them
selves about the bridge; one says four
spans, another five, while still an
other says: Zone grand sweep" but
the Socialists replied ''What matter
such details? Our plans agree on all
essential points and any of them will
bridge the stream that none may suf-
fer. This thing is urgent, for people
perish hourly"


Then certain liable minds" resolved
to damn Socialism with faint praise,
saying "they mean well and are not
without merit. But there Is virtue in
compromise and danger in haste. Let
us have more reform boats, that we
may save here and there sone. To save
ALL by a Socialist bridge were too
radical and revolutionary.

aged Indian suuaws of Victorville have
started on their fortieth pilgrimage
to the mountain wilds of Big Bear
valley on their annual foraging expe-

Meldua and Iasia, known to the whites
of Victorville as "Ann" and "Sarah."
and they are the remainder of tribe
that a score of years ago annually
sent most of its families to the for
ests to harvest the pinon crop.

and the pinons have rapidly disap-
peared. There are now few members
or the once populous tribe left and
there is also a great shortage of
pinons. For 10 years the two squaws
have driven their shaggy ponies to the
spot and brought down what few
pinons they could harvest.


The white hunters of the little nuts
shoot the cones from the pine trees
upper branches with rifles, but the two
Old Indians use their primitive bows
and arrows.

left this morning for the same region,
north of Big Bear valley, to harvest
their annual stock of pinons, of which
the pioneers are fond.

cabin passengers Miss Eleanor HOFFMAN,

and the iifeboat was compelled to return

the missing woman.

one on the vessel noticed anything UNI
usual about her during the voyage up to
the time she took her fatal plunge. The
day before she spent her time quietly

rational in every respect.

NEW YORK, February 1.-THE most
serious traffic block that the BROOKLYN
bridge has known in years brought the
rush-hour throngs across into Manhattan
on foot this morning.


The block. which began at $40 O'Clock,
and was not cleared until the rush hours
were almost over, was caused by q Lex
ington avenue express train coming in
from Cypress Hills. Where the bridge
tracks branch near the Manhattan end to
allow trains choice of the north or south
side of the terminal platform this train
took an indecisive course. The first
truck went to the south and the car was
sent straddling over the tive tracks,
knocking the third rail of its supports
and tipping the second car over the iron
guard rail above the central promenade
for pedestrians. The forward trucks of
the third car were jostled from the track,
but that car settled steadily upon it's
underpinning and its passengers were
not hurt


Hurt by Flying Glass.


Flying glass terrified many persons and
cut some in the first and second cars.
Policemen. who rushed to help the i'm
prisoned passengers out. first sent i'm an
ambulance alarm to the Hudson Street
and other hospitals. The Oak street sta
ton police reserve, reinforcing the bridge
command rushed over the tracks regard
less Of the exposed third rails, and broke
open the end doors and the platform
guards on the first and second cars. Then
they lifted down the 100 passengers of
the two cars. and passed them TO other
policemen, who assisted them over the
railing to the promenade walk.


One woman. who disappeared before the
police could learn her name, was hurled
partially through q window OF the second
car and was caught by policeman on
the promenade walk. over which the car
had lurched. She was the only woman In
the car. and she was lifted out through
the broken window to the walk quite
badly cut about the face and bruised
She complained to Policeman Brown OF
the bridge squad that her purse was in
side, and he went through the window to
get it. On coming out again he handed
it to her and turned to find an ambulance
surgeon. When he next looked for her
she had disappeared along with all the
others, none OF whom had waited for the
ambulances to arrive.

deaf she heard neither the door nor the

finally restored order. Miss Crawford is
forty-five years old.

don and other universities. Oxford
was the only British university not

devote four days to actual farm work

sight into the conditions Of Canadian
agriculture. From Winnipeg the party
will cross the border and visit Madi-
son, Wis; Chicago, Pittsburg, Wash
ington, Annapolis, Philadelphia, New
York, New Haven and Cambridge, Mass.

of the Rhodes scholarship idea, and
after the plan had been worked out

BOSTON, Oct. 26.-The $500 900

the British steamer Kaisenga has just
brought to this port were carried
across the seas amid many perils.


The Kaisenga's trouble began on
July II last, when she was four days
out from Colombo for New York. The
steamer ran into monsoon on that
day, and simultaneously the crew had
TO fight a fire which had broken out
in a bunker. Before the blaze was
subdued it had done damage estimated
at $4,000.


The Kaisenga rode out the storm
safely A coral reef then brought trou-
BILE, the steamer scraping over it on
August s between Singapore and Kobe,
but managing to work off without seri-
Gus damage.

ia on September for Boston than she
ran down and sunk a native fishing
schooner. There were no casualties.

ga, nearly pushing the Kaisenga into

An Arab fireman, crazed by the heat

was not seen again.

an ill-conceived joke there was little
sleep in Panama last night. The jok-
ers were Jailed today


The public has been made nervous
by reports of the earthquake devasta-
tions in Costa Rica, and when word
was passed along last evening that
seismologists had predicted Panama
would be shaken by an earthquake
during the night and the city of Colon
disappear beneath a tidal wave, -anic
prevailed.


The alarm spread from this city to
Ancon and Colon. Many persons fled
into the country and those who stayed
in the towns camped in the streets
and parks. Many spent the hours in
prayer.


The police and firemen remained at
their posts ready for any emergency.


When morning came with no harm
having been done the people realized
they had been hoaxed and the police
got after the jokers.

Professor Metchnikoff and other IA

fruits and vegetables on the ground

microbes. The skins of tomatoes,

breeding grounds for the microbes of
all diseases, and the surface of lettuce,
celery, watercress and other vege-

almost equally adapted to the multi
plication of the maleficent little germs.

subject that among health faddists
and extremely particular people there
has arisen a prejudice that might be
called microphobia. Many people will
eat nothing raw, thus depriving them
selves of all salads and all but cooked

PHILADELPHIA. December 17.-An
unusually pathetic story, in which
death and disease laid a heavy hand
upon an alien family, was made public
today by the immigration authorities
stationed in this city.


John Pike. sturdy shoemaker, came
here two weeks ago from Russia on
the North German Lloyd steamer Cas-
sci. with his wife and six young chill
dren, to seek their fortune in the new
world. But at the gateway of the
promised land they were stopped by
the immigration officials.


They found that three Of the children,
all boys. were suffering from trachoma
The other three, all girls. were i'll with
measles.


There was nothing for the immigra-
tion officers to do but to send the boys
back across the ocean. A family council
was held and it was decided that the
father should take the boys back to their
grandmother in Russia, while the mother
awaited the return of the husband.


There was an affecting parting between
the mother and her boys. AS the ship
sailed away she and the little girls were
sent to the municipal hospital.


The heartbroken. mother was assisted
by the kindly nurses in the care of

FISHGUARD, Wales, Sept. 5.-The
steamer Mauretania arrived here to-
day, hoving on board Captain Pinkham
and fifteen of his crew, who were
picked up by the Cunarder after they
had been at sea in a small boat for six
days following the burning of their
vessel, the British tramp steamer West
Point.


Captain Pinkham said the fire on the
West Point started in the engine room
on August 27. The flames drove the
engineers from their posts and spread
so rapidly that soon the donkey en-
gines operating the pumps were dis
abled by the heat.


An attempt was made to extinguish
the fire by a bucket brigade, but the
hopelessness of the effort was quickly
apparent and the captain ordered small
boats lowered. From the bunkers the
flames made their way to the store
room and galley and prevented the
provisioning of the boats, the intense
heat repeatedly driving back the sail
ors who hoped to secure food sufficient
to keep them until they were picked up
by a passing vessel.


CREW STANDS BY SHIP


Though pressed hard by the fire the
crew stood by their ship until Sunday
afternoon, when the captain ordered
all hands into the boats.


Throughout that night the boats,
each carrying sixteen persons, cruised
in the vicinity, and in the morning
another attempt was made to secure
much needed stores. The burning
craft, which was then sinking, was
again boarded, but scarcely anything
of consequence was secured.


Monday evening the ship foundered.
The two small boats last Wednesday
drifted apart. The other boatload was
picked up by the LELAND line steamer
Devonian Friday morning, while Cap
tain Pinkham and his companions were
rescued by the Mauretania Friday
night.


The captain and the men suffered Sc
yerely, and only by dint OF hard work
saved their boat from sinking.

Pinkham, in telling his story. I'VE

Telephone communication between
Nova Scotia and Prince Edward island
will be established in the near future.
The Maritime telegraph and telephone
company of Nova Scotia has commenced
work on the laying of a cable across
northumberland strait, from a point
known as Waterside, just beyond Car
riboo island, nine miles from Pictou,
Nova Scotia, to Wood island near Char
lottetown, Prince Edward island. The
distance is about 35 miles.


The Nova Scotia telephone exchanges
have connections with those in New
Brunswick, Portland and Boston, and
thus communication by telephone from
points in the United States to Prince
Edward island can soon be had. There
is only one other cable connecting
Prince Edward island with the main
land, which is owned and operated by
the Anglo-American telegraph company


The Prince Edward Island telephone
company has now established tele-
phonic, connections with every part of
this province The telephone is found
in many farm houses. The rates now
charged for telephone service on Prince
Edward island to farm houses are SIS a
year. Long distance rates. if to point
more than 30 miles from the exchange,
are % cents for minutes conversa-
ton; if less than 20 miles, / 5 cents

blocking the traffic and amusing a

after several efforts quelled the aquatic
vagrant.

order all the passengers inside and eX-
ceed the speed limit in a dash through

burst with all of the bravado Of an
"over Niagara artist"

posite the flower garden of the Pacific
Mutual company. The falling water
flooded the flower beds and when a
slight breeze blowed. drenched the
west side of the Pacific Mutual build
ing. The sun shining upon the water
produced remarkably Deautitui rain
bow effect

from the main because of the danger
of explosion of boilers in the neighbor-
hood which draw their water from the
big pipe. Last night after business
hours all companies who might be
drawing upon the pipe for water sup
ply We're notified, the water was shut
off and workmen repaired the injury.


1t took some delicate 'plumbical'
surgery to stop the storm yesterday
afternoon. Four of five water COM
pany physicians were all but drowned
in the operation. Time after time
when they thought they had the leak
plugged ii would break out anew and
the force of the stream almost caused
them to aviate. One man had his hat
carried fifty feet into the air and into
the garden across the street.

The Motuans of New Guinea have q
curious story about the origin OF yams.
They think that yams first grew from
bones. This was how IT happened. A
Motuan girl who had five brothers mar
ried a cannibal who lived some dis
tance away. says the London Globe.
The brothers came by turhs TO visit her
and four Of them were eaten by the
cannibal husband. The wife, however,
kept their bones, and when the fifth
brother came, instead of being eaten
like the others, he succeeded in killing
the cannibal husband and returned to
his home with the bones of his brothers.
The bones were duly mourned over and
buried. When the relatives visited the
place where the bones were buried some
time later they found strange plant
growing upon the grave, and on dig
ging up the bones they found they had
turned into yans OF different colors
and sizes.

uel Bonilla is promoting in Spanish

lief of passengers arriving here today

turned to Estrada's army week ago,

their efforts toward tearing through

olating the lottery ordinance and was

Two nights ago a band of brigands at
tackled the railway station Of Rosetti on
this line. Choosing the hour OF midnight,
they approached the station, which is
! desolately situated. and commenced their
attack on the dwelling Of the telegraph
clerk. which stands some 200 yards from
the station itself.


This official possesses a savage watch
dog, but the brigands silenced IL by
throwing to II dead fowls stolen from the
adjacent shed. Then they proceeded to
force an entrance by a back window,
thinking they had an easy task, the only
inhabitants being the clerk and his wife.


They reckoned, however, without their
host, for hardly had they begun TO force
the window when a door was thrown
open and a shot from q Martini rife
stretched one bandit dead This threw
the others into disorder.


They rushed from the yard, the clerk
Following, but seeing he did not fire again
(haying recklessly advanced without load
ing), they turned on him with the knives
and axes with which they were armed,
and for moment his death seemed GER
tain, when his courageous young wife ran
forward and fired with a shotgun with
which she had armed herself. and another
brigand fell wounded. Picking up their
companion. they, fairly cowed, now took
TO their heels. The clerk and his wife,
loading, followed them, but unfortunately
both fen IN the dark. the band making
their escape.


The gendarnerie have already arrested
some members of the band, known crimi-
mails, lately come into the district. They
have confessed their completely, and say
that being burdened with the wounded
man and afraid If they left him OF his
denouncing them, they threw him. still
living, into a deep well, where his body
has been since discovered.

SAN RAFAEL, Aug. 9.-Two wreck
ing crews carried to the scene of the
Ignacio collision late Monday night
and early yesterday morning worked
with block and tackle and AK and crow
bar clearing away the tangled mass
of iron and broken wood until sunrise.
The heap of wreckage was piled high
along the sides of the track, and the
torn, sprung tracks were Strengthened
and made firm for the resumption of
traffic


So quickly was the work performed
that the regular schedule was main
tanned yesterday morning. Passengers
passing along the route yesterday saw
engines, battered and twisted, on either
side of the line. Remnants of the splin-
tered baggage car and fat workcars of
the freight were dumped to the side
also, but the damaged coaches and the
smoker of the passenger were towed
q mile away from the scene.


The smoker still has a section of the
baggage car driven into it's fore end.
This was the attraction of crowds of
persons from the nearby towns who
journeyed to view the car of death.
The shattered sides and the broken
woodwork are red with the stain of
blood. The marks of the axes and bars
with which the rescuers worked fran
tically to free the imprisoned victims
were examined by the curious


At the scene of the collision the
greatest difficulty that confronted the
wreckers was to move the engines
that-driven into each other at awful
speed-were wedged tightly together.
This was done with block and tackle
Strong posts were driven into the sides
of hills and ropes attached to the en-
gines. One was drawn to either side
and the taut ropes wrenched them
apart at the same time, the engines
falling with heavy crash on the side
of the track.


Both engines were smashed and
broken beyond the hope of repair. The
trucks Were wrenched from one, while
wheels and aXles were twisted and
ch1pped. The tender of the passenger
engine parted from the cab and for
ward section and was driven back into
the forward section of the baggage
car. Had not the engine crews jumped
from the flying locomotives they would
have been killed

The 304 miles from Cincinnati, O.,
to Vandalia, ILL.,, over roads deep in
sticky mud proved the hardest test the
big touring car on the Franklin trek
has met in its 3500-mile journey. This
run was made Saturday and Sunday.


1t had been raining steadily and at
last reports still is, in this portion of
the territory covered by the Trek


route, and the four men from Syra-
cuse comprising the crew were strong
ly advised against trying to continue
the Journey until road conditions I'M
proved. But they decided to keep
going, and Saturday, the sixth day of
the "Trek," they made Terre Haute,
Ind, 204 miles. The next day they
reached Vandalia, 100 miles from
Terre Haute. Monday morning the
start for st. Louis was made.


Sunday proved the most trying day
of the entire trip. In the hundred
miles covered not another automobile
was seen by the party, and in many
places even wagons were abandoned,
men and women resorting to the old
time horseback method of travel when
travel was necessary. AT times the car
sank half way to the hubs in the
ooze, and low gear was used for all
but five miles of the distance covered.


In spite of this severe test the air
cooled engine did not oVerheat ana
delivered it's power SO reliably that the
car was pulled from every mud hole
and slough into which it sank. The
light weight of the car and its large
wheels and tires were a material aid
in successfully making days run
that automobile experts in Terre Haute
declared impossible for any motor
car.

Two three-masted Schooners-the Silver
and the Renold-both heavily laden with
lumber narrowly escaped being wrecked
in Hell Gate late yesterday afternoon,
when, In tow of the tug Atlas, of the New
town Creek Towing Company. they at
tempted TO force a passage into the East
River against a flood tide which was racing
toward the Sound at a rate of between four
and five miles an hour


its first burst of speed spent, the tug
progress grew slower and slower until IT
finally became stationary between the cur
rents. In the next instant. schooners and
tug, helpless. were being carried broadside
back toward the Sound.


In the sudden reversal of things the tug
got mixed up with The two schooners in a
hopeless tangle. The captains OF the
schooners dropped their anchors just as the
current swung them toward the jagged reef
of Scaly Rock Still entangled with its tow
the tug was swung first against one
schooner and then against the other, but
the anchors held until help came.


Two tugs and the police boat Patrol
Strengthened out the tangle and the Silver
was left anchored at Scaly Rock and the
Renold off the iifesaving station on the
Astoria shore Two hours later the current
turned ard the journey through the treach-
erous passage was accomplished in safety.

grow fat and unpicturesque under fed
sral auspices. When the jack rabbit and

Divide Until that far day arrives, how

rabbit remains the most skillful four

bay at the moon by night and keep just
out of rifle range by day. The coyote
knows more about traps than Canadian
.'voyageur," is an expert on strychnine
and never falls for the dead-fall. He is
rather fond of lambs and calves, but
rabbits are the oatmeal of this phan-
tom highlander, and as Diamondfield
Jack Davis would say. where two or
three of these are gathered together
there you will find the coyote, seeking
to stow one of them into his midst:'

and this morning 1t went over the sea
wall about the Potomac Park, and flooded
all the low lands on the Virginia side OF
the river. In OccoQuan creek the freshet
came down with q rush Sunday, and YES
sells that were lying in the creek were
torn from their moorings and taken down
the stream in spit Of all efforts to hold
them.


The barges Totuskey and Patuxent.
which were lying at Occoquan loading
ties for Philadelphia. were taken
by the current and carried about three
miles down stream from their moorfng
places before the men aboard them could
get the anchors to hold. Reports state
that the vessels were not damaged, nor
has any damage been done by the high
water. The tug Capt. Toby was yester-
day sent to the assistance OF the two
barges, but, In consequence of the down
rush Of water, she was unable to reach
the boats.

red. The Maryland bird was two ounces

many crews of fire fighters that have
been sent out from the Missoula head
quarters of the forest service, near
western Montana. The smoke of a
number of fires within plain sight of
the city made the day cloudy and the
heavens glowed tonight. From the
Flathead forest, many miles to the
north, a heavy pail of smoke is sweep
ing over the foothills toward Missoula.
From. the Blackfoot canyon, east of the
city, comes word of more new fires,
and from the Bitter Root forest, south
and west, four new fires are reported
today, all bad and one serious.


The worst is near Stevensville, where
a steady fight has met with but little
success. Three more fires were re-
ported in the Bitter Root valley today,
all south of Hamilton. The fire nearest
to Missoula is gradually eating its way
to the Lolo national forest. .

From the Electric News Service.


There is no longer any reason why even
the farmer Of moderate means should not
enjoy all the home comforts Of his city
cousin. The day when bath tubs, light
Ing plants, water systems for fire pro-
lection and heating furnaces were to be
found only in the larger villages and in
the cities has gone forever. Today there
are few rural villages too small to boast
Of all these things. and the farmer has
caught the spirit Of the times. and his
up-to-date farmhouse is lighted with cleo
tricity and heated by steam. 1t is sup
piled with fine bath rooms and running
water and other modern conveniences.


A few years ago the electric light and
power plants installed on farms were very
few and far between. A few adventurous
farmers had dared to harness their noun
tain pasture streams and turn their water
energy into electricity for use about the
house and barns; a few more had insta led
gasolene engines for the same purpose
These early installations proved a sue
cess from the first, and 1t was not long
before their worth had been talked and
written about until almost every well-to-
do farmer was considering the question OF
q similar installation.


Aside from the many benefits and econ
omies of electricity for lighting, heating
and cooking in the farmhouse, it readily
assumes most Of the hard work about
the farm which in the past has been a
most discouraging factor in securing farm
labor Electricity easily does the milking,
separating and churning, as we'll as turn
ing the washing machine and the wringer
In the barn it is applied to feed cutters.
corn shelters, feed grinders and to all
other small machinery, such as the grind
stone, lathe and small buzz saw for
cutting fire wood. The threshing machine
and tanning mill are very easily belted
onto the portable motor. In Germany ana
a few other foreign countries electricity
Is also used to advantage to pull the
plows, harrows. rakes, cultivators, bind
ers, mowers and other outdoor machinery.

Nothing could be more appropriate than
that Col. Roosevelt should take advantage
OF his Italian trip at this juncture to view
Mount Etna in eruption He has been
called the greatest human volcano in mod
ern times. Both friends and enemies have
Hkened him to the great natural vents in
the earth's surface, channels Of vast
power, stupendous forms of natural ex-
preston. Those living in the vicinity of
Mount Roosevelt have always experienced
the same uncertainty and in some cases
the same apprehension the jewellers of
the slopes OF Nesuvius and Etna and
other chimneys of the world Repeated
lava flows cannot drive them from their
chosen places: fierce outpourings of
scoriae and hot ashes and gas have with
cred them. but still they cling to their
precarious positions, perhaps from sheer
love of danger.


But, metaphor aside, a mountain like
Etna would naturally appeal strongly to
q man like Roosevelt 1t stands for the
same unquenchable fire that burns within
him, for the same underlying impulse that
drives him forward. the same unexpected
ness that has always kept his world
guessing. One can imagine the colonel
standing at some convenient though not
especially safe vantage point, watching
the awe-inspiring vision Of the volcano at
work and restraining himself with diff
Guilty from going even closer The specta-
Gle of Col. Roosevelt contemplating the
sphinx does not nearly so well express the
worlds concept OF the man the prom
ised picture of the hero OF San Juan Hill
standing on Mount Etna and observing
nature in her most convulsive mood.

mand. Both men were ''tenderfeet"
and too weak after their 80-mile desert
ride to make a fight.

morning.

Announcement was made yesterday
of the conclusion of a deal which will
give the Western Pacific railroad entry
into Eureka, Los Angeles. Olympia.
Santa Barbara, Seattle and Tacoma and
will permit the Gould line to book
passengers to and from these places
via San Francisco at the same fares
that now prevail over the Southern
Pacific, Santa Fe and northern lines.


The Southern Pacific, which controls
the land transportation situation north
and south from here, has refused to
interchange passenger business with
the Western Pacific. Under these cir
cumstances the Western Pacific could
not sell ticket to Seattle or Los An
geles or to any of the coast points
above mentioned. and travellers in those
places could not book over the new
line without first and at their own ex-
pense making the trip to San Fran
cisco. This has now been changed.


The Western Pacific has consum
mated arrangements, effective at once,
for an interchange of passenger busi-
ness with the Pacific Coast steamship
company, whose lines running out of
this port will bridge all the gaps that
until now have restricted the Gould
line to San Francisco as the only point
it touched on the Pacific coast


The new arrangement settles for the
Western Pacific what looked like a
serious problem and gives to the resi-
dents of the towns affected the choice
of another route to the east.

A short walk along this path which

brought the visitors facing the gar

The charming hostess, herself ac-

realms behind the scenes, had able as

door, played their parts with quite as

''votes for women" woman must find

In poor exhibition of soccer, the
Vampires yesterday afternoon defeat
ed the Burns by score of to at
the Preside grounds and won the per-
petual challenge cup of the California
soccer football association. The i'm
portance of the occasion proved too
much for the players and team work
was at a discount throughout the game.
Although defeated, the Burns proved in
no wise inferior to their opponents,
and if the game was replayed the
Scotch laddies would probably prove
the winners. The Vampires had all the
football luck and this, combined with
the excellent work of McFarlane in
goal, brought home the bacon for the
men from Alameda.


The Burns won the toss and elected
to play with the wind behind them in
the first half. McFarlane was tested
early, Doig and Welsh sending in well
directed shots which caused the Ala
media goal keeper considerable worry.
The Vamps never had a lookin during
the initial period, the Burns being in
close attendance to McFarlane during
the entire half. Shots from all angles
were rained upon the custodian, but he
managed to get the ball away, although
he was forced to concede many corners.
The Burns secured 13 corner kicks in
the initial period, but were unable to
score.


Referee James Duncan got his
lamps crossed and called the first half
seven and a half minutes too soon. The
linesmen called his attention to the
mistake and the time was made up
after the intermission The Vamps
started strong when they had the wind
at their backs and for time the Burns
defense had merry time There was
nothing doing, however, until 20 min
utes from the finish, when Swaine
reached the net with a fast shot.
Swaine had been playing a classy game
and his success was we'll deserved. The
Burns went into the game with re-
newed energy after this reverse, but
were unable to equalize. Munroe was
of little assistance to his side in the
last period, the clever forward having
been injured shortly after the resump-
tion of hostilities. Doig, Melville and
Welsh were best for the losers, while
McFarlane, Middleton, Hunter and
Swaine performed deeds of valor for
the winners. LeCoutier, who took
Jacksons place in the Vampire team,
played good game but was lacking in
backing up his forwards. Jackson was
injured in the practice.

feated the United Caledonians, to l.,
in a game played under the auspices
of the Bay Counties soccer league at
Freeman's park, Oakland.

OKOLONA, Ark, Feb. &c. A. Con-
lin, who escaped from prison at Hot
Springs Wednesday night, was cap
tured here today, but not until he was
seriously, perhaps, fatally, wounded.


For twenty-four hours a posse had
searched all passing trains. Late today
Deputy Sheriff Jesse Hayes and a
posse tagged a freight train, and as
they entered the caboose Conlin, aban-
doning his personal effects, ran from
the opposite door and made dash for
the woods.


Members of the posse opened fire and
a bullet entered Conlin's back and
passed through his body. He will be
removed to Hot Springs tomorrow if
his condition permits.

BY Monday things were improved enough

when the captain was able to get an OBJ

obstacles in the development OF this
years team will be the unfamiliarity

VICTORIA, B. c., Aug. 5.-Brief
messages received from Juneau, Skag-
way and Cordova says there was no
panic when the Princess May struck
the reef north of Sentinel island this
morning, but the women and children
suffered much from cold in the small
boats, the majority having left the
sinking ship scantily clad.


Captain Mcleod and his officers took
the situation coolly and managed to
get all the passengers and the crew
away from the sinking steamer before
she foundered. The boats hugged the
shore until daylight, when landings
were made.


In the meantime steamers were sent
from Juneau, where the distress signals
were received from several sources.
The steamship Victoria picked up the
call at sea, and it was also heard by
the United States naval station at Cor
dova. The ships boats bearing the
survivors will reach Juneau late to-
night.


All the mail, including gold from the
Yukon sent as registered mail, was
landed on Sentinel island.


CAPTAINS REPORT


A message received tonight from
Captain Mcleod says the liner ran
ashore at o'clock this morning on a
reef at the north end of Sentinel island.
The vessel began to sink Immediately,
and wireless messages were sent by
Operator Keller asking for assistance,
until water flooding into the engine
room rendered the apparatus useless.
The passengers and crew were all
saved and landed on Sentinel island.
When the landing was completed Pilot
John Richardson was sent with a
boats crew to Juneau, where he ar
rived tonight.


The steamer probably will be saved.
Wrecking apparatus will be sent north
at once to begin salvage operations,
The foreh Id and engine room are filled
with water, but the vessel is not sub
merged.


A cablegram from the Skagway
agent Of the Canadian Pacific says the
company's steamer Princess Ena,
which was on the way up Lynn canal,
was advised of the wreck of the Prin-
cess May and was ordered to the scene.

with machine guns from the United
States gunboat Paducah, today threw
up line Of defense about the Ameri-

duty until the impending crisis in the
Nicaraguan war is passed. The con-

Blueields. The Madriz and Estrada

three miles Of the city. Outpost fight

deciding conflict will undoubtedly
soon be in progress.

slow In taking up their last lines Of
defense yesterday, were attacked by a
Madriz division. The skirmish lasted
more than an hour before the Estrada
forces could retreat successfully and
the losses will probably reach 100
men about SO dead on each side.

refuge near the American consulate
and the bluejackets have been sta
toned about the public square. Ameri-
cans fear the marines will not be able
to awe the Madriz forces into remain
ing out of the city. The Madriz fac
ton claims that Americans really
started the revolution and say they
will sack the city. In this event the
marines would be forced to fight a
force greatly outnumbering them.


The Madriz gunboat Venus, which
was driven from the Bluefelds harboT
yesterday by the Paducah, landed 300
soldiers below the city last night,
strengthening the Madriz army.

The work of discharging the cargo
of the quarantined liner Nippon Maru
into lighters was begun yesterday. To-
morrow the empty ship will be taken
once more alongside the fumigating
hulk Omaha and filled with fumes that
will insure the death of every rat that
survived the first fumigation. The ship
will then be towed to the Pacific Mail
wharf, where the work of loading the
return cargo will begin.


Passengers and crew have been land
ed at the quarantine station and will
remain there until Friday. While the
ship was being fumigated the personal
effects and clothing, from overcoats to
shoes, of everybody that crossed the
Pacific on the liner We're cooked to
turn in the big sterilizer. While their
clothing was undergoing this treat
ment its owners were given antiseptic
baths, after which they wandered about
in sterilized kimonos until their own
clothes were returned.


The quarantine station is beautifully
located and the passengers are making
the best of the situation. Harold Mac
Grath, the writer, is busy gathering
material for new novel, in which Doc
tor TrOtter of the quarantine station
will be the villain and Captain Smith
the heroine.

BALTIMORE, January 27.-The Bal
timore and Ohio Railroad Company s
"Oyster Special for the west ran into
the engine Of work train at Relay last
night about TAO o'clock, because of a
misunderstanding of signals. The two
engines were greatly damaged and turned
turtle, and the engineers and fremen
of both were injured. Traffic was de-
layed. but the tracks were cleared by 2
o'clock this morning.


The injured are Leonard G. Rout. engi-
neer of the work train, leg sprained and
decorations about the body; T. ]. Welsh,
fireman of work train, scalded about the
body; John Fl. Deminnis, engineer of the
oyster special, rib broken; j. NJ. Strick-
lev, fireman of the oyster special, lacera-
lions.


1t was stated last night that the work
train had a clearing signal from st.
Dennis and was under control of the
dispatchers Investigation also showed
that a red light had been set for the
oyster train to stop, but because of his
injuries Deminnis was not permitted to
make any statement.


/ The work train was crossing from the
passenger to the freight tracks when
the accident occurred.


The work train engine keeled over on
its side, and the tender, which had been
thrown UP by the impact, came down on
top Beneath the wreck Rout and Welsh
were temporarily Gagged, and the steam
escaping from broken valves poured over
Welsh's body, causing him excruciating
pain Both say they feared they had
been caught in a deathtrap until they
found a small aperture beneath the en-
CINE. where it had gouged a hole in the
ground by its weight. and they emerged
on their hands and knees. Welsh later
became unconscious from pain.


Strickley. the fireman of the oyster
special, escaped almost unhurt, and his
good fortune, with that of his engineer
Deminnis-was considered remarkable.

FTER leaving the beavers lodge


~ Hiawatha went down to the big
1 y oak tree to see Mrs. Bushytail,
the gray squirrel. The little Indian boy
knew all of the secrets OF the wood
folk. so It was not necessary for him
tn ask the little squirrel mother what
she was doing. 1t was busy time for
her. as she was working to fill her store
house with nuts and acorns. She knew
that the cold winter would soon come,
with its ice and snow. In that kind OF
weather squirrels are more comfort
able in their snug nests than frisklng
through the woods trying to gather
food. Hiawatha knew something about
the coy nests Of the squirrel family,
because he had often seen their little
summer homes made at the ends OF the
hong tree branches. just where they
forked into smaller limbs. He knew,
too. that where the large branches
forked from the trunks there were
often holes in the trees. 1t was In these
holes that the frisky squirrels built
their wintry homes. They lined them
with dry leaves and twigs, woven SO
neatly than even the heavy storms
could not destroy them.


Mrs. Gray Squirrel was not the least
bit afraid of Hiawatha. for she often
scampered upon his back and shoulders,
but she never talked. That is. she never
could make the Indian understand just
what she said. Hiawatha often wondered
why the gray squirrels were not more
friendly with the ground squirrels that
wore such pretty striped coats. The
Indian liked the way the ground squirrels
or chipmunks built their storerooms I'M
der ground. You know that they always
make two doors to their storeh0uses, be-
cause they are afraid that pna may be
closed during the winter. They are
rather particular house builders, for they
have several underground halls leading
off, from the main tunnel. At the end of
each passageway there is a room for
some special kind of nut. One room may
be filed with acorns. another with chezt-
nuts and another with hickory nuts. In
all a chipmunk stores away about tenN
pounds of provisions for the wintry
weather.


Another cousin of Mrs. Gray Squirrel
is Mrs. Flying Squirrel. who can fly from
tree branch to tree branch because her
fore legs and hind legs are Joined by,
loose flesh. making sails. One Of the
secrets which Hiawatha might have
known was that the word squirrel means
shadow tail" 1t suits the little animals
exactly. because they may almost hide
in the shadows Of their own bushy tails.

excuses were offered for Withholding
the money, declares Mrs. HeyndrfKS.
1t was not until yesterday, two months
since the case was dismissed, that the
$4,000, without interest, was returned TO
her.

NOANK, Conn, Oct. 22.-When the
auxiliary fishing schooner Ada Bell
put in here last night the crew told
of how near they came to being hit by
the equilibrator of the Wellman air
ship.


Sunday morning, during heavy fog,
hey said, big, dark object appeared,
'hich they took at first to be more
mick fog. But as the object approached
they saw something heavy humping
along the water, and they started
their motor just In time to get their
boat out of the way, the airship pass
ing not more than thirty feet from
them.


The captain could easily make out the
crew of the airship, but neither crew
made any effort to speak, and the ball
oon passed by and was soon lost in
the fog.


The crew of the Ada Bell did not
know that Wellman had started across
the ocean until they put into port last
night.

London, May 2e.-The Russian steamer
Lituania, which sailed from Copenhagen
on May "a for New York, had a narrow
escape from being wrecked on Friday
evening. The Lituania had twelve hun
dred emigrants aboard and was proceed
ing very slowly, owing to the fog, when
she struck the rocks off Old Head Point,
Pentland Firth, between Scotland and
the Orkney Islands. The steamer held
fast. and many of the emigrants, greatly
alarmed, fell on their knees and prayed.


Fortunately the fog lifted, and after
wireless communication was established
with the warship Bellona, at Invergor-
don, and with Copenhagen. the engines
were reversed and the liner floated off.


The bulkheads kept the water from the
main hold, and the Lituania reached
Tynemouth. where repairs will be made.

WASHINGTON, July 12.-Weather
generally favorable for harvesting and
vegetable growth prevailed last week
in the great corn and winter wheat
growing states, according to the week
ly bulletin issued today by the weather
bureau.


The bulletin says in part I'm the
northern portion of the corn belt there
is still a general lack of rainfall and
vegetation is suffering.


I'm the spring wheat belt there were
light showers over most districts and
the change to somewhat cooler and
partly cloudy weather gave some re-
lief from the adverse conditions that
have prevailed for so long in those
states. Light showers during the week
afforded temporary relief only. how
ever, and heavy, soaking rains are still
badly needed.


Dry weather continues over the
western portion of the great plains re-
gion, and as result the great ranges
are dry and vegetation scant.


From the Rocky mountains west
ward the weather has continued very
dry and much injury has resulted to
dry farming interests. In the irrigated
districts the water supply has held out
better than expected, but the streams
are now falling rapidly and rain is
needed to augment the flow."

ceased long ago. The children are en-

plots; the Rosedale garden, with 90
plots and the Speedway garden, with 81
plots. These gardens were open forty-one
days during June and July and the total
attendance was 1910, the average daily
attendance being 100. The number on the
rolls at the end of the month was 100.


The work was begun In the spring, the
children coming once a week during
school time. Each boy may have his
own plot, usually not more than eighty or
ninety square feet The crops consist
for the most part of radishes. lettuce,
parsely. beets, carrots, tomatoes, turnips
and onions.


The gardens are open three mornings a
week from $50 until 1890 O'Clock. Not
only are the children taught practical
gardening and to respect the property of
others, but they are allowed to have
all their own crops to take home, and
some of them provide their families with
many vegetables during the summer.

Despondent because she failed to re-
ceive Christmas gifts from her rela-
tives in Germany, Anna Brier. 81 years
old, attempted to end her life early
yesterday morning by inhaling illu-
minating gas in her room at the home
of Rev. c. A. Nolte, 1923 Cherry street,
where she was employed as house
maid.


The young woman had been melan-
choly for the last several days. She
stated she was expecting letters and
presents from her relatives, and when
she failed to receive them Monday
night she became discouraged and
cried bitterly.


A short time before o'clock yester-
day morning Martin Nolte was pass
ing in the hall, when he detected the
odor of gas. He made an investiga-
ton and traced the odor to the room
occupied by Miss Brier. He forced an
entrance into the room, found the
young woman lying on the bed and
the gas jets wide open.


The unconscious woman was taken
to the receiving hospital. where she
regained consciousness after being
given stimulants, The police surgeons
say she will recover.

made the run to Big Bear valley, over
the Santa Ana Canyon road and re-
turn on the crest road through Little
Bear valley and Pinecrest in eight
hours and seventeen minutes. The
Santa Ana canyon road is the steepest
and most rugged in the mountains.
Not since the washouts of January,
which badly damaged long stretches OF
the road. has an automobile reached
Big Bear valley over it.

George Wood of Riverside and Opie
L. Warner of San Bernardino.


In addition to accomplishing the feat
which teamsters and others familiar
with the route said was impossible, the
party had the experience of being
chased by a mad bull, which rushed at
the automobile with lowered head and
threatened damage to the tires. Hey
ser, who drove the car, fled from the
animal with all the speed possible over
the rocky road. Three burros, which,
like the bull, had never seen an auto-
mobile, followed the machine for sew
eraI miles

Produces Interesting Theory.


Paris April 1.-THE study OF the pre-
historic skeleton discovered last fall in
the French department Of Dordogne has
produced an interesting theory concern
ing the primitive races of Europe and
their origin. II may be recalled that this
tho first absolutely perfect skeleton OF
q man from the older stone age was
named Homo aurignacensis hauseri, after
Prof. Hauser, who first located il in its
blocked up cave.


Prof. Klaatsch Of Breslau found that
1t represented an entirely different race
from the famous Neanderthal men and
all other known primitive men. The
Aurignac race was slight and graceful,
had very straight bones and proportions
which Indicate that dexterlty had al
ready to some extent replaced brute
force. He now announces that the find
proves that in the glacial epoch Europe
had two absolutely distinct races Of men
which after a fight for mastery at a
central European point blended together.


The modern population of southern
Europe, Prof Klaatsch says, IS descended
from this mixture. On the other hand.
the Germanic people sprang directly
from the Aurignac race. The Neander-
thai men came first from Africa with an
African fauna. The negroid races, the
gorilla and chimpanzee. are remote rela-
uves Of this race.


The Aurignac race probably came from
Asia, and the orang-outang is their near
est monkey relative. Further back both
races originated in the vanished CONT
nent OF Lemuria, which lay between
Africa, Asia and Australia They ar
rived in Europe by different paths.

Little Luke Hays could write his
name. He brought his slate to show
his mother what round. clear letters
he could make.


Would you like to make your name
grow, Luke?' said his mother.


"I never saw name grow" said
Luke.


Then his mother took him out into
the garden. She gave him stick with
a sharp point and made him write his
name in large letters in the middle of
a bed of black earth; then his mother
sowed mignonette seed along the let
ters.


Now" said she, din a few weeks you
will see your name growing tall and
sweet"


Luke went away the next day to visit
his grandmother, and when he came
home again, three weeks later he ran
at once to the garden. There was his
name, Luke Hays" in pretty green
letters, just as he had written it. Luke
was delighted and has never failed to
grow his name every year since.-Se3
lected.

CHICAGO. Dec. 25.-Not all laments
for the old-fashoned New Years
have ceased, but the new sort-the New

when the epidemic of college inns

100000" histrionic star with

But he was wrong; the country is
speckled now with college inns ga
lore and of all sorts, from Seattle 10

record.


The spread of the college inn, not
only to college towns and cities north'
south, east and west, has in fact been
startling phenomenon. New YORK,
though il lifts its eyebrows disdaln-
fully when anyone mentions the possi-
bility of anything new originating IN

SPREAD OF COLLEGE INNS


From New York to Lafayette is a
big jump i'll point of population, but
the HooSier college town has a better
imitation of the original than the east
ern city and its college atmosphere
is much truer to the standard than
the Gotham cafe. Milwaukee has re-
produced in detail the Chicago original
and the Cream City's copy is the near
est approach to the original college
inn" of any of the many imitators,
some of which are poor counterteltS.
They will be poorer counterfeits by
comparison when the Chicago proto-
type moves into its handsome quarters
in the new $3,000,000 Hotel Sherman
during Christmas week. If New York
and Milwaukee and Lafayette and the
other cities which have college inns
want to keep up with Chicago they will
have to 60 some.


The college inn" idea, like other sue
cesses, came suddenly. Joseph Beifeld,
having secured control of the old SJ1er-
man house, was impressed with the
need for a grill room that would be
something more than q mere place to
eat. He thought if he could make the
place more attractive without being
cold and formal he would be bene-
factor both to that part of the public
which must eat in hotels and to him.
self.


In talking il over with his son. DR..
William Beifeld, the latter suddenly
advanced the idea of calling the grill
room the college inn and redecorating
it to carry out as we'll as possible the
name. This was done, college flags and
colors were used in the redecorating
scheme, few stalls were put in at one
end Of the grill room, partitions and
other things that made for formality
were eliminated and the college inn
was success from the start. The
reason ascribed for the widespread sue
cess of the idea is that it revolution
ized the old way of looking upon cafes
as mere eating places and introduced
a more cozy, neighborly, cordial atmos-
phere without sacrificing any individual
rights or tastes. People liked the col
ors and the spirit of the college inn.
The New Years eve receipts for the
last three years of the College inn
were: 1906, $10,000 1907, $4,000; 1905,
$4,000.


EUROPE LENDS SUGGESTIONS


So successful in fact was it that
when it was decided to tear down the
hotel and erect a modern fifteen-story
hostelrS the College Inn was not closed
but carefully moved to temporary
quarters in Clark street. 1t has been
doing business in the smaller quarters
while the handsome new structure was
being erected at Clark and Randolph.
on the site which has been occupied
by five hotels for seventy-five years.
The new College Inn was opened dur
ing Christmas week-and for New
Years eve, and has been made the
largest and probably the most beauti-
full grill room in the United States, a
creditable original of the college inn
idea, upon which millions of dollars
have been lavshed. With the kitchen
and bar it occupies the entire base
ment of the big hotel building-a quar-
ter of a block. The old and the new
worlds were searched for suggestions
that would aid in carrying out a
scheme for decoration and comfort.
The decorations are of the Elizabethan
period, with silver~d oak paneling to
the ceiling, which is of ivory. the Sc
Vereness of the white relieved by bright
colored small frescoes.


About the walls are enameled wood
shields representing all the prominent
English and American colleges, the
decorations which have been copied so
widely. Along the south wall there is
a row Of booths like those of the old
English coffee houses which were fire.
quented and made famous by Thack-
cray, Ben Jonson, Sheridan, Dickens
and other literary and theatrical celeb
rites


There are two entrances--one off the
main entrance to the hotel on Clark
street and the other from the lobby
The main entrance is of beautifully
carved oak and gothic windows with
heraldic designs in loaded glass. Open
ing off the grill room are seven private
ming rooms, with accommodations for
from six to twenty-four persons. Each
of these rooms has its Individual dec
oratve scheme. every detail CARRYING.
out some special period In fact, there
is vastly more study and work put into
the decorative scheme of the new Col
lege Inn than visitors realize, but the
general erect is one of warmth and
friendliness, and that was the idea that
set the college inns to blossoming so

Barely to escape from death in the
great refrigerators of the United
States army transport Logan was the
thrilling experience of Lieutenant
Colonel Albert d. Kniskern of 2S21
Elmwood avenue, Berkeley, purchasing
commissary of the transport service,
just before the troopship last sailed
for the Philippines


Locked in the icy cold storage com
partment with companion Colonel
Kniskern was in imminent peril of
having to remain in the frozen tenn
perature in the bottom of the ship
until the vessel reached Manila a
month later. Death was the only ap-
parent promise of relief from the tor
ture which the two men faced.


The army officials have kept the facts
quiet, and the secret came out only
yesterday.


Colonel Kniskern, as purchasing COM
missary of the transports service, has
charge of all.army purchases shipped
out of San Francisco.


The Logan was to have sailed March
., but. owing to delays in the arrival
or troops from the east the sailing
was postponed until March T. That
day the last of the refrigerated goods
were stored in the vessel and Colonel
Kniskern and an aid went into the
cold storage hold to make final in
spection before the compartment was
locked for the voyage. When the off,
Ger entered the room was lighted by
electric lights.


Without warning the lights went out
and the officer and his aid found them
selves in the depth of the ship, with no
means of making quick escape from
their icy prison.


Carefully they grouped their way to
the wall of the compartment and
worked around to the door


To their horror they found the great
double self-locking doors of the ice
house shut.


Through the steel keel of the ship
they could hear the great propellers of
the vessel churning in the bay, and
they believed that the troopship had
Stdi lCo OH It's way 10 the OTiGHl.


Made desperate by the terror of the
situation, they threw all their energy
into beating at the prison door which
barred them from the world. Hour
after hour passed. The propellers
turned and rested and the vessel rocked
in the tide. The soldiers did not know
but that the lines had been cast off and
the voyage had begun.


One, two, three, four, five hours
passed in the terrible vault. The arctic
temperature froze and stiffened the
men. but they fought off the chill and
battled and battered on the great door


For six hours they made their reso-
lutte fight.


Then down the companionway of the
vessel passed sergeant making his
on the ship. The men in the
prison could not hear his footsteps, but
the sergeant heard the faint rappings of
the incarcerated He could not locate
nor define the sound, but the regularity
of the taps moved him to make a report
to the officer of the ship. 1t was imme-
diately ordered that the refrigerator be
opened.


AS the great doors swung out Colonel
and his companion tottered
in to the light and fell exhausted, numb.
across the threshold


Mrs. Kniskern, when seen at her home
in Berkeley yesterday stated that Col
onel Kniskern had now recovered from
the effects of his dangerous experience
and that it was believed that his health
was in no way affected by the ordeal
he had undergone.

entering. There were about sixty men on

stricken. they rushed back into the boat

ing crash, the Camden struck her sister
craft.

wenonah's women's cabin. There fol-

Added to the confusion.

RENO, Nov. 17.-wrecked In his
most successful flight before the Reno
public, Fred Wiseman of Santa Rosa
narrowly escaped injury at the race
track today when his bipIane was prac-
tically demolished. Rising 40 feet from
the ground the birdman was caught in
an air eddy from the grandstanG,
which he overtopped. This overset his
machine, sending 1t crashing to earth.
Wiseman was thrown out, but stls-
tanned no injuries. When up about 40
feet the biplane commenced to drop,
diving straight toward the earth, when
Wiseman managed to regain control
and altered its course slightly, bring
ing it back to an even keel It plunged
to earth, the motor spinning furiously,
and struck squarely in an frrigating
ditch, thus preventing the wheels from
revolving and allowing a safe alight-
ing.


There was a crash when the wheels
crumpled underneath and jammed
through the bottom plane and one of
the wings bent and snapped.


The birdman shut off his engine as
he struck, preventing the propeller
from tearing the car to pieces. The
sudden shock threw Wiseman from his
precarious perch straight into the
wires and stays. He was caught in
these and wavered to and fro for a
few seconds as the machine quivered
Then he extricated himself and jumped
away from the debris.


The aeroplane will probably be taken
apart and the broken planes and
mechanism packed away for shipment
to California. Wiseman Prentice and
the half dozen mechanicians that ac-
cop1panied the outfit left the race
track for Reno tonight

schools said Hello, Christmas" this
morning. To the tune of tinkling lit
tie Christmas carols and by the light of

scientific, high-minded affair.


Big Christmas Trees.


In every one of the many kindergartens
and first grade schools today there were
big Christmas trees. Yards upon yards
of Christmas greens were garlanded

The trees were gay with the red things

That was the keynote to the whole
Christmas tree celebration in the lower
grades. 1t was the Christmas of giving
and not of getting. The idea was worked
out all through the school system, espeei-
ally where the children have not yet be-
gun to lose faith in the identity of Santa
Claus.


For several weeks past the children
have been busily weaving paper mats,
making calendars of their sketches and
odd little water-colors, and making things
to ornament telephone call pads. In the
third grade some have even become so
pragmatic and unitarian that they have
made pink and red wooden flat-iron hold
ers, and tea pot holders, and the like of
that.


All these things hung on a forest of
widely separated Christmas trees today
The makers of the gifts sat, with ill con-
cealed impatiense. until the teacher gave

ed like baby sun to take the gift. hand

Plays by First-Grade Pupils.


LII SOluc VI tie grace TOOUlS ltleTe

Little CinderellaS sat by gloomy ashes
today and waited for their handsome
young prices. Fairy godmothers played
their parts without a hating line In all
the plays there was nothing but simplic-
ity and nothing but the pure strain of the
simple little stories for children that SIM
ply can't be crowded out, no matter how

The main celebrations today were in the

The Hague, July 1.-George Turner, OF
counsel for the United States, closed his
argument to-day before the arbitration
tribunal which is 10 decide the Newfound-
land fisheries dispute between America and
Great Britain.


During the eight days on which Mr.. Tur-
ner spoke he developed the contention that
the United States had an equal voice with
Great Britain in legislation involving the
fisheries on the Newfoundland coast and in
the enforcement of the regulations arising
therefrOm. IN other words, Mr.. Turner
held that Great Britain in the treaty of
1918 gave the United States equality in the
sovereign rights now at issue. and sup
ported his argument with long extracts
from authorities on international law.


In his peroration Mr.. Turner said that,
although he had spoken freely. he had
desired throughout to show the greatest
respect to England. The United States and
England, he said. were common in blood,
history, legislation and language. Perhaps
the disputes between the two nations were
due partly to the close relationship. for
when the British lion reared across tine
waters American blood grew hot, and a
defiant roar was sent back, though peace
and silence quickly again held sway

LONG BEACH, Aug. 22.-Anna Rut-
ledge, aged 13 years, daughter of Mrs.
Norman Rutledge Of San Jose, allowed
baby buggy containing her 8-months-
old sister to get away from her last
night on the Pine avenue incline lead
ing to the beach. The buggy swerved
from side to side, finally turning into
the curb and spilling the baby out on
the walk, cutting its face The girl
slipped and fell in her attempt to catch
up with the runaway carriage, sprain-
ing her right hand.


She had been playfully releasing her
hold on the buggy and then catching
the handle again. The time came,
however, when she failed to regain her
grasp. The baby was asleep during
it's wild ride, but screamed in fright
upon it's rude awakening.

struck the eagle in the head, stunning
it, and before it could arise again the
bows pounded it to death with other
stones and sticks.

over seven feet from tip to tip of its
wings. Jarrett, the lad who performed
the David-like feat on this Goliath Of
the air, is years old, and to his well
directed shot his brother Mart owes
his safety.

STOCKTON, May 23.-Norton Ball, a
molder employed at the Stockton iron
works. battled for his life yesterday
with a vicious bulldog while swimming
in North street canal.


Ball and three or four companions
were enjoying themselves in the canal
when a German and his bulldog ap-
peared on the levee. Without any warn
ing the dog sprang into the water,
swan out to where Ball was SWIM
ming and made a lunge for his throat.
The young man protected himself with
his arm, the CANNES teeth sinking in
the arm


1t was with difficulty that Ball fought
off the dog and kept his head above
water Being good swimmer he made
his way to the bank by swimming
with one hand, the dog continuing his
attack as he SWAN alongside him.


When they reached land the bulldog
discontinued his attack and ran along
the levee. Balls arm was badly torn
and was bleeding quite freely. His COM
panions, who Were some distance be-
low him, came TO his assistance and he
managed to make his way across the
stream again to the other side, where
he had left his clothing. He dressed
and hurried to the emergency hospital,
where his injuries were attended. The
tendons were torn loose and the flesh
badly lacerated.


The boys later secured guns and re-
turned to the canal in the hopes of
finding the dog, their intention being
to shoot him. The German, however,
had disappeared with his canine.

police believe the deaths are due to acct
dent.

Robertson, his brother, forty-three years
old, and William Thompson. forty years

room at LAT 10th street. They had been
out last night with Thompson, whom they
brought home with them.


This morning Robert Anderson, who
lives at the same address, and works in
the Erie basin, wondered why the Rob
ertsons did not come down to breakfast

the door and saw the three men lying
unconscious on the bed.

stones throw from the bank

Liverpool June 21.-The first travelling
party of university men, made possible by
the benef1cence of a philanthropist whose
name has not been made public, left here
to-day for Canada and the United States.

bridge, Durham, Edinburgh, London and
other universities. Oxford is the only

cities of Canada as far west as Winnipeg,
near which place the men will devote four
days to actual farm work as a practical

and visit Madison, Wis: Chicago, Pitts
burg. Washington, Annapolis, Philadelphia.
New York, New Haven and Cambridge.
Mass.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 1.-The long
established passbook system used in
ordinary savings institutions will be
adopted for the government postal
savings banks. The committee that
has been perfecting the plans for the
postal banks had been considering
what is known as the coupon system
for postal banks deposits, but has now
decided that while having some ad-
vantage that system might produce
complications.


According to the coupon system de-
positors would receive with each de-
posit a slip representing their deposit,
together with a coupon for the amount
of interest that would be paid on their
money. The committee decided there
were many objections to flooding the
country with millions of deposit slips
with coupons attached, many of which
would represent values of only few
cents.

washed the solution away. Later ap-

chip soap in the proportion of ten

oil: to this add one hundred gallons Of
water, the whole being boiled together

for arraignment, but the judge said

Her attorney then asked for reduc-
