OAKLAND, May 23.-That she would
be shot out of the witness chair if she
gave testimony in the suit now being
tried before Judge Ellsworth over the
property of the late John Drusedom
was the threat made to her by Maggie
Mann, Drusedoms former house keep
er. according to IA year old Hazel
Mann, who testified today. The two
are not related.


Hazel Mann, the witness, said that
Maggie Mann, the house keeper, met
her in Fourteenth street and told her
her life would be worthless If she tes-
tif1ed. Last Saturday night, the wit
ness continued, the same threat was
made to her by Miss Mann over the
telephone.


The contest was brought by Mrs.
Anne Waterman to set aside as fraud
ulent a deed to property valued at
$4,000 which Drusedom gave Maggie
Mann shortly before his death. Mrs.
Waterman says that her father, who
was 73 years old when he died, was of
unsound mind and unduly influenced
by the house keeper when he executed
the deed.


Testimony has been given in the case
to the effect that he changed materi-
ally after Maggie Mann became his
house keeper, showing frisky and
youthful traits. One witness testified
that his behavior was scandalous and
that right on the front porch where
all the neighbors could see it, Maggie
Mann used to kiss and hug him.

PHILADELPHIA, May 3O.-Because
Miss Cora Diehl, a dressmaker, of
Seventeenth street. near Arch, did not
have her dress completed on schedule
time, Mrs. Della Williams, next
door neighbor, had her arrested.


Miss Diehl explained to Magistrate
Scott in central station that she had
been i'll, and consequently could not
do the work as she had promised. She
said she would have the dress finished
next Monday, if given a chance, and
the magistrate held her in bail to keep
her promise.


The dressmaker was allowed to sign
her own bail bond of $400. She will
have further hearing on Tuesday. If,
in the meantime, the dress is finished,
the case will be dropped, Mrs. Williams
having fallen into the spirit of con-
cession and agreed to this.


According to Mrs. Williams, the dress
should have been delivered last Mon
day. She said she gave the material to
the dressmaker five weeks ago, and
that she felt she was being imposed
upon.

TIONESTA, Pa, July 9.-Pretty lit
tie Lillian Gilfoyle, five years old, liv-
ing with her mother near LickingVllle,
yesterday was given permission 10
gather wild strawberries in the field
back of the house, and within half
an hour came running in with small
laceration on the side of her tiny
hand.


Lillian was crying and overcome
with such terror that she could make
no coherent disclosure of what had
happened to her. Bees had stung her,
she said at first, then a snake had
fastened itself to her hand and she
had dragged it half way to the house
in her frightened effort to escape, she
lisped Later, she said two snakes
had struck at her.


The mother was frantic. The near
est doctor lived in Lickingville. She
had no antidotes about the house. She
bound up the wound and ran to
neighbours, a mile away. Word was
sent in to town with all possible speed,
but seven hours had elapsed before
the doctor rushed into the house.


There was little for the doctor to
do. Little Lillian lay in sort of
stupor, having suffered seven hours of
agony of the most fearful intensity.
Sedatives were administered and the
piteous throes of the dying child ale
waited. During the night she died.


Neighbors searched the field and
found two large rattlers. One lay
much nearer the house than the other,
and there were evidences that the
snake had been dragged a consid-
cradle distance. Just what happened
to the little one is not known. Those
who found the rattler believe that the
girl was struck. perhaps by both of
them. and that her death resulted.

offer conditional upon similar action

river. The agreement provides the men
shall be taken back without discrimln-

ing the strike.

nies and their employees does not affect
the strikes of chauffeurs, cab drivers

demands of their, own.

details reached here today of race
riot near Harrisville, Simpson county
on Sunday. Several hundred white
men are now searching for fugitive ne
groes. one white man, Luther Buck
ley. and a negro have been killed. The
trouble started when two negroes quar-
relied with a white farmer and left him
living unconscious from blow on the
head. A posse started in pursuit of the
colored men. Shortly after dark yes
terday, while one of the searching par
ties was riding along the public road,
fire was opened by the fugitlVes, and
Buckley, a young FARMER, was shot
dead from his horse.


The posse gave immediate pursuit
and a negro named Jones was captured
and shot to death.

STOCKTON, June 27.-Fire started
from sparks from an engine this after
noon ran through the big barley fields
of Union island, in the southwestern
section of San Joaquin county, and
burned more than 1000 acres of grain
that was expected to harvest from
forty to sixty bushels an acre.


A lucky turn in the wind changed
the run of the fire to the river bank
and stopped the destruction The losses
fell principally on renters on the Will
liams and Bixler lands, but they were
nearly all insured. The grain crops
of that section are very heavy, and
the farmers feared the flames would
run through the whole district.

suffering fractionally. The home rails

labor dispute in the coal trade. Despite

sta,c Of the national finances. the under

NATE -SZALKA, Hungary, March 26.
The village of Oekoerito and the ada
cent districts have been thrown into
mourning by terrible disaster at the
former place last night which resulted
in the death of between 800 and 400
persons and the serious injury of 100
others.


A public ball was announced to De
held at the hotel, where the coach house
had been fitted up as ballroom. 1t
was a great barnlike structure, deco
rated with tinder dry June branches
left from a previous entertainment to
which were added for the occasion dec
orations and Chinese lanterns. The fes-
tivity attracted pleasure seekers from
the surrounding country and the build
ing was so packed. just before the ball
commenced that the single door that
afforded entrance and exit was nailed
up to prevent the admittance of scores
who clamored outside.


DREADFUL PANIC ENSUES


While the dancing was in full swing
a pine branch caught fire and fell to the
floor. 1t blazed furiously and almost
instantly the dresses of several women
burst into flames. The fire spread with
astonishing rapidity. A dreadful panic
ensued, the jewellers losing their heads
completely. Many of them, with flames
shooting out from their garments.
rushed toward the barred exit. where
surging mass was jammed together.


Women and men fell and were tram
pied under foot Those in front vainly
endeavored to tear open the door, but
were crushed helplessly by the pres
sure of the crowd behind.


WRECKAGE BURIED VICTIMS


Soon the roof crashed in, the blazing
wreckage falling on the helpless vic
tins so that many of those who had
hitherto escaped the flames were struck
down by beams or buried under debris


When the door was finally broken
open some few persons escaped, but
most of these collapsed before they
got far Inside the building were
heaps of charred corpses. Screams
and groaRs still were audible from the
smoking piles. A detachment of troops
was ordered to the scene to clear the
wreckage and help bury the dead.


The official estimate. as given to-
night, states that 29o persons perished.
but it is believed that the total death
roll will prove much larger than this,
as many persons have not been ac-
counted for.

TRENTON, " j.. January S.-Although
she might have saved herself instead OF
her patient, Miss Elizabeth Coombe, a
nurse in the Mercer Hospital here, sacri-
feed her life today in performing her
duties i'm the institution.


The young woman was crushed to death
in an elevator shaft in the hospital, but
the patient whom she saved does not
know of the nurses heroism. The young
woman will be buried tomorrow.


Miss Coombe was one of the most pop
ular young women of Trenton. She met
death bravely. and but for her display OF
courage two lives would have been sacri-
feed instead of one.


The nurse was instructed to convey a
helpless patient from the third floor in
the hospital to the first, where the oper-
ating room is situated. In this work she
operated an elevator alone, and stopped
the elevator at the first floor. She was
just removing the cot bearing the invalid
when she felt the elevator moving up
ward


Instantly she pushed the cot backward
into the Enclosure to prevent the pa
tient from being injured. but as she did
so the elevator shot upward, crushing hel
head, dragging her for a distance anC
then dropping her into the pit twenty
feet below.


The patient did not suffer even a
scratch, but the youthful nurse died q
few moments after the hospital internes
arrived at her side. Her face was
crushed beyond all recognition.

LONG BEACH, Dec. 1S.-Nine young
people, of whom five are high school
seniors, were held up by two masked
men near Eighth street and Chestnut
avenue. about 1 O'Clock this morning
and robbed of $25 and silver watch.
The parties held up were in three sep
arate groups and about forty-fve min
utes elapsed between the time the first
group was stopped by the footpads and
the termination of the proceedings.


The victims of the footpads included
young married couple, four young
men and three young women. They
were: Mr.. and Mrs. Hal Barber, Miss
Myma Taylor, Miss Frances Wood,
Miss Mabel Anderson, William Sven
ingson, M. T. Hiatt, Loring Jones and
Bert Mason. Miss Taylor and Miss
Wood and Hiatt, Mason and Swening-
son are high school seniors, who had
been attending a senior class party at
Alamitos bay.


Mr.. and Mrs. Barber and Jones and
Miss Anderson were standing on West
Eighth street. between Chestnut and
Cedar avenues, when two men passed
them. Just around the corner the two
men put on smoked glasses, drew re-
Volvers and returned, commanding the
four to hold up their hands. AS they
did so Sweningson, Hiatt, Miss Wood
and Miss Taylor came along Eighth
street. They had alighted from car
at Seventh street and Pine avenue and
were walking toward Miss Taylor's
home, across the street from the scene
of the holdup.


VICTIMS LINED IN ROW


AS the last four appeared, one of the
holdup men ran to meet them. and,
while his companion made a search of
Jones and Barber's pockets, the other
robber marched the others up to where
the first victims stood and lined them
all UP together.


About this time Mason appeared on
the scene. He had escorted the young
woman who accompanied him to her
residence and was hurrying to his own
home. One of the highwaymen stepped
out, stopped Mason and placed him in
the line.


The two crooks then completed their
search through the pockets OF the
young men, brandishing their revol-
pers as they made the search in a
leisurely and methodical manner.


The girls were not searched, but S5
cents was taken from purse which
one of them had given to her escort to
carry. The highwaymen overlooked
$5.05 in the same purse.


All their victims were warned not to
resist or make an outcry.


After searching their victims the
robbers backed into the shadow of
big palm tree, retreated behind the
tree. then turned and ran.


Miss Taylor at once notified her
father and the police were informed of
the case. That section of the city was
secured thoroughly by patrolmen and
detectives, but no trace of the holdup
men was found. This morning two
suspects were arrested, but were re-
leased soon afterWard, there being no
evidence that they knew anything of
the robbery.


Meager descriptions were given of
the robbers. They were said to be
about five feet seven inches tall. and
both wore white sailor caps.

SAN BERNARDINO, March 10.-The
California limited, which left Los An
geles at 10 o'clock this morning, mar
rowly escaped a disastrous wreck as 1t
was leaving San Bernardino before l
o'clock this afternoon. The leading
locomotive struck a partly opened
switch at the junction point of the
main line and loop in the northern part
of the city, and both engines with the
buffet car left the track. Although the
two locomotives were drawing the
train at a fast rate of speed, the engi-
neer at the instant he felt his engine
leave the rails applied the emergency
brakes, which brought the train to a
stop before more than the leading car
had been derailed. Neither engine
turned over. The cars which were not
derailed were returned to the yards,
while the wrecker rerailed the engines
and repaired the track. Traffic was
demoralized for four hours. No one was
injured.

SAN LEANDRO, July 21.-Though
the large tank of oil in the engine
room of the burning electric plant and
pumping station threatened to explode
from the heat at any moment, Mrs. I.
w. Hellman, Jr, the wife of the prom
inent San Francisco banker, stayed
bravely by the blazing structure and
coolly directed the efforts of her en-
ployes this morning in preventing the
spread of the flames, which, once
caught in the dry grass, would have
destroyed the beautiful country home
of the Hellmans at the head of Dutton
avenue.


Despite the efforts of the volunteer
fire fighters, who included even Mrs.
Hellman's maids, the extensive power
plant, which supplied light and
water to the estate and was valued
at $4,000, was completely destroyed.
But for Mrs. Hellmans GOODNESS and
bravery, the loss would have been
much greater.


Notifies Mrs. Hellman


The fire, believed to have been
started by crossed wires, was discov
cred by the estate engineer shortly
after $50 o'clock. He at once notified
Mrs. Hellman, who was giving orders
to the housekeeper. Hellman had left
but short time before for the city
and Mrs Hellman wos the only member
of the family at home


Realizing the need of quick action,
Mrs. Hellman notified the Melrose fire
department and then, throwing a wrap
about her shoulders, hastened out to
the burning building, located at some
distance from the house. When she
arrived, sparks were already catching
in the dry grass and foliage that
separated the home from the plant.


Summoning every available employee
on the place, Mrs. Hellman quickly or
ganized a bucket and garden brigade.
Needless of the sparks that burnt
every time they hit and the dense,
pungent smoke, Mrs Hellman directed
the little band of fire fighters, despite
the admonitions of the engineer that
oil tanks might explode, and prevented
the spread of the fire to the grass,
which would have meant the destruc-
tion of the house.


Plant in Ashes


When the fire department arrived
from Melrose, after a five mile run, the
plant was in ashes. The building con-
tained one of the finest storage battery
systems on the coast and had been
installed by the Dunsmuirs before the
Fellmans acquired possession of the
improved part of the old Souther
farm, which theyshave since made their
home. 1t was purchased from Edna
Wallace Hopper. the actress, who got
it from the estate of Mrs Josephine
Dunsmuir, her mother.


Mrs. HelIman is a society leader and
has been identified with the 400" of
San Francisco for many years. Her
husband is the president of the Union
Trust company of San Francisco.

In all my street railway riding In
Germany have not yet seen a crowded
street railway car Only once have 1
seen passengers standing inside a car.


The Germans recognize the necessity
Of making street railway service flexible,
to provide for variations in travel at
different times. and they attach trail
cars behind the motor cars. In even
such small cities as Heidelberg train
consisting Of a closed motor car haul
ing an open trail car is regularly run.


American street railways have pro-
vlded for increased traffic by putting on
larger and heavier cars. but the Ger
mans nave met the same problern bv
running trains OF two or three cars
The advantages of the German system
TO tho public are extremely great and
l believe they are almost as great 10
the street railway. The floors of Ger
man street cars are low. Ike the Ameri-
can street cars Of dozen years ago.
They are far easier to get in and out
or than our high-hoored American cars.
which are designed TO accommodate the
car builders rather than the convenience
OF the travelling public.


The German street cars are clean
They are even cleaner than the Boston
street cars; and those who know how
high the Boston street railway service
stands compared with that Of most other
American cities VIII appreciate what q
compliment this is. Not only are the
cars clean. but they are attractive. They

they look. in fact, like an American car
just out Of the shops


And not only are the cars clean. but
the employees are clean. Their uniforms
are immaculate. their brass buttons shin.
ing, and the men themselves are cour

With shouts of childish joy, Remie
Vache 8 years old, whose cute ways
and manly bearing endeared him to
the matrons in the city Jail since he
was placed in their care Tuesday
night, ran down the corridor of the
gloomy Jail building last night and
leaped into the arms of his mother,
who burst into tears when she saw
the little fellow.


For several minutes Mrs. Eugene
Vache knelt on the concrete floor of
tightly to her breast She was too
overcome to speak, and the little boys
inquiries of "Where has 90 bin, muz-
zer?" were not answered


The jailer and the matron who wit
messed the happy reunion of mother
and child silently walked away and
left the happy pair to themselves until
the mother had recovered her COM
posure and indicated that she was
ready to take the little fellow to her
home.


Mrs. Vache, who lives at 636 Wall
street, explained how the child hap
pened to be left in the care of Ada
Robinson, a negress of S32 San Julian
street, and told such a pathetic story
that those who listened to the recital
turned away and furtiYely brushed
tears from their eyes.


According to her story, Mrs. Vache
was divorced last February and
awarded the custody of the child. At
that time she was practically penni-
less and in i'll health. Although hardly
able to attend to her own housework,
the unfortunate woman obtained light
employment and managed to feed and
cIothe the child by depriving herself
of many comforts which she formerly
had enjoyed.


STARYEs FOR CHILD


Owing to the fact that she was
compelled to take the child with ner
because she was unable to pay for
his board at a children's home, Mrs.
Vache frequently had to give up work.
Some days she went without eating
because of not having enough food for
both. She had several offers from
persons VINO wished to adopt the child,
but her love for the little one was too
strong to consent to parting with him.
No matter how little money she would
have the mother always provided for
the lad and kept him dressed neatly.


After several weeks of almost des-
titution, Mrs. Vache obtained a posi-
ton about ten days ago in a tailor
shop at 2091 West Fifth street. She
took the little fellow with her, but
found that she was unable to do her
work while he was clinging to her
skirts and begging her to play with
him.


Mrs. Vache was unable to hire per-
sons living at the same house where
she had a room to care for the child.
and was told that the negress, Ada
Robinson, was a reliable person and
would keep the little one for a nom
mai price.


Dhe child was taken to the home of
the negress September IL. Mrs. Vache
explained that she was without funds
but would return within a few days
and pay for the lads board.


The following day Mrs. Vache re-
ceived her wages and found that after
paying her own room rent, which then
was past due, she would not have
anything left. The unfortunate woman
was SO worried over the matter that
instead of explaining her condition she
sent the childs clothing to the negress
without any message.


The Robinson woman became
alarmed when the mother failed to
appear and gave the child in custody
of Patrolman H. B. Wallace Tuesday
night and asked him to investigate
the matter.


! Mrs. Vache stated last night that
she had made arrangements to have
the child cared for at her own home.

Az Rome the Tiber Is threatening &c

ings being destroyed.


The interior Of Spain is practically

blocks many of the Alpine passes and

eral years and most OF the smaller

There is no longer any reason why
even the farmer of moderate means
should not enjoy all the home comforts
of his city cousin, says the Electric
News. The day when bath tubs. light
ing plants, water systems for fire pro-
lection and heating furnaces were to
be found only in the larger villages
and in the cities has gone forever.
Today there are few rural villages too
SIN II to boast of all these things. and
the farmer has caught the spirit of the
times and his up-to-date farmhouse is
lighted with electricity and heated by
steam. 1t is supplied with fine bath
rooms and running water and other
modern conVeniences.


A few years ago the electric light
power plants installed on farms were
very few and far between. A few ad-
venturous farmers had dared to har-
ness their mountain pasture streams
and turn their water energy into cleo
tricity for use about the house and
barns; a few more had installed gaso-
line engines for the same purpose.
These early installations proved
success from the first and 1t was not
long before their worth had been
talked and written about until almost
every Well-to-do farmer was consider


ing a similar installation.


Aside from the many benefits and
economies of electricity for lighting,
heating and cooking in the farmhouse
it readily assumes most of the hard
work about the farm which in the past
has been a most discouraging factor
In securing farm labor. Electricity
easily does the milking. separating and
churning, as we'll as turn the washing
machine and the wringer In the barn
it is applied to feed cutters corn-shell-
ers, feed grinders and to all other
small machinery, such as the grind
stone, lathe and a small buzz saw for
cutting firewood. The threshing ma
chine and flaming mill are very easily
belted onto the portable motor. In
Germany and a few other foreign
countries electricity is also used to ad-
vantage to pull the plows, harrows,
raIes, cultivators, binders, mowers
and other outdoor machinery.

TORONTO, October 22-Practically
every inhabited spot in middle Canada
from the islands of the great lakes to
the arctic circle, however isolated, is, or
within forty-eight hours will be, alert
to ascertain the fate of the aeronauts
who drifted away from St. Louis last
Monday aboard the balloon America ii
in the international race. Up to late
hour tonight no reassuring word had
come through the rapidly growing net
work of search lines. Allan r. Hawley,
pilot, and Augustus Post, aid, of the
American aeroctat have not been heard
from.


Realization that each hour means less
ened probability Of escape from the in
evitable rigors of climate and dangers
Of the wild regions into which the sky
racers probably have been carried has
made the search strenuous. The hard
ships today recounted by the Azureaus
crew. who, upon landing in the AIgoma
district, were confronted with a wild
bison, and who fought for many hours
through blind forests and across streams
before reaching civilization, brought to
many the first -ealization of the hazards
attending these unprepared and unpro-
tected aeronauts in the vast unopened
areas to which those striving for dis
tance records may have been tempted.


Watching for the Balloonists.


Tonight scores Of those who know the
signs Of the skies, the trails of the for
ests and the ways of the lakes, are using
their trained senses in watching for or
seeking the balloonists. Indian runners,
forest rangers, frontier constables, Cana
dian mounted police, lighthouse keepers
along the lakes, trading and hunting
camps. railway construction gangs and
lake patrols have had instructions and
are on the lookout. The requests, official
and personal for cooperation in the
search, sent out from New York. where
two of the aeronauts live. from ST. Louis
and from the Canadian government have
been flashed wherever wires can carry
them.

w. Smith was shot and instantly killed
yesterday by Mrs. Daisy Fischer. the wife
of E. v. Fischer of this city. Smith
appeared at the hear door Of the Fischer
home armed with revolver. Mrs
Fischer opened fire with a Winchester
rife, and sent FIVE shots into his body,
one of which plowed through his brain.

Mrs. Fischer and her husband say that
Smith was her sutton ten years ago in
Hannibal, Mo. Smith continued his at
tentions Notwithstanding her marriage.
Frequent quarrels occurred between the
husband and Smith and finally. to avoid
conflict, Fischer and his wife left Han
nibal and came to Oklahoma. Smith fol-
lowed and frequently made visits to their
home against their protest. Several en-
counters occurred between Smith and
Fischer.


Smith made his appearance here March
10 and attempted to enter the Fischer
home. Mrs. Fischer locked the door and
telephoned her husband, who came post
haste to her relief, and dubbed Smith into
insensibility. He continued to hang
about town and frequently came into
contact with the police on various
charges.

charge of her husband. Public opinion

through the dense fog. The Tacoma
was rammed above the water line, a
hole being stove In her starboard bow

the Tacoma sprang a leak and the
Isthmian stood by until 1t was learned
that the vessel was in no danger, The
Tacoma was picked up by tug ana
towed into port here. She was in
bound from Nakneck, Alaska.

NHICAGO, April 23.-The eastward


moving storm, manifested yester-
day in rain and high winds, de-
veloped snow and freezing tempera-
lures in the western lake region and
in the upper Mississippi valley today.


In the fruit belts of northern Indiana,
western Michigan, Illinois, Iowa, Mis-
souri,, Minnesota and Wisconsin, fruit
was damaged to the extent of millions
of dollars, according to reports from
the sections affected.


At Chicago, Milwaukee, Dubuque and
other cities in the path of the storm
the thermometer dropped from % to 2S
degrees over night.


Lake Michigan was lashed into a
fury. The Goodrich line steamer Iowa
was washed ashore between Kenosha
and Racine, Wis, but was not serious
ly damaged. Her passenger list was
small. The tug u. I. Morford has been
sent to her relief. 1t is not thought
any serious damage has bee ndone, al
though the vessel has been aground
since o'clock this morning.


The City of Benton Harbor of the
Graham & Morton line arrived here
several hours late today after an all
night battle with the wind and waves
on it's way from st. Joseph, Mich. On
account of the binding snow the
steamer was unable to locate the har-
Dor here early today, her ice-encrusted
hulk showing inside the river several
hours late.


The steamer Puritan, leaving Chicago
at 1870 last night, bound across the
lake, was beaten back to her dock to-
day by the gale.


The small lumber steamer Cora was
caught thirty miles out by the storm,
and experienced the gravest danger in
making her way back to her wharf.


The official report of the local weather
bureau states that the weather in the
Great Lake region probably VIII con-
tinue unsettled, with snow squalls.

Topeka, Kas., Jan. lathe Kansas
river rose ten feet during the night and
stood at is feet this morning. The
bridges at Willard, Valencia and Lee
compton have been swept away.


Ice jams We're responsible. The Le-
compton bridge Withstood the 1903 flood
but those at Willard and Valencia were
destroyed and had been rebuilt.


The gauge shows that the water
reached its maximum height early this
morning, and it is now falling slowly
The ice gorge in the Kansas river
reached Lawrence today, carrying out
a wagon bridge and causing several
thousand dollars loss between Lecomp-
ton, eleven miles west, and Lawrence.
The ice was tossed forty feet high.


All Traffic Stopped


All traffic between Lawrence and
North Lawrence was stopped and the
electric light plant was shut down.
Schools in North Lawrence were closed
The weather bureau notified business
houses along the river that the flood
stage was likely to be reached within
twenty-four hours if the ice below st.
bility of the gorge breaking.


The ferryboat Madison at Venice, H.,
was sunk by the ice.


On the Marais des Cygnes river an ice
gorge formed against a bridge two
miles east of Ottawa, and by this morn
ing it had extended to that city,
blocking the channel.


The water was rising rapidly this
morning, and a fore of men started out
to dynamite the gorge in an attempt to
prevent a flood.

I'm UraI Mountains.


Mans inventions follow natures lead
The cold storage of fruit is a modern de-


vice for the supplying of man with fruit
long after the fruit-ripening season is


over. but nature has done the same thing
from time immemorial. Seebohm, the


English ornithologist. surprised from Ma


ture her secret and discovered her great


cold storage system, says Harper s
Weekly


In the course Of his researches he was
led to visit the Penhora River. which
flows from the Ural Mountains into the
Arctic Ocean, near Nova Zsmbia Along
the lower part of the river he found what
seemed a most uninviting district-an un-


Inhabited. treeless swamp. stretching on
| either side of the stream, and known as
the tundra. Higher up the river was the
great Siberian forest, but here in the tun-
dra was nothing but hard frozen snow.


Yet this unattraetive spot was found to
| be the summer home Of half the bird
population Of the Old World


The investigator reached II in the be-
ginning Of April. Forest and tundra
were as bare of life as the Desert Of Sa-
hara. but a change was coming. Suddenly
summer broke over the scene, and with
It came the birds The ice in the river
split and disappeared. the banks steamed
in the sun and innumerable birds of all
sizes and colors appeared within forty
eight hours after the first warmth.


The once frozen tundra now showed
itself TO be moor. with here and there a
large bog and numerous lakes. 1t was
covered with moss, lichens. heath-like
plants. dwarf birch and millions of acres
Of cloudberries, cranberrles, and crowber-
ries. This was the storehouse of the
feathered tribes.


The perpetual sun OF the arctic summer
causes the plants TO bear in wonderful
profusion. so that fruit is abundant But
fruit-bearing does not come before bios
soming, and fruit cannot be perfected in
forty-eight hours. The little travellers
were arriving by the thousands The
fruit would not be ripe until the middle
or end of the arctic summer, and If the
birds had to walt till then they must
needs starve.


Not so, however, does nature provide
for her pensioners. Long before the snow
melted provision had been made for their
maintenance. Beneath the snow lay the
whole crop of last years fruit, perfectly
preserved.


Each year, when the berries are ripe
and before the birds can gather them, the
snow descends upon the tundra, effectu-
ally covering the crop and preserving it
in perfect condition until the spring sun
melts the snow and discloses the bushes
loaded with ripened fruit, or, in some
cases, the ground beneath the plants Gov
cred with the fallen treasure waiting for
the hungry strangers. The berries never
decay beneath the snow. but keep in per-
feet condition. and are accessible as soon
as the snow melts


Nor need the visitors depend on fruit
alone for sustenance The insect-eating
birds are also provided for, and all may
take their choice of fruit or flesh The |
same heat which frees the fruit also !
brings into being the most prolific insect |
life in the world. No European can live |
there without veil after the snow melts. |

having murdered his wife and thrown the
body in Lake Como. appears before Judge
Blair, in court of oyer and termner in

formally move for the dismissal of the
case on the ground that the Italian gov
eminent has made no formal demand for
him.


The treaty expressly provides that no
citizen Of the United States shall be re-
turned to Italy for trial without for
NAL demand on the State Department by
an authorized officer of the Italian gov
eminent. This demand. they are con-
WINGED, has never been made.


Inquiries at the State Department for
the last six weeks have produced only
evasive replies If the demand has not
been made, Charlton Is practically free
man. for the treaty also provided that
the papers shall be filed with the State
Department within forty days after the
date of the arrest.


The attorneys say that the State De-
partment has committed several blunders,
and that through these blunders the Ital-
ian government will try to extradite

ATLANTIC CITY, June 6.-Jumping

J. Lawrence, a wealthy Philadelphia
sugar broker. and former college ath-
lete, pulled stroke oar with a volunteer
crew who went TO the rescue of the crew
of the steamer Brazoria of the Atlantic
City transportation line. Tie freight
laden vessel struck the inlet bar yester-
day and snapped off her rudder.


Unable to persuade Capt. Lynch and
the crew of the freight steamer to aban-
don the craft to the heavy breakers,
the volunteer rescuers pulled the life
boat through the heavy seas, and with
the new government power boat dragged
the steamer into deep water, where she
is now lying safely awaiting repairs.
Thousands of spectators on the Board
walk cheeTed the volunteer crew when
it returned to the beach.

City station was on duty alone when
the freight boat struck the bar. The
lighthouse keeper. Frank Adams; Thomas
Nixon, one of the government crew la iii
off duty by government order during the
summer months; Edward Harrison. Marx
Brown, Harry Topham and William Al
len, skilled boatmen. had boarded the
life-saving craft when Lawrence left "A

ing lightered ashore and she VIII be

JEFFERSON CITY. Mo. June Ga
fully equipped counterfeiting plant. which
has been in operation at the state peni-
Tertiary for twenty years: was raided yes
terday by Government Inspector Edward
j. McHugh Molds. fire pots. spurious
coins and paraphernalia were confiscated
and two prisoners taken. Both confessed
having made counterfeit half dollars
quarters and five-cent pieces.
The plant, Inspector McHugh says. has
been in the penitentiary for twenty years.
and has been handed down from prisoner
10 prisoner. The men arrested are Lee J..
Jaynes. a five-year man from Kansas
City, and Joseph Vail. another long-term
prisoner from there.


A Quarrel between four prisoners oc-
cupying the same cell regarding the divi-
sion of the spoils was responsible for the
raid.


Gov. Hadley has announced that he will
pardon both men in October, when the
federal court convenes, that they may be
prosecuted.


Molds Hidden in Cell.


When Warden Andrea learned that
prisoners were making spurious coins he
placed watch on the suspected men in
the hope of catching them in the act. His
discovery was made last Thursday.


Three molds made by counterfeiters
were found hidden in the cell occupied
by JAMES and Vail Two sets of these
were for fifty-cent pieces, one for quarter
dollars and the other for five-cent pieces.
A small plaster of Paris furnace used for
heating the metal was dug from under
the cell floor.


This furnace was constructed to re-
ceve a receptacle four inches square.
Charcoal was used for fuel. Hidden in
the beds of the prisoners were found
eight fifty-cent, two twenty-five-cent and
two five-cent pieces.


The appearance of the furnace showed
it had been in operation but short
while. 1t is the opinion of Inspector Nc
Hugh that the men did not have chance
to put any of their coins in circulation.
Jaynes and Vail were simply following
out the course of former convicts


Circulated Coins at Carnivals.


1t is custom at the Jefferson City
prison to hold carnival twice year,
one on Christmas day, when a three
days feast is allowed the long-term men,
and the otner on the Fourth of July. 1t
was for this latter holiday that Jaynes
and Vail were preparing.


When the carnival is held concessions
are granted to the long-term men, and
they have stands en- which are various
articles for sale. For twenty years the
carnivalS have been an eSta blished Gus
tom, and invariably after their celebration
counterfeit coins have been found among
the prisoners Even prison officials, who
parroniZed the stands, were sometimes
made victims.

One Of the most daring hold-ups that have

OAKLAND. May 25.-Seven persons
were injured in a collision between a
Key Route special and Twelfth street
streets shortly after II o'clock this
morning. The cars were about to pass
each other at the point of the acci-
dent, when the traction car, suddenly
oereiled by a rock in the roadbed, was
thrown in a slant across the path of
the oncoming special.


Among those injured were Miss Ma
tilda Brown, sister of Judge Everett
Brown; Mrs. ]. Flynn of Tenth street
Mrs. W. c. Coffet of Alameda, Mrs. T.
Jackson and three men.


Motorman E. Hayes, who was in
charge of the Twelfth street car, mar
rowly escaped serious injury when the
special car crashed into the side steps
and rails. crumbling them into kim
ding wood. The fact that the injuries
were not more serious is due to the
GOODNESS of Motorman Kerwin of the
Key Route car, who, when he saw the
derailment of the car so feet ahead
threw on his emergency brakes and
succeeded in checking the headway OF
his car before IT struck.


Miss Brown. who was riding inside
the traction car when the accident oc-
Cured, was thrown across the aisle
ana was severely cut over lne eyes ana
about the head by broken glass from
the car windows, and was also bruised
about the breast and shoulders. She
was unconscious until taken into the
manual training high school building
near by, where school teachers dressed
her wounds. She was later taken to
the Fabiola- hospital, where she was at
tended by surgeons, after which she
was removed to her home, SIS Twenty
ninth street.


Mrs. Flynn. Mrs. Coffet and others
were thrown from the car into the
street by the shock. Mrs. Flynn and
Mrs. Coffet both sustained serious
bruises about the limbs. Mrs. Jackson
was cut about the face and shoulders
by broken glass and was bruised The
three unidentified men were bruised and
slightly cut. None of the Key Route
passengers was hurt.


Superintendent ]. P. Potter person
ally directed the work of the wreck
ing crew, and after tying up Twelfth
street traffic for more than two hours
the wreckage was cleared away.

MILA4, Nov. 27.-Bisceglia cathe-
dral in the province of Bari, has been
by shocking cholera riots.


The city was just beginning to re-
cover from commercial depression
when a fresh outbreak of Asiatic
cholera occurred. The Red Cross corps
was hastily summoned and began a
thorough disinfection of the cathedral,
which apparently was the scene of
contagion. Soon after bowling crowd
of the church and rushed upon the
Red Cross officials, trampling them
under foot and destroying the disinfec-
tion material and pumps.


The fanatics then persuaded them
selves that the images of the saints
were scowling and sweating with rage,
so tearing out their own tresses they
began washing and polishing the faces
of the statues.


About 300 lshermen, whose calling is
languishing because of the general
prohibition against the sale and con,
sumption of fish, came upon the scene
and turned the Red Cross out of the
building. Some ascended the belfry
and set all the bells ringing violently.
In a few minutes practically the whole
of the population assembled eager for
the opportunity of attacking the local
authorities for their vexatious cholera
measures.


Reinforcements arrived, and pitt
less hail of stones and missiles of
divers kinds was hurled upon the heads
of the soldiers from the upper windows
and balconies of the adjacent streets.
Once inside the cathedral they were
confronted by a mob armed with dag
gers and reyolVerS. During a fright
full display of barbarity that ensued
one man was thrust through with a
bayonet, and there was pool Of blood
at the foot of the high altar.


The edif1ce resounded with the roar
of firearms and the piercing shrieks of
the fanatical throng Besides casual
ties among the civilians, a number of
soldiers fell wounded with bullets and
knife thrusts in various parts of the
church. The populace were left in un-
disputed possession.

Nothing is too luxurious in furs.
This season fashion simply demands
the best.


Just another instance that proves
that Parisiennes are leaders of fash
ion. Last summer fair Frenchwomen
wore stoles of ermine with lingerie
frocks-regardless of heat or cold.
Now, that winter is here. heavy FUR
garments are their whim.


The increased popularity Of motor
ing has called forth fur coats of an
entirely new type. These garments
are fashioned on the lines of smart
mannish topcoats and, of course.
unique furs were necessary to make
the vogue a success-as every one al
ways wants something different
Leopard skin, antelope and baby deer
are quite the most popular, although
pony skin and raccoon are also note
worthy.


Fur-lined coats for motoring. as Of
yore, are favored by conservative
women. These luxurious topcoats are
mostly of heavy broadcloth, lined with
squirrel and with large shawl collar
of skunk or Persian lamb.


Caracal coats of generous length
are most befitting for shopping and
daily events. Broadtail and Persian
lamb are also included in the same
category.


Evening coats-also worn for for
NAL afternoon affairs-are simply
superb.


Full length coats of Russian sable
or ermine are the most queenly One
exquisite coat recently seen was of
snowy ermine with broad band of
skunk around the bottom. which
curved gracefully at each side of the
front Sable and ermine are fire.
quently combined, while white fox
and sealskin is another joyous har-
mony.


Muffs are simply enormous and abb
solutely fiat. Indeed. some are SO
large and fiimsy that they are almost
burdensome. Quite the most extreme
styles have wide centers of Persian
silk. or velvet, with wide bands of
fur. The large ctoles to match are
fashioned likewise, only SO wide that
they are more like shawls than mere
neckpieces. These particular modes
were created by Madame Agnes-and
Parisiennes have thoroughly approved
them.


Women of moderate tastes are quite
satisfied with the round and pillow
muffs of conservative size. and stoles
of usual proportions.

killed in the civil war, was the original
commander. sat down to a banquet last
night at the Wellington Hotel. 1t was
the last reunion. The roll was called for
the last time, and never again will the
Chicago Zouaves meet under the old flag
to recount the tales of war and battles


Very few are left in the ranks. Once
they were 40 strong. They CHALLENGED
the world. Their, was not better drilled
corps in the nation. They claimed the
championship, and the claim was not dis.
puted. They travelled all through the east
and south in 1860 to find competitors who
would march beside them. They went TO
West Point, and the greatest masters of
military technique passed them for all
that they claimed. and added praises that
were not expected.

SALT LAKE CITY, Utah, Feb 10
There will be no through trains over
the Western Pacific railroad for a
week, perhaps longer period. dis
aster similar in kind, though of lesser
degree than that which overwhelmed
the San Pedro, Los Angeles and Salt
Lake, befell the new Gould road during
a short lived tempest yesterday after
noon.


Lashed by the wind, mighty waves of
salt laden water beat down the West
ern Pacific roadbed where it crosses
the shallow southern arm of the Great
Salt lake, tore out long stretches of
track and piled masses of debris on
other portions. Examination today
showed that 10 miles of the line must
be repaired and two or three miles re-
built before trains can pass.


When the line was constructed the
lake was several feet below its pres
ent level and the elevation of the rails
was ample. The subsequent rise of the
waters brought them within splashing
distance of the ties and ii is no secret
that the officials have long realized the
necessity for reconstruction.


Freight, through and local. has been
handled by the Western Pacific for two
months. Passenger service has not
been established.

ELY. New. Sept. 11.-One man was
fatally injured and two were seriously
hurt in pitched battle with a gang of
four robbers, who entered the Southern
club this morning and made a partly
successful effort to seize the cash at
the gaming tables. For time shots
flew unfortunately


= The bandits. heavily armed. entered
the club at an early hour and COM
manded the crowd. consisting of a
hundred persons. to hold up their
hands. The order was complied with.
the men backing against the walls, and
the robbers proceeded to throw the
money from half dozen tables into
canvas sacks which they carried.


After taking the money from two
tables the bandits approached a third
where Clyde Tilford back of the table
refused to obey orders and drew a gun
to resist. The action was the signal for
resistance from all parts of the room
and a general melee began which
lasted fifteen minutes with the com
batants firing from behind tables and
bars.


The robbers were finally repuIsed, but
not until several of the frequenters of
the place had been wounded. George
Mill was wounded in the left lung,
probably fatally. Clarence McFadden
was struck in the leg by a spent bullet
and Tilford had his head cut open by
blow from the gun of one of the des-
peradoes-


After being driven out of the place
and firing several shots through the
windows, the robbers fled into the hills.
taking about $1,000 with them.


Indians have been requisitioned to
trail the outlaws and 90 special officers
in automobiles and on horseback are
in pursuit. Tex Hall, owner of the
Southern club and democratic candi-
date for sheriff. is leading the posse

lines has been lost, the Trinity & Brazos

connection, being owned jointly by the
Rock Island, now a rival of the Frisco,

the Burlington.


President lovett's Statement.


President Lovett of the Southern Pacific
yesterday made the following statement
concerning the scope of the new arrange
ment:


The north and south lines of the South
ern Pacific system extend from Galveston,
Houston, Port Arthur, Sabine Pass anu
Beaumont. on the Gulf, to Dallas, Fort
Worth Sherman. Denison and other north
ern Texas cities, but we have no lines cross
ing the northerly border of Texas Formerly
these lines received considerable business
from the Missouri, Kansas & Texas, with
which they connect at Denson. and from
the Rock Island system and the Colorado
& Southern system, with which they con-
meet at Forth Worth. But the Missouri
Kansas & Texas for some years has had
its own line to the Gulf, and some two
or three years ago the Rock Island sys-
tenn and the Colorado & Southern system
jointly constructed line from Fort Worth
TO the Gulf. The Frisco system has lines
from st. Louis and from Kansas City
through Missouri, Kansas and Oklahoma
to Denison, Dallas and Fort Worth, where
they connect with our lines.


Traffic Agreement Wholly.


An agreement has been made by which
these lines and the east and west lines of
the Frisco system in South Texas shall
work preferentially for traffic between
South and Central Texas and St Louis,
Kansas City, Oklahoma and other points
north. 1t is a traffic agreement wholly,
neither party having any running rights
on the lines of the other and no financial
commitments of any character being In
volved. The lines connect directly, and
ing together for the business mentioned
against the several other systems having
through lines from St Louis to the Gulf,
which neither of these alone has.


A similar agreement for the Interchange
of traffic was made in 1909 between the
Hartman lines and the Kansas City
Southern Railway, which operates a line
from Kansas City to the Gulf at Port
Arthur, Tex, and it is understood that that
arrangement will not be affected by the
new Frisco alliance.


President Winchell of the st. Louis q
San Francisco said yesterday:


Our traffic alliance with the Southern
Pacific is both offensive and defensive. 1t
means a new through route for US from
Galveston to Kansas City and Chicago,
and is practically the same as running
over our own tracks. It gives three hun
dred miles of new track over the Houston
& Texas Central, connecting our main line
with the division running from Browns
vile to New Orleans"

What is described as the largest
stalactite cave in Europe was recently
discovered near Schoenbergalm, in the
Dachstein mountains, Upper Austria.
Recently party of Austrian and Hun
garian scientists spent twenty-four
hours in thoroughly exploring the
cavern. The principal tunnel was found
to extend over a mile and a quarter,
with numerous side passages of vary
ing lengths. In traversing the main
tunnel the exploring party had to cross
by rope ladders an ice crevasse rs
feet deep and more than 100 feet wide,
says the Pail Mall Gazette. The cave
is divided into two levels. In the upper
were found two immense ice halls con-
tanning precipitous Subterranean
glaciers, some 300 feet long. Phenom-
email ice formations were also found
here. In the lower level was an end
less series of halls, the largest more
than 600 feet long and 100 feet high.
Traces of subterranean water courses
in the form of sand and rubble were
discovered in the main tunnels. There
were also some beautiful flowershaped
stalactites. Among the palaeontogical
discoveries made were petrified Bra
chiopoda and remains of cave bears
(ursus spelaeus).

the glad Christmas time has mostly vanished

the appraisement OF his bounty. and who ever
heard of much sentiment being attached to the aP-
oraiser job2 Already each woman has segregated
the useless presents and also the ones that arc
nice but not necessary.


Possibly the man has done the same thing, but
he is not so resourceful as the woman. She knows
how to turn the useless thing to account and she
does Already She is figuring where she will save
money by carefully slowing away the rejected
gifts with labels them for the persons to whom
she intends to present them next Christmas
Dainty little things that women have embroidered
usually share this fate. and the woman who is lay
ing them away this year may have received them
from some other woman who went through the
same process a year ago, so that even the most
trivial Christmas gilt enjoys measure OF immOr-
tality Still one shudders at the blighted friend
ships that would result if by any chance one OF
these creations ever should complete the circle by
coming back to the original maker after having
posed as first aid TO Santa Claus for the previous
five or ten years.

time one cannot blame the wise housewife for get
ting practical use out OF thing that is useless
But there is a precedent Tor it. it will be remem-
bered that Fiji Potter daughter of Mrs. James
Brown Potter, sent all her useless and duplicate
wedding presents TO a public auctioneer in New
York and realized enough money to buy the things
she really wanted Her action shocked the other
members of the -Four Hundred" at the time. but
they later forgot it and the ones who had sent the
useless presents were too ashamed of themselves
10 ever admit that their gift to the bride had been
among those that went under the hammer.

over again but they usually forget all about them
by the time Christmas comes back.

Philadelphia, April 29.-Although the
football rules committee. IN session at
the University Club, got along swimming
ly to-day, and apparently have all but
decided upon the rules that shall govern
the game hereafter, there was no off,
cial information to be given out tonight.


Secretary z. K. Hall. Of the committee.
who has been its spokesman at all the
conferences this winter. said tonight that
the committee surely would give out all
its new rulings tomorrow; that these
were practically decided upon. but that
this evenings and tomorrow morning.
session would be necessary to frame the
rules in appropriate text


All day to-day the committee was in
session at the University Club, the mem
bers converting early in the morning and
finally adjowning only when midnight
was approaching. The entire committee
was present. together with several alter
mates, and the decision OF the new rules
began only after various reports from
the various colleges that have held real
football practice since the meeting of the
committee last month, had been received.


The committeeman to-day were not as
accessible as they were at the New York
meetings. and the nothing doing" sign
was hung out after each adjournment
for luncheon or dinner. However. Il may
be said that the two great questions that
were being debated were the forward
pass and its future. and what means
should be taken to bring about more open
play without destroying present princi-
pies OF the game. Long before the COM
mittee adjourned tonight, the report was
spread that the forward pass surely
would be. retained. and that a vote 10
this effect had been taken.

sumed sad countenance, and assured his jesty

mournful fact that all his relatives would die be-

majesty's presence wore glad face. For your

7 was very disagreeable day. A


hot Santa Ana wind was blowing
- and dust came in such thick

dows. Miss Brown. our teacher, had
a headache and asked questions sharp
ly, expecting prompt answers. Jimmie,

most, failed utterly in one lesson and

Across the street from the school

and pollywogs liked. Jimmie found a
large, green frog and, when Miss
Brown was in the rear of the school
house, put it in her desk. Another
frog he took out on the yard and put
1t in small girls lap. The little
child was very startled and gave a
cry. When Miss Brown came to her
she scolded the girl for being afraid
of such harmless animals as frogs.


just after school had taken up, Miss

studied hard. Then as the lid was
opened, out jumped the frog. Miss
Brown screamed and then fell to the
floor in a dead faint. Jimmie, who had
not meant any harm, rushed and got
some water. When Miss Brown re-
yiyed her headache was worse and
she went home, after eXcuslng us Tor

The next day turned out beautifully.
Anyone who had only seen Miss Brown

nized her She was sweet and lovely

Your niece,

SAN PEDRO. Aug. 22.-It is report
ed that the Pacific Coast Steamship
company is to have another large
steamer built for the run between
Puget sound and Southern California.
The growth in the passenger business
on the coast during the past two
years, 1t is said. has determined the
company to put on a third steamer Tor
through traffic.


When the liners President and Gov
ernor were brought to the Pacific
coast five years ago 1t was not thought
there was business enough In South
ern California to make their operation
profitable, and they were run for the
first two seasons between San Fran
cisco and Seattle only. AS an expert
ment they were put on the southern
run for the summer time three years
ago, with the expectation of taking
them off again in the winter. Business
continued so good late In the season
that 1t was decided to continue the big
boats during the winter on a weekly
schedule. They did a good business,
even in the winter months, and the
second winter had all they could carry,
Notwithstanding new competition.


The Alaska Pacific line put on the
steamer Admiral Sampson, and later
added two more steamers on the run
between Los Angeles and Puget sound

day schedule. Still the Pacific Coast
company ran we'll filled with passen-
gers, although five steamers were ply

was none before.


Competition between Los Angeles
and San Francisco was still further in
creased a few weeks ago, when the
San Francisco and Portland Steamship
company entered the field with. three
big steamers, the Beaver, Bear and
Rose City, on a five-day schedule.
Eighteen months ago there were but
five steamers running out of this port
on a regular passenger schedule. Now
there are twelve. The North Pacific
Steamship company, running the Ell
Ter and the Roanoke, are in the fore
front of the business.


Besides these there are about twenty
lumber schooners fitted with passen-
ger accommodations that make round
trips to northern ports in about twelve
days with irregular sailings. These,
as we'll as the regular passenger
steamers, have all the passenger busi-
ness they can handle, and at this sea-
son are generally sold out several days
in advance of sailing dates.

ance.

Paris, Jan. 21.-With the Seine the Rhona
the Ardeche and the Gard and their tribu-
taries surging over their banks, East and
central France tonight are still being
swept by damaging floods, which show
no signs OF abatement. Along the banks
OF all these streams much damage al
ready has been done and the people in
numerous instances have been forced to
leave their homes and seek safety In high
places Factories have shut down because
OF the raging currents and numerous small
craft have been carried away and wrecked.
Hundreds of persons are entirely homeless
and the government is rushing to them
much NEEDED supplies.


In Paris large portion Of the uncom-
pleted north and south subway line here
has been practically destroyed, and the
underground section of the Orleans road
is flooded. II is feared the Boulevard st.
German, under which the subway extends.
will give way. The electric factory from
which all the public clocks are worked is
inundated and all the clocks are stopped

The yell of astonishment that greeted
her appearance from the besieged had
hardly died away before she started
the ascent.


She raced quarter way up with hard
ly a sign of decreased speed. But the
drumming of the motor grew louder
and more strained as she reached half
way Still, she must have been going
at a great clip, for the three-quarters
distance was made at rate faster
than a man could run-but the last
quarter!


Slower and slower the chained
wheels turned over the snowy crest yet
steadily they forced her up with
scarcely a slip as they gripped the icy
slope. And now the Zip came within
range of the sharpshooters, who un-
nercifully peppered the onrushing foe.


Would she do it? Up, up into hail
of snowballs the besiegers sped. They
had naught but their snow shields,
which they crouched behind for what
protection they gave. Finally only so
feet separated them from the crest.
Could they make it? The putting mo-
tor was just able to complete the
climb where it hurled the Zip over the
crest directly at the base of the fort,
into the massed ranks of the besieged.
who had come out to repel the enemy,
though they had not dared to run
down to meet the oncomers on account
of the slippery hillside The top was
gained al last.


Then came the fiercest fighting of the
whole campaign. Franks confidence in
his followers was not misplaced, but
more than once they were all forced
down the hill by Ben's force, who out
numbered them two to one. Yet every
precious moment gained brought
Franks reinforcement creeping nearer
to the top.


Ben was no coward, and he and
Frank finally grappled with each other
just at the critical moment They
were equally matched, but Frank was
lucky enough to down his enemy, and
Ben's fall threw his ranks into great
confusion, and all the while Franks
second army corps" climbed higher.


The momentary panic gained time
enough for them to reach the top,
where they literally moved down the
tired and disconnected enemy, who had
been too busily engaged in fighting
off the Zip's crew to notice their APP
proach They pulled Frank off Ben,
who rose to find himself a prisoner
with all his army,


But what happened next was most
humiliating of all. over a dozen sIeds
were captured among the spoils of
war. When Frank learned OF this an
idea struck him. He turned to Ben:


I'VE can't make you fellows walk
the plank but we can make you ride
the sledr" and then each prisoner was
forced to ride ANONYMOUSLY down hill
on the very sled he mad brought up


Frank reserved Ben for the last
Frank had a little ceremony he want
ed to perform, especially for his cap
tive's benefit. Still kicking and fight
ing, Ben was forced to watch Frank
remove the little flag upon the PROV
of the Zip and stick it on the crest
OF Fort Tomahawk


Then Frank said:


Il brought this flag % miles 10
plant II on Tomahawk hill, and when
you want 10 declare war again lust
remember that. Now, boys. give Ben
his little ride"

class of laborers for the island.


Mr.. Keefe praised the Russian immi-
grants brought from Siberia and consid-
cred them more desirable than the Fill
pinos, but said that the immigration Of
Americans from the mainland would best
solve both the labor problem and the
Americanization of the island. The COM
ing here Of Americans, however, in the
opinion of the commissioner, was de-
pendent upon higher wages than are now
being paid in the island.

who declared that mysterious voices
had threatened her life and that of her
son over the telephone. She intimated

declared, she warned her son to pro-
tect his life against possible injury.

the small dagger which he used with
almost fatal results when attacked by
Brodenstein.

YUMA. Jan. 2S-John Richley
Charles blackburn and w. A. Reid are
in from a prospecting trip in the For
tuna mountains. They have brought
with them some rich rock found in
ledge two and half miles southeast
of the old Fortuna mine. Samples
taken along the ledge horned large
values in free gold, and though the
discoverers have not been able to ex-
nIore the deposits to any considerable
depth, having practically exhausted
their grub supply by the time they
made the find, surface indications
Justify the belief that they have made
a rich find.


The vein was traced for a distance
of 900 feet, and though only two feet
wide thes rock was found to be rich
for the whole distance. Five claims
were located. The discoveries expect
70 return to camp and begin active
development as soon as they can get
the necessary outfit together.

WASHINGTON. March S.-Retail
meat dealers today placed upon the
farmers and the packers responsibility
for the higher price of meat in testt-
mony given before the senate commit
tee Investigating the increased cost Of
living.


Five retail men from New York.
Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washing
ton were heard, and Walter Brown, a
Washington dealer who kills his own
meat, was the only one who did not
admit that the price of meat had gone
up at least 10 per cent during the
last five years.


Each witness vigorously denied the
retailers were responsible for prevail
ing prices, and none would admit that
any agreement on prices existed
among them. While no one charged
that the packers were in a combina-
tion, all witnesses who had dealings
with them declared there seemed to
be no competition for retail trade.


John Rohlman, who conducts
market in New York city, told the COM
tailers in New York was so keen that
they had been unable to keep pace with
the steadily increased prices.


Asked by Senator Simmons why the
retailers had not added something to
the price to the consumer to cover
this increased expense for help and
rent, the witness said:


THE merchants in New York city
are being crushed to the wall by the
wholesalers, who represent the pack
erS."

ascertained that the case of fever re-

smallpox.

Cal One hundred men have been dis
charged and paid off. and have left
for their homes in various parts of the
country The wives of several officers
came to Port Townsend and have vis-
tied them frequently.

head: John u. KING, former postmaster
at New Castle, injured about the stom-

conductor on freight car, face severely
cut.

to the Delaware Hospital here in an am
bulance and has remained with him. 1t
is not known whether the wreck was due
10 slippery rails or a misunderstanding OF
signals. There was a heavy fog at the
time.

the announcement that the tong war

murders may be added to the already
long list. The acclamations of peace

low waiting for the other side to make
the first move. The highbinders are
being watched closely by the police,

and murderous battle than the tongs
have yet had.

Miss Florence Mary Pardee. the beau
tiful university girl who met death
Sunday afternoon in an automobile ac-
cident near Corte MADEIRA, Marin
county, took place this afternoon at
o'clock from the home of her parents,
former Governor and Mrs. George C.
Pardee, at 672 Eleventh street

impressive simplicity by Rev. Charles
r. Brown, pastor of the First Congre-
gationaI church. who made his remarks
brief but full of feeling, paying tribute

been good and bright and beautiful and
full of promise. The speaker referred
to the cheer with which she had in
spired not only her own home, but all
those with whom she had come in con-
tact, and invoked the comfort of a
higher power for the bereaved parents
and household.

miliar songs that were dear to Miss
Pardee and her parents, were sung by
the quartet of the First congregational
church, Mrs. Carroll Nicholson, con
tralto; Mrs. Alma Bergeland Winches-
ter, soprano; Howard Pratt, tenor, and
III. D. Mustard, basso.


The beautiful Pardee home was made
still more so by the endless banks of
flowers that filed the interior and were
everywhere visible. each a silen ex-
preston of the widespread sympathy
felt throughout the state for the be-
reaved family. A great cluster of red
roses, which Miss Pardee loved, was
the message from her Alpha Phi sisters
of the state university, and a similar
offering came from Doctor Pardee's 5
brother Masons. Both the chamber of
commerce and the Oakland club. in
which Doctor and Mrs. Pardee had
taken active parts, closed their doors
during the funeral hours and suspended
business.


> The body was inferred in the family
vaule at Mountain View cemetery. the
services there being private. The pail
bearers were young friends of both

streets drying his clothes.

landed.

passing down the Delaware bay last

water into the hold. The captain
did not believe the fire would amount

last night following a mass meeting
called to protest against the introduce
ton of pay-as-you-enter cars by the

principal car lines Of the city two weeks
ago. 1t caused general dissatisfaction
because. it was asserted. the company
failed to provide proper cars.

A mass meeting was called for last
night at Massey Hall. The call was
issued by the board of control through
Mayor Geary, and was intended merely
to voice a protest against the innova-
ton. Many fiery speeches were made,
however, and upon leaving the build
Ing the audience became q mob
They attacked the street cars, dragged
of the conductors and motormen, and
then proceeded to wreck the cars. All
available police were called out, but
they were unable to control the situa-
ton.


Mayors Appeal Vain.


Mayor Geary personally appealed to
several sections Of the mob, begging
them to desist and go home. His pleas
were ignored


Twelve cars were wrecked and the
windows in 100 others were smashed.
Eighteen persons were injured. Rioting
ceased at midnight. Twelve arrests

SANTA MONICA, June 13.-Narrow-
ly escaping destruction on the rocks
of the Malibu, toward which their
boat was drifting, three Italian fisher
men from San Pedro tonight owe their
lives to K. Ogura and S. Tani, Japan
ese boys, who went to their rescue.
Unaware of their danger, the fisher
men, Mike Nyoncichi and two COM
panions, were sleeping peacefully In
the bottom of their boat when Ogura
and Tani reached them.


Nyoncichi and his fellow fishermen
arrived here last night in launch on
an all-night run from San Pedro.
They passed the day sleeping in a
little dory attached to the launch,
which was moored near the long wharf.
In some manner the dory became freed
from the lavnch and drifted north
ward toward the jagged rocks, which
meant certain disaster if it went
ashore. Their predicament was dis
covered by other fishermen at the
wharf and the Japanese boys were
notified. Without hesitation they
launched a small boat and rowed rap
idly toward the dory of the slumber-
ing Italians, reaching them just in
time to awaken them and warn them
Of their peril.

shot a hole through the pillow and
placed an empty rifle shell on the floor
seems probable in the light of testi-
mony yesterday afternoon.

that the health officers took sufferers to
the ships to secure their eyes and hearts
for the compounding of medicine and the
health officers were assaulted. Rioting

Corps was called out to protect foreign
ers and property.


The recent outbreak against foreigners

nastic followers.

was not until 5000 troops were sent that
the uprising was suppressed. Churches
and property were destroyed in Leinchow
and Sanchang. but no foreigners lost
their lives.

SPOKANE, Wash, Aug. 25.-A spe-
cial to the Spokesman Review from
Tekoa, Wash, says: James Rhine of
Missoula, who was one of a party of
fifty fire fighters working near Avery,
Idaho, of whom twenty perished last
Sunday, arrived here tonight and told
the story of his perils.


The crew were on hill four miles
from the cook camp and two miles
from Avery. On Sunday afternoon they
were warned to flee for their lives by
a man who rushed past them with a
warning that they had no time to lose.


The fifty men started down noun
tain side three miles long and very
steep. Ahead of them the gale blew
furiously, tearing down trees and
throwing them across the trail, but no
one was injured.


Arriving at the cook camp they
found it deserted and notice tackled
up warning all to leave while there was
time. The men ran to a point where
the fire had burned off the timber. All
but twenty-three men then started for
the railroad.


The next morning before daylight
three of the men who had been left
behind arrived at Avery. The others
fingered too long and were swallowed
by the moving furnace.


OF the dead Mr.. Rhine knew the
name of but one man (Murphy), whom
he remembered because the men all
liked him.

witness the death of thirty Italian fire
fighters without being able to help
them; how they saw them huddled to-

men to death, leaving after the smoke
arose only a heap of black objects.

hundred yards above them were thirty
italians lighting a blaze which was
coming down the canyon. The creek
bed was dry where the Italians were
working, but there was little water
below where Miller and Weston were
stationed.

flame had caught her fiimsy robe and
was spreading rapidly. Falling to the
floor she rolled upon the blaze.

quickly put out the fire.

standing up. Women were screaming

1t was all over in q moment. and when

not injured she was greeted with loud
cheers and applause. Then she. resumed
her dance.

before noon today, a large whale en-
tered the harbor, and for short time
entertained the passengers on the fer
ryboat Sausalito by playing his huge
bulk in the choppy waves almost along
side the craft.


The discovery was first made by
James Hinman, whose experiences on
the whaling vessels which have left this
port for the past few years have given
him a keen sight for leviathans.


AS the Sausalito was proceeding qui-
etly along her course Hinman suddenly
jumped to his feet, and, dancing along
the lower deck to the rear of the boat,
yelled.


"There she blows!"


Immediately there was a rush to the
vessels side, everyone being eager to
get glimpse of the rare visitor, which,
after giving one more roll, and then for
good measure a switch or its tail, dived
and disappeared.

Recent consular reports indicate that
American interests in Liberia are reviv-
ing. Data of our commerce with that
country have had a special place in the
monthly official returns of exports and
imports. The amounts are small, but
they are growing. Exports rose from
s49,S63 in 1908 to 1854 in 1909. I'm
ports in 1909 were nominal. AS early
as the fifteenth century Liberia was
the first country to send cotton cloths
to northern and western Europe. That
industry is reviving for home consump-
ton in a recent report.


The population amounts to 1850, 900.
No white man is allowed to hold land
or to acquire citizens rights. Slavery
is Illegal. Complete religious tolera-
ton exists. English money is current,
though accounts are kept in dollars and
cents. English weights and measures
are used.


miles A large proportion of the peo-
pie speak English. The government
is modelled after that of the United
States, says the New York Sun. Mon
rovia, the capital and port. population
5000, is on Cape Mesurado.


Iron ore abounds in Liberia, and cop
per and other metals are found Cot
ton f1ourishes, and sugar cane and cof-
fee are easily produced. The most i'm



wood, teak. mahogany, hickory, poplar.
birthstone wood ESQ called because of
its yellow COLOR, sassa wood and many
other woods valuable in shipbuilding
and cabinet work. Ebony. camwood
and other dye woods, the acacia, which
yields gum arabic, and the copal trees
are found. There are several useful
varieties of palm, especially the nut
bearing palm from which palm oil is
made. The country is rich in medicinal
plants, among them the copaiba tree,
which gives croton oil, and the castor
oil plant. Several varieties of maize
and rice of excellent quality are cul-
tivated, and good crops of wheat, bar
ley and oats have been raised. The
vegetables are almost endless in their
variety-almost every kind of garden
vegetable known in America. The
fruits are numerous and fine, including
the mango, lemon, lime, orange, guava,
tamarind, pomegranate, cocoanut, plan
tain. banana, rose apple, African cherry.
pineapple, avocado pear and the Afri-
can peach. Wild animals, formerly
abundant, are now rarely seen.


The Liberians build coasting vessels
and possess ships trading with Great
Britain and the United States. A large
number of the inhabitants of the At
rican interior depend upon Liberia for
their supply OF European and American
goods. The more important articles of
export are coffee, sugar, palm oil and
palm kernels, cocoa, arrowrOOt, caout-
chouc, IVORY and kola nuts. The
yearly foreign commerce amounts to

The crows were once beautiful birds,
loved and admired by all the fowls Of the
air. The crows Of that time dressed in
the most gorgeous coiors and their heads
were decorated with red feathers that
glistened like fire when the sun reflected
upon II. The crows had many servants
who attended upon them. The wood
peckeT was the head servant. and his
helpers were the sap suckers, yellow ham
mers, and the linnets. They faithfully
performed their duty OF eombing the
beautiful heads of the crows. and would
Row and then pluck feather from the
crows head and stick It in their own. at
the same time making the excuse that
they were pulling at a snarled feather
or picking nits from his head


So one day the crows got very angry
at losing their beautiful feathers from
their heads, and when the servants heard
Of this they Immediately formed a plot
against the crows.


So one morning as the servants were
attending upon the crows they over
powered them and plucked all OF their
red feathers from their heads and rolled
them in heap Of charcoal, thus color
ing them black to this very day Any
one can see for himself the crows are
not on friendly terms with their former
servants. for they still possess the red
heads that the crows once had.

ANGELS CAMP, Sept. 27.--Hiram w.
Johnson, Republican nominee for gov
ernor, finished here tonight the most
strenuous day he has had since the be-
ginning of his present campaign tour.


Since early morning he has been on
the road over the mountains in his
automobile. He made nine speeches and
crossed the greater part Of three coun-
ties.


rhe reception accorded the Republi-
can leader in Eldorado. Amador and
Calaveras counties has been enthus1-
astic. Before reaching Plymouth, where
the first speech was made to about 100
men gathered on the main street, john
son was met by two automobile loads
of Republicans from Sutter Creek and
Jackson, who accompanied him until
late In the afternoon, when he crossed
from Amador county into Calaveras.


other speeches were made during the
morning at Dry Town, Amador City
and Sutter Creek, where practically the
entire population was out. School was
dismissed all along the route Of the
ride, and hundreds of children were In
the various audiences.


Johnson stopped for lunch at Jackson
and made an address of half an hour
from the porch of the National hotel.
His afternoon stops we're at Mokelumne
Hill and San Andreas, and tonight he
made two addresses in Angels Camp.
The opera house could not hold half the
crowd that gathered to hear him, and
following the meeting Johnson ap-
peared on the main street and talked
to hundreds gathered there.

text:
TACOMA, Sept. 27.--The Democratic
state convention, after hot fight
over some features, adopted today a
radical platform on general issues. 1t
demands actual reduction of the tar
iff, physical valuation of railroads,
control of express companies, election
of senators by direct vote, and apply
ing the Oregon plan until the national
constitution is amended


The platform favors a progressive
inheritance tax, graduated income
tax, direct nominations, the recall and
the initiative and the referendum. It
also demands that money received
from the sale of national resources be
used for the benefit of the state in
which they are situated.


The initiative and referendum, recall
and Oregon plan met with strong op-
position, but motion to strike them
out was almost unanimously defeated.

PASADENA, Nov. 13.-Long Beach
high school and Throop academy foot
ball teams played to game yester-
day on Throop's field. Most of the
game was played in a drizzling rain.
The first and second quarters were
characterized with perfectly clean play
ing, but there was enough rough work
in the last half to make up for sew
eral games, Long Beach besting Throop
slightly in this manner OF play.


In the first quarter Long Beach used
the forward pass four or five times for
long gains. Throop, with Herds boot
ing, gained from ten to twenty yards
on each exchange of punts. The quar-
ter was played through with no time
out.


The second quarter of the game went
fairly even until near the end Of the
period, when Long Beach punted forty
yards from the 20-yard line, and Call
of Throop carried the ball back twenty
five yards. Herd place kicked for
Throop from the S5-yard line. Follow
ing a few minutes punting back and
forth, the period ended with the ball
in the center of the field.


In the third period Keats of Long
Beach carried the ball back to the CEN
ter Of the field following Throop's 40
yard kickoff. With a succession of
forward passes Long Beach took the
ball to dangerous territory for Throop.
The latter recovered and punted the
ball into Long Beach territory. Throop
was penalized twenty yards for side
line coaching. With long gains through
the line they took the ball to the 95-
yard line, where Herd tried a place
kick and failed. Throop recovered the
ball on the 25-yard line, gained five
yards and place kicked from the 20
yard line. After an exchange of punts
the ball was within fifteen yards of
Throop's goal when the period ended.


Referee Rheinschild called the game
on account of darkness, and after nu-
merous verbal forward passes," Long
Beach prevailed on Throop to continue
the game. After a few minutes play
in the fourth period Long Beach scored
a touchdown following several forward
passes from the 15-yard line, where the
ball was put in play. A kicked goal
tied the game
