WOODLAND, Dec. 5.-Word was re-
ceived here today that the supreme
court has reversed its former ruling
in the celebrated sidewalk case.


About five years ago D. Balfour and
". P. Wilbur put down sidewalks in
front of their property. A short time
afterward the city council ordered side
walks put down for the entire district
in which Wilbur and Balfour lived.
These two refused to pay their pro
rata Of the cost, claiming they were
not benefited inasmuch as they already
had sidewalks. Both were, sued by the
city.


Balfour's case came up first and the
lower court held he did not have TO
pay the assessment. The supreme
court reversed the decision and de-
manded that the lower court find for
the city.


Wilbur's case was tried afterward,
and Judge Hawkins held that he did
not have to obey the mandate of the
supreme court in the Balfour case, and
that Wilbur did not have to pay the
assessment. The supreme court sus-
tained this decision, reversing its de-
cree in the Balfour case

a failure, Mrs Charles Henry Israels,
editor of "The Survey" a journal of
philanthropy, said in an address be-
fore the Young Women's Union, 422
Bainbridge street. that the remedy
for present conditions is the establish

pal dancing academy.


All of us are interested in the work

she said 1--WE inquire as to the work

hours The sewing circles and millin-
cry classes for working girls have
failed, because a girl who makes tucks
from morning till night all the year
around, is not interested in embroider-
ing at night. She wants to meet
friends and make the acquaintance of
members of the opposite sex, and she
naturally drifts into the dance hall.

now asking the city to establish mu-
nicipal dancing academies This, she
declared, is the only practical solution

are led astray and find their way into
white slave dens.

MADRID, Oct. 5.-Premier Canale-
jas tonight made public the following
accounts of events in Lisbon, which
he had just received:


About 1880 a. m. Tuesday the pop
ulation of Lisbon were awakened by
the booming of cannon. Everybody
rushed into the streets or opened win
dows to see what was happening. The
streets rapidly filled with people, rush
ing hither and thither, while the bu-
giles sounded the assembly


Here and there rifles cracked and
shouts of rallying cries were heard.
The revolution had broken out and
the twenty-one guns was the signal
for the mobilization of the police. They
threw themselves gallantly upon the
insurgents, but were received with a
fusillade of small bombs. Seeing that
they were powerless, the police sum-
moned the troops, but the soldiers
soon split into two bands, one going
over to the side of the revolutionists,
the other remaining faithful to dis
cipline and monarchy.


"A fierce engagement soon devel-
oped. officers and soldiers dropped
dead or wounded in large numbers.
Artillerymen served the guns with
desperate energy. The revolutionists
succeeded in seizing the barracks con-
tiguous to the royal palace where King
Manuel was staying. The king was
informed of what had occurred and
left the building, accompanied by four
confidential attendants, who took him
to a place of safety.


"The battle continued to rage in the
streets. The revolutionists had thrown
up barricades and sent detachments to
hold bridges and telegraph lines. Dur
ing the day detachments Of troops
from provincial garrisons arrived in
Lisbon and Joined the soldiers who had
remained loyal, so that the rival forces
practically were equal"


Premier Canalejas, in giving out this
statement, said:


81 believe Queen Amelie has not left
the palace at Cintra, and l know that
in the other Portuguese provinces the
seditious movement has received little
support"


At midnight the government received
further advices confirming that the
revolutionary movement originating in
Lisbon had gained no ground in the
provinces.


The Radical club tonight illuminated
it's building in celebration of the ris-
ing. It's members sang the Mersel-
laise, while the public collected under
the windows. The police entered the
club and turned out everybody. The
clubmen then marched to Puerto del
Sol, where the police again dispersed
them. One of the men was arrested.
Beyond this incident, all is quiet in
both Madrid and the provinces.


Details of the lighting in Lisbon in
dicate that two regiments, one of which
was artillery, in conjunction with citi-
zens and thousands of peasants, who
arrived from the country the night be-
fore, maintained a bloody battle on
Tuesday with a loyalist regiment.


They soon were joined by another
regiment and the numbers of the re-
volutionists were swelled hour by hour


Members of the cabinet went to
Necessidades place and implored the
king to flee for safety, for they were
unable to answer for his life.


The first step Of the revolutionist
troops was to dynamite the railroad
bridges and thus prevent the arrival of
loyalist Troops.

NEW YORK, November 16-How hero
| ism and steadfast hope won in the face
| Of apparent disaster was told yesterday
| by the crew. whose rescue from the sink
| ing schooner Lucy E. Friend was re-
| lated briefly in dispatches. Capt. and
Mrs. Frank E. Lowry, Byron Wallace, a
steward, and four negro sailors. who
composed the crew Of the lost schooner,
arrived here on board the Livingstone, of
| the Atlantic Fruit Company's line. An
interesting member Of the rescued group
| was a French poodle, a pet of Mrs.
Lowry.


1.-THE Lucy E. Friend, a three-masted
schooner. lat feet long and registering
All tons, left Newport News last Satur-


day with a cargo q pig iron. bound for
Bridgeport. Conn. All went well until
and heavy sea rose. The schooner,
which was of the coast of Maryland, was
pounded heavily and her hull, more than


twenty-eight years old, sprang leak.
Woman Helps in Pumping.
Two steam pumps were set to work and
later two hand pumps, but these made no
Roadway against the water that steadily
was filing the vessel. Mrs. Lowry took
her turn with the negro sailors. Wallace,


the steward, although seventy years old,
also did his part.


When the water had risen so high that
1t put the steam pumps out of commission
kCapt Lowry ordered the pig iron thrown
overheard. Mrs. Lowry worked with the
others until her hands were SO torn by
| the heavy pieces of rough metal that she
could lift no more.


Toward evening two steamships passed
the schooner. but no attention was paid
| to her signals Of distress At midnight
Capt. Lowry set fire to several tar barrels.
An hour later the lights of the Living
stone were seen. But the schooner was
settling and Capt. Lowry ordered his wife
and crew to take to the yawl. Mrs. Lowry
| tied her pet cat and dog In separate bags
| and tried to take them with her. The cat
| jumped overheard, however, in its sack
| and disappeared.


Yawl Beyond Reach.
Before the captain and steward could
leave the schooner the yawl was washed
| out Of reach and they had to jump over
board in the darkness. although neither
could swim. By good fortune they caught
ropes thrown to them from the small boat
and were drawn aboard. Half an hour
| later the crew was lifted on board the
| Livingstone.


Capt Lowry is from Portland, Me. He
has been at sea for thirty-nine Of his
forty mine years The schooner was about
thirty miles east of the Winter Quarter
lights, on the coast of Virginia, where
| she was abandoned.

DENVER, Sept. 2S.-State legislators

that State Auditor Roady Kenehan
had refused to honor the second APP
preparation bill passed by the legis-
lature, allowing $4,000 for its own ex-
penses. The bill as approved by the
governor, read that the sum "shall be
paid out of moneys not already APP
propriated," the conventional form Of
appropriation bills.

the regular session of the legislature
had appropriated every cent in sight
and all the money available for two
years. Until the bill is brought back
and amended, therefore, or new bill
passed, the legislators and employees
will be without pay.

MADISON, Wis, Sept. 2S.-For the
last five years the first word to be
said about Badger football prospects
was that they were ''most promising
of a championship team" This year
they are the exact opposite. For five
years, from a promising start, the
Badgers have finished in disaster, and
the prayer this year is that the rule
of opposites will prevail.


Prospects here are about as bad as
can be. Only one veteran, Alfred
Buser is eligible, and only three others,
Captain Dean, Center Arpin and Guard
Macmiller, have a chance to take spe-
cial examinations to remove scholastic
conditions. Halfback Culver, FullbaclS
Wilce, Quarterback Fucik and Tackles
Boyle and Osthoff have graduated.


The scholastic ban also rests upon
the best of last seasons freshman
eleven, including the two Lampere
boys, Lloyd and Hanberg. 1t is be-
lieved that these young stars can
square themselves with the faculty.


Keckie Moll is In great condition, but
all to the bad in his class work, and
he declares that he is looking for q
Job as a high school coach and will
not return to the university.


Assuming that the conditions can be
worked off, the leading candidates for
the varsity eleven will be Captain Dean
and johnson, ends; Buser, Pierce,
Arpin and Macmiller, linemen; Ander
son and Lampert, halfbacks; Lloyd,
quarterback, and Tanberg, fullback.


Coach Barry and Captain Dean claim
the season is too young for them to tell
who will make up the team, but they
admit that faculty action and gradua-
tion have spread dire poverty of ma
terial over the Wisconsin situation this
season.

STOCKTON. Aug. 19.-Joseph Co
oaugh Waugh. aged %. and Miss Alice
Letitia Floyd, aged 10, both of Stock
ton, were principals in near marriage
affair last night that bordered very
closely on the line between a practical
joke and the stern reality.


The affair went so far as the issu-
ance Of marriage licence and the sum-
moning of Justice A. c. Parker. The
tying Of the marital knot was started
when Waugh most seriously declared
that it had gone far enough


The young people. who have been
acquainted only two weeks, were in
company with the young lady's aunt,
Marguerite +. Nolan, and friend, Mrs.
L. Tanner, about o'clock last evening
when Chief Deputy County Clerk Fred
II. Johnson happened by in his buggy.
he stopped and conversed with the
members Of the party, and some one
Jocularly asked him whether he would
issue marriage license to Waugh and
Miss Floyd


Certainly I will" said Johnson


The dare was made and the parties
started toward the courthouse. John
son expected them to turn back before
they had proceeded very far, but they
continued on and followed him up
stairs in the courthouse to the county
clerks office He unlocked the doors,
and invited them inside.


The customary questions were asked
and the license book opened. Thinking
the joke had reached its climax, the
clerk inquired:


You really want me to issue a IL
cense?"


Both answered in the affirmative and
the document was made out. They
signed the license and the seal was
affixed.


Send for Justice Parker" suggested
one of the party.


Ten or fifteen minutes later the jus
tice appeared. He was introduced to
the couple and informed they wanted
to be married. He asked them whether
that was their wish, and they told
him it was.


You wish the ring ceremony" in
quired Justice Parker


They stated they would dispense with
that formality, and he added:


You will join hands"


The young Lady thrust out her hand
toward Waugh. but he did not respond.
Something had to be done and it was
apparently up TO" Waugh.


This has gone far enough" he
stammered.


All joined in joking him. even the
young lady. The party finally departed,
leaving Johnson out So for the marriage
license and Justice Parker minus the
fee

WITH the disappearance of the old


w southern Christmas there vanished
two holiday customs which are now moth
ing more than "reminiscences. One was
the John Coonahs'' parade, the OTTER
the 'gander pulling The former was

Florida and New Orleans.


The coonahs made their appearance
some time during Christmas week. They
were a band of negroes, dressed pic
turesquely to the point of weirdness, but
with the general characteristic Of being
ragged. The majority were armed with
banjos. bones, flies, drums, castanets and
all sorts of instruments. At their head
was a leader, the most gaudily arrayed
and armed with whip. The procession
made its way frrin one plantation to
another, taking in all in the neighbour
hood.


When a plantation was reached the
leader would crack his whip. At the sig
nal all the instruments would start up
the Coonah song would burst forth from
many lips and the dancers would spring
from the lines. Faster and faster would
sound the barbaric music and faster and
faster would fly the nimble feet until,
dropping out one by one. only the leader
and one other would be left TO show their
best steps.


When this had been concluded an oid
negro would pass around his hat to re-
ceive the shower of coins he knew would
be waiting for him. Then the little folks
OF the great house would come out
with raisins, nuts, fruits and other Christ
mas goodies for the eXpectant crowd.
After the excitement Of gathering them
up had subsidized the leader would crack
his whip again and off he procession
would wind TO the next plantation.


The "gander pulling was Eastime OF
the backwoods of Alabama. This is also
credited to North Carolina over a CEN
tury ago. The game consisted in hang
ing a gander, usually aged, from pole
set in a vacant field. The contestants,
all of whom must be mounted. would
have to gaIlop past the Sander and try
to pull it's head off. AS the animals head
was we'll creased. and as a man usually
stood close by to urge tagging nass into
a gallop the efforts were many and the
results mostly ludicrous But finally one
would succeed in securing the coveted
head and would thereby win the prize

When Mrs. A. Morris Lowe, tour

terms in California penitentiaries.

ficers began Investigations and found

Mrs loves apartments, where he had
hidden while watching an opportunity
to enter the rooms. Other roomers
said Brown answers the description of
a man who has been lettering about
that neighborhood for the past several
days.


The police records show Brown was

source of supply his capture is doubt
fu.

afternoon comes as the climax of the
sensational man hunt that has been
carried on for the last three days.
News that two Japanese had been seen
at a cabin near a deserted mine this
morning lent fresh zest to the pursuit,
and a posse quickly left for the place
where the Japanese had been seen.
On the way the horse ridden by
Stanley Hackett of Chicago, who had
ioined the posse. stumbled and fell, car
rving his rider with him. Hackett suf-

side. Haekett hobbling behind him,
emptying his revolver as he ran.

ridge. and those familiar with the

off his retreat, believed the man cor
nered. When the posse reached the

cliff. swinging from rock to rock with
superhuman agility.


According to Hackett, the japanese
had evidently hidden not more than
100 yards from the trail taken by the
posse.


Unaware of Hackett's mishap, and
believing that his pursuers had passed,
he emerged from his hiding place IN
the bushes, and catching sight OF
Hackett fed up the mountainside.

BY Telegraph 10 The Tribune


Poughkeepsie, n. Y. June 25.-The ex-
pected and the unexpected happened on
the Hudson this afternoon: Cornell
swept the river, as the most confident Of
her admirers believed she would. and
Pennsylvania had the crew that gave
battle to the veteran and well trained
oarsmen from Ithaca to the end.


Rowed in the dark, with the water
rough, and under conditions that could
hardly have been worse, Pennsylvania
suddenly jumped into fame. For three
miles, and all through that gruelling,
heartrending fourth, the Pennsylvanians
fought the Cornell eight, losing out at
the finish by less than half length
after as stirring and wonderful a squirt
as any crew has ever made on the Hud-
son.


Columbia, which has been second to
the winners for the three preceding re-
gattas, was left behind at the tWomile
mark, when Cornell and Pennsylvania
forged to the front and fought it out to
the finish The New York crew was not
outclassed; it simply did not have the
Drawn and muscle in the shell to carry
it through the rough and heavy going
of the course far out in the middle of the
stream. Syracuse and Wisconsin were
left in the ruck and lost in the gloom
that surrounded the crews when they
swept across the line.


Race a Brilliant Duel.


The race was a brilliant duel between
Cornell and Pennsylvania, with the tide
OF fortune favoring the one and then
Just as quickly switching to the other. 1t
was much the same as race here three
years ago, when Columbia had her sec
ond birth and came into prominence In
rowing after years Of obscurity. When
the two crews swept under the bridge,
that monument of the strength and
weakness of all crews that row under
it. there was nothing in the form dis
pIayed by either to indicate the victor
The Ithacans tried their famous spurt
but they mad once again found crew
that could match that squirt with one
equally good There was momen-
tary gain for the Cornell shell, but 1t
was momentary only, for the Red and
Blue oarsmen gamely responded to the
call of their coxswain and sent up their
stroke.


The Pennsylvania shell kept shooting
along in the same even tenor which had
marked its progress all the way down
the course. and for another half mile
the Quakers hung to the Cornell shell
with the perseverance of bulldog; but
age and weight told at the three and a
half mile mark, and then the Ithacans
made the bid that pulled them half
length ahead and kept them there to the
finish. which was shrouded in the murk
and gloom of an evening mist.


Cornell Makes a Clean Sweep.


IT was a Cornell day from first to last.
E,verything went the Ithacans' way, the
four-oared race, the freshman race ana
the varsity race Cornell supporters
had all they could do to contain them
solves when their crews swept down the
stream to victory in the first two races
When the crews We're lost IN the dark
ness near the finish line in the race of
tho day and it became impossible to dis
.;reuish who had won, their confidence
NAV have wavered for moment. but
tbe flashing signals and bursting bombs
,,,,ickIv told the story of another Cornell
SWEEP" and the JOY of the Ithacans
knew no bounds


Aside from the wonderful perform
a,ces made by the Cornell crews, the
poughkeepsie regatta of 1910 will go
down as a colossal piece of misnianage-
,,ent Had 1t not been for the rowing
os the crews, once they were started

bred yards.

boats will be pulled off before the close
of the regatta.

An unsinkable, $4,000, armor plate,
forced steel target lies at the bottom
of the sea near Manila, and the whole
United States navy department is
scratching its official head and wonder
ing how it happened. And at that the
answer is simple: Uncle Sans tars
took to firing at the nonsinkable affair.
1t was a case of "Toot, toot! Good
by!'


This is the news that has been re-
ceived by naval officials at Mare island.


The squadron of the Pacific fleet, sta
toned at and around Manila bay, eight
cruisers in all took to practicing No
vember %, and the new steel target
sent from the Brooklyn navy yard,
shipped to the Philippines in sections
and put together there, was hauled out
to the firing line for the initial trial.
The usual wooden targets got full of
holes and went to the bottom, and the
navy department sent out this new
tangled affair because it was air cham
bered, and, among other things, the
navy department fondly believed it
would never Sink.


First of all, the cruiser Charleston
swung up into position, carrying a
bone in her teeth. and the boys in the
turrets took good squint at the pat
ent target Then they spat on their
hands and, as the wardog circled and
steamed back along its course, turned
loose with the port six inch gun. 1t
was jolly broadside and the target
was noted to become restless and shake
itself as the shots came out.


Next came the starboard six inch
battery, and the target just naturally
gave up Men piled into the launches
and steamed toward the steel affair,
but the launch could not travel fast
enough When the boat was still sew
eral hundred yards away there was a
gurgle and gasp. and the $4,000 target
just naturally started for the bottom
of the sea. The Charleston had pune
tured each of its air chambers

prise that the Easter" eggs. Will
bring


They will not be cold storage eggs
either" said the warden. THE cons
need an innovation now and then to
break the monotony of their lives

decorating the prison chapel for the

e. o. Jones, the night superintendent,

badly burned and bruised. All the

Two girls from Buffalo-Mary Meni,
ten years old. and Nelsie Beforpa, eight
were found unconscious in a Lackawanna
freight car at Secaucus. n. J., yesterday
after a narrowing experience On Tues
CAV afternoon the children were play
ing in the Lackawanna freight yards at
Buffalo. when they were told by some boys
that if they would climb into one of the
cars they would find some fine bananas.
The children got into the car, and they
had no sooner done than the boys
locked the door and ran away. The chill
dren beat on the door and cried for help,
but no one heard them. The car soon
started for Secaucus.


When the children did not return to
their homes their relatives notified the


police in Buffalo, who learned that the
missing girls had been seen playing about
the freight yards and suspected that they


had been carried off in a car. Word was
sent TO the Lackawanna offices The yard


master at SecauCus was ordered to search
all the cars on their arrival from Buffalo.


The children were found lying in cor


ner of the car with their arms around


each other. They were unconscious, and


at first il was feared that life was ex-
tinct They were taken to the Young
Mems Christian Association headquarters


at Secaucus and DR.. Ring was summoned.
The physician had great difficulty in re-
viving the children, but finally brought
them around. They were then turned over


to the Lackawanna officials pending in
structions from Buffalo.

OAKLAND, May 6.-While playing
house" this morning with a toy lamp
as part of her equipment, 8 year old
Agnes Camorra of 2S3 Third street,
lost her life when the oil she had
poured into the lamp exploded. She
was hght1ng. the lamp, as she had
seen her mother do, little thinking that
her clothes would be set afire.


The child's mother was away from
home, having to work in a cannery be-
cause her husband deserted her some
time ago. Only the aged grandmother,
Mrs. Maria Fernandez. was present to
take care of the tot and she was out
OF the room when the explosion oc-
CURED.


Some one gave the child a toy lamp
a few days ago, with capacity of only
few teaspoonfuls of coal OIL and with
no wick. This morning, after her
mother had gone to work, she stole
into the cupboard, took down the
can and poured the oil into her lamp.
Then she applied a lighted match


Her shrieks brought Mrs. Fernandez
into the room. The grandmother
wrapped a blanket about the girl and
rushed out-of the house. Two strangers
were passing in a buggy, and Mrs.
Fernandez stopped them and fairly
threw her granddaughter into the We
hlcle, while she shouted directions to
drive to the receiving hospital.


The strangers did so at full speed.
but without avail. The girls body
had been frightfully burned and she
expired short time after reaching the
hospital. An effort was made to get
her mother to the child's side before
she died, but when she arrived at
the hospital she was confronted by the
charred remains of her lifeless child

scramble to escape from the flames which
destroyed Young's Hotel at Winthrop
Beach early today a mother and her son
leaped from the windows and We're SO
frightfully injured that probably neither
can recover, the thirty-five remaining
guests escaping uninjured. The hotel
was burned to the ground, together with
the garage in the rear and two adjoin-
ing cottages known as the Idle Hour and
the Commonwealth. The total loss prob
ably will be considerably in excess of
$4,000


The injured are Mrs. John c. c. Beggs
and her son, John c. Beggs, jr., aged
seventeen years, of Springfield. They
were asleep on the second floor of the
building when the fire broke out. at ?
am. They rushed out into the hall and
started down the stairs. Then suddenly
they turned back with the evident pur-
pose of recovering something from their
apartments.


Jump to Sidewalk.


When they returned the halls were
filling with smoke, and thinking that
escape was impossible save through the
windows, they again retraced their steps
and frantic with terror jumped to the
sidewalk below.


Both were unconscious when picked
up. At the hospital to which they were
taken it was found that their injuries
would probably prove fatal. The boy
sustained fractured skull. Mrs. Beggs
had both Of her thighs broken. her right
knee pan splintered and her left foot
dislocated.


Shore Drive Threatened.


The fire was the most obstinate with
which the Winthrop department has had
to deal in years. Aid was sent from
Boston and Revere. and not until am.
was the blaze under control. For a time
the entire shore drive, on which the hotel
was located, and which Is lined with cot
tages, was threatened.


The blaze originated in a linen closet
over the furnace.

NEW YORK, September 2O-Dixie Kid,

Nelson last night at the Olympic Athletic

his belt. as he expected to, before he sails
for Paris. The colored boxer was pretty
badly beaten by his white opponent. Dixie
Kid Will probably enjoy easy picking
among the Paris clubs, as did Willie
Lewis, but there are several velters around
New York who will give him a good fight
whenever he comes home.

night than he has been for some time,
and his condition and stamina earned him
the decision. He received much punish
ment, but was always able to stand 1t
and always came back for more. The
bout, on the whole, was fast one from
the second round, but Nelson forced the
pace and scored the most telling blows.


The Dixie Kid exhibited quite a bit of
wildness, much more than usual. but
this was due to the bad scare he received
to the canvas by quick right to the
jaw that bewildered the spectators equal
ly as much as the recipient.


The round had just opened, and after
the men had been separated from a clinch
they both squared off and were feinting
at lon. range, when the white boxer saw
a quick chance and sent In the punch that
sent the colored'man to the floor.
This gave Nelson a good start over
Dixie Kid and he continued to force
the work all the way and never let up
The first round was the only tame session
of the ten. as both men were slow to get
into action.

Roosevelt party, bringing news that

rhinoceros family, besides considerable
lesser game. Quentin Grogan, who was
reported ill earlier, has recovered, and
the others of the party are in excellent
health.

February 8. Nimule is to the north, in
the province of the Nile, and will be
reached by boats up the river Bar-eI-
Jebel. The party had an interesting
experience on their second day at
Rhino camp. A grass fire accidentally
started threatened to burn up the
whole outfit, which was saved only by
the energetic work of all hands.

rancher. So many adventures have be-

ming several hours from dogs who were

buck. 1t came YEARLY across the field
and tried to force it's way through a
picket fence that skirts the front yard
of the McAdams home In some man
ner its head became wedged between
two pickets.

endeavoring TO break into her fathers
garden, ran down to drive him away.
Selling a picket she struck the ex-
hausted animal over the head, break
ing one of its horns. The tired deer
tried to back away, but at the next
blow it dropped dead.

two days In trying TO escape alive out
Of the fire zone.

Point on a ST. Paul train, which for
miles ran through the forests between
two veritable walls of fire. So terrific
was the heat that at times the cars
took fire and rushed blazing through
the forests.


Monday night the entire train caught
fire and was consumed so quickly that
ali the passengers were. forced to
abandon their clothing and fed
through the forest on foot In their
night clothes. When Northern Pa.
cifc train picked them up their. condi-
ton was pitiable. They were brought
into Helena yesterday.


The refugees declare the havoc
wrought by the Idaho and western
Montana fires can scarcely be exag'
gerated For miles upon miles, they
said, they ran through burning forests,
unable to see in any direction on
account of the dense smoke. Every
where crops are burned. farmhouses
destroyed and settlements wiped out

danger.

Even more extraordinary was an
oversight of the foreign office many
years ago. The inhabitants of one of
the Palmeston islands, in the Pacific,
under our rule, were dependent for
much of their food-apart from what
their own island produced-on the
shipping supplies arranged for them
by our foreign office in Whitehall. But
for nine months not a ship came to
the islands, and as the extreme heat
was killing the cocoanut trees and
every other eatable fruit, the plight of
the islanders was desperate The peo-
pie were without food, and the actual
owner of the islands died from want;
whilst most of the residents were per-
ishing, and many had actually died,
when at last a vessel named The EN-
pire CHANGED to call, and thus enabled
them to get some food. Then it was
discovered that the Whitehall rulers
had entirely forgotten to arrange for
the usual supplies during that year.

SAN FRANCISCO, Feb. 11.-Jewelry
and clothing worn by the girl whose
skeleton was found on Mount Tamal-
pals February were identified yester-
day by four men as having belonged
to Anna Jensen, a domestic employed
in a local boarding house and who
has not been seen since April !, 1909.


THESE men. who lived at the board
ing house, which was conducted by
Miss Helma Carlson, and whose meals
were served by the Jensen girl for
several months, are positive in their
identification not only of the mountain
victims bracelet but are also certain
that the murdered woman's dress, hat,
watch and hair were those of the for
mer house servant.


Further they assert that the eSti-
mated height and weight of the victim
were the same as Anna Jensen's. One
of the identifiers recalls that Miss Jen-
sen, just before she left the boarding
house, purchased pair of shoes from
a San Francisco shop whose label was
found on the dead girls shoes.


Men Live Far Apart


The four men now live apart, and
none was aware of the fact yesterday
that the others had connected the
Tamalpais mystery with the Jensen
girl.


An effort will be made to trace the
movements of Miss Jensen after she
left the boarding house last April.


David Borland and George Brown,
who lived at the boarding house while
Miss Jensen was employed there, are
now in Los Angeles.


Another solution of the mystery is
advanced by Michael Jargans of San
Jose, who says he recognizes in the
clothing and jewelry Of the murdered
girl the effects of a Mrs. Rose Shook,
whom he brought to this country from
Germany eight years ago.


Last June, he says, Mrs Shook, then
a widow, came down from Seattle on
the steamer Watson, and during the
voyage she was married, with alleged
questionable ceremony, to a travelling
salesman. Later they were regularly
married. Since then she has not been
heard from.


Jargans' identification is said to be
the most minutely accurate yet made.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 20.-President
Taft and the members of the senate
and house are being besieged by aero
nautic enthusiasts, who are urging on
the authorities the necessity of sup
plying the military and naval forces
of the United States with war balloons
and aeroplanes.


1t has been pointed out to President
Taft and the legislators by General
James Allen, chief signal officer of
the army, in charge of the experiments
in aviation; Cortlandt Field Bishop,
and other men interested in the sub
ject that the United States is far be-
hind other nations in the matter of
military aeronautics.


The army of this country has one
dirigible balloon and two aeroplanes,
and the navy has none at all, whereas
Germany has now in military service
fourteen dirigibles of six different
models and five aeroplanes, France
has seven dirigibles and twenty-nine
aeroplanes, Italy three dirigibles and
seven aeroplanes, Russia three dirig-
ibles and six aeroplanes, Austria two
dirigibles and four aeroplanes, Eng
land two dirigibles and two aeroplanes
and Spain one dirigible and three aero
planes.


Altogether it is known that European
military and naval forces are today
equipped with thirty-two dirigibles and
fifty-six aeroplanes. One of the Brit
ish aeroplanes is the Cody machine, in
vented by Colonel S. f. Cody, formerly
an American citizen, but now Brit
ish subject.


The Japanese are devoting much
time and money to experimenting with
military balloons and aeroplanes, and
plan to equip their army with all mod
ern devices in the way of airships.

Gravesend and Belmont have been

SAN ANSELMO, June 1o-Mrs.
George Van Orden, wife of a well
known San Francisco dentist residing
here this summer narrowly escaped
death today with her two children and
a friend, Mrs. Charles Bluxtom, when
the horse which Mrs. Buxton was
driving became frightened at an auto
mobile and ran away, hurting the oc-
cupants from the carriage into the
roadside ditch.


Mrs. Van Orden and her two little
children. Edith and Allan, were in the
rear seat of the carriage when the ac-
cident happened. The horse reared and
plunged suddenly forward as the auto
mobile passed. Mrs. Buxton clung
bravely to the rens, but was unable
to hold the frightened animal Fear
ing that they would crash into a tele-
graph pole, Mrs. Buxton succ eeded in
forcing the horse over a sloping bank
into the ditch.


Although thrown to the ground, none
of the occupants was seriously injured.
Mrs. Van Orden held both little chill
dren in her arms as she fell and saved
them from being hurt. She received a
few bruises. as did Mrs. Buxton.

Time was when doctors used to bleed
weak and emaciated patients. and thus
make them weaker and more emaciated.
In those same good old days" consump-
tives were kept in close. unventilated
rooms and slowly put to death by mis-
directed kindness.


And in that same era SchoOlchildren
who lacked muscle and strength and were
less vigorous and healthy than their fell
lows were coddled at home, and in school
were kept near the hot stoves and away
from every draft of fresh air. They
breathed the vitiated atmosphere of the
ordinary schoolroom which had been
breathed over and again by all the other
scholars in the same room Every avenue
to good health was closed against them,
and most of them died.


What change has taken place I'm the
past few years. Doctors rarely, il ever,
bleed patients now. Consumptives are
turned out of doors, away from heaters
and stoves and registers and puny school
children are now taught in tents. in warm
weather and in cold, with no fires to burn
the oxygen out of the air and no other
walls than those Of thin canvas to protect
them from drafts.

SAN PEDRO, Nov. 80.-Flying the
flag of Japan, the cruisers Asama and
Kasagi are expected here early tomor-
row morning and will anchor in the
outer harbor for nine days. The cruis-
ers left San Francisco yesterday morn
ing, but are proceeding under slow
speed. A wireless received today stat
ed that they were at Santa Barbara,
and they will probably arrive here early
tomorrow morning.


AS the cruisers are being used for
training purposes, the stops made are
prolonged to permit the naval cadets to
observe the various places through
which the fleet passes The cruisers are
on their way to South America. The
Asama flies the ,admiraIs flag, the
cruiser being under command of Rear
manded them during the Russo-Japan-
ese war The Asama was in half a
dozen battles, and her commander was
distinguished for gallant action. In
one battle the after deck was shot away
by Russian shells.


Local Japanese are making much
preparation for the visit. There was
considerable excitement among the
boatmen this afternoon over the privi-
lege OF carrying visitors to the cruisers.
A few weeks ago X. Yamamoto, a jap
anese gardener employed by John T.
Gaffey, chartered all the launches of
the san Pedro Transportation company
for a Japanese syndicate to carry Wis
itors to the cruisers. With this he got
the exclusive landing privilege claimed
by the ferry company at the foot Of
Fifth street.


Although the Southern Pacific gave
an easement to the public over Fifth
street a few years ago, the ferry COM
pany claims the exclusive commercial
rights at the landing. Long Beach boat
owners who have been landing passen-
gers there threaten to enter the busi-
ness tomorrow and break the monopoly
of carrying passengers to the cruisers.
After much negotiating and interpret
ing this afternoon a compromise was
made by which the Long Beach boats
will honor tickets of the Japanese syn
dicate and pay Kamamoto 40 per cent
of the receipts.

SAN BERNARDINO, Jan. 5.--To re-
ward the brave act of Walter Baker,
the fireman of the ill-fated Southern
Pacific paper train, which Sunday
morning plunged into the Santa Ana
river near Cotton, an effort may be
made by fellow railroad men to secure
for him a Carnegie medal.


Baker not only saved the engineer,
John Rhinehardt, from watery grave,
but, risking his life among the waters
of the rushing torrent, swan to the
opposite bank and, tagging a passen-
ger train which was following, saved
it from destruction at the side of the
submerged engine already at the river
bottom.


After pulling Rhinehardt, who was
badly injured to the bank, Baker, re-
membering that their orders read that
another passenger train was following,
plunged into the seething river and
after a desperate struggle in the rush
ing waters, filled with floating trees
and stumps and lumber, reached the
opposite side.


He clambered from the icy waters
lust in time to halt the onComing pas
senger train, filled with passengers,
who never knew that it was only
through the act of the fireman in risk
ing his life in the torrent that their
lives were saved.

San Francisco, taking 500 tons of as
phalt from the Salt Lake wharf. To-
morrow the big steamer Lucy Neff will
sail for Seattle, having as ballast 300
tons of asphaltum.


The lumber-carrying fleet of steam
ers have little cargo on the return to
the north, but with the demand for
asphaltum and plaster on the northern
coast many of the steamers can now
secure an occasional cargo.

CLEVELAND, o., Sept 1.-Racing
with a fast Lake Shore mail train,
Glenn H. Curtiss, the aviator, today
drove his biplane over the water from
Cedar Point to Euclid Beach, an air
line distance of sixty miles, complet-
ing a 12O-mile round trip flight be-
gun yesterday and establishing an uh-
questioned worlds record for over
the water flights. He beat the train
into Cleveland by seventeen minutes.


Encountering contrary air currents,
Curtiss was unable to maintain high
speed, taking an hour and forty min
utes for the flight. The total distance
traversed, estimated at the United
States photographic office, was 64.75
miles.


The first ten miles were covered in
thirteen minutes, but after that the
breeze grew gusty,- necessltating many
dips and maneuyers. Off Cleveland
harbor the breeze blew only twelve
miles an hour, but was unsteady and
the 100000 persons lining the lake
front and perched on the tops of every
available building had opportunity to
Judge the difficulty of air navigation
under unfavorable conditions.


Tonight the aviator was entertained
at banquet given by the Cleveland
Aero club.

The problem OF protecting the forests
Of the country from fires Is receiving
considerable attention from associations
Of private owners. associations Of lum-
Der companies. State forest wardens. and
the national government. In spite OF all
that has been done. however. probably
60 per cent Of the private forests have no
adequate system of protection.


There are three classes of forest fires
surface fires. which burn the surface
layer Of leaves, dry grass, brush. and
small trees; ground fires. burning the
deep accumulation OF vegetable mold.
and crown fires. which accompany sur
face fires and burn the crowns Of the
trees


Surface fires are the most common.
and may start under ordinary dry condi-
lions. The severity Of the fire. Of course.
depends largely on the amount OF accu-
mulated leaves and brush and the
strength of the wind. Surface fires XIII
seedlings and young trees. but In many
cases do not kill the larger trees Under
some conditions they may kill everything
in the area which they cover.


Ground fires occur only when the vege-
table mold has become thoroughly dry.
They burn slowly. but with intense heat.
and are exceedingly difficult 20 extin-
guish. They have been known to burn
ali winter, creeping along under deep
layer Of snow. Ground fires usually de-
stroy all trees, killing the tissues Of the
roots. and the trees die and are blown
down.


Crown fires almost invariably accom-
pany surface fires, and occur only when
the woods are very dry and there is a
high wind Usually all trees Rre killed
Sometimes. however, where there are a
great many hardwoods in mixture with
coniferous trees. single trees or groups
OF trees may escape injury.

Starkville. Colo Oct Sat 10 o'clock
last night a gas explosion wrecked the
big coal mines of the Colorado Fuel and
Iron Company. Fifty-eight men are
known to have been entombed and the
number may reach 100. There is small
hope that any are still alive They were
nearly all Americans.


Rescue parties have been endeavoring
to enter the workings at intervals since
the explosion, but at 9 o'clock tonight
none had succeeded in penetrating more
than 300 feet. The last party of eleven
men were overcome by gas and barely
escaped death. companions who were roped
to them and twenty feet behind them
dragging them out unconscious.


The explosion tore out about forty feet
OF the entrance, which eaved in, render
ing rescue work through this entrance
impossible until the debris has been
cleared away. Timbers, steel rails. dirt.
and rocks were hurled from the en-
trance for hundreds of feet by the force
OF the explosion.


The whole interior of the mine is be-
lleved 10 be a wreck. The imprisoned
men are believed to have been behind
the explosion. If this is true, they may
escape through the Eagleville mine.
which is connected with the Starkville
property, but which. years ago. was
walled off with a cement wall. If the
miners are stlll alive they may make
their way TO the wall and chop their way
out


Their failure to give any signals for
nearly twenty-four hours indicates that
they are all dead, although the company
officials say the workings are so Sxten-
sive and air galleries so numerous that
some may survive. Supt. Thompson ex-
poets a modern equipment for the res
cuers at II o'clock tonight and viii then
go in with a strong force

VENICE, May 21.-Countess Maria
Tarnowska and her accomplices, law
yer Prilukoff and DIR. Nikolas Nau-
mon, have been sentenced for the
murder OF the countess husband. The
two years that the trio have been In
prison, awaiting trial, will be deduct
ed from the sentences imposed yes
terday, which will make the countess
term at solitary imprisonment, six
years and four months; Prilukoff's
eight years, and Naumoff's, six years
and one month.


These sentences were what the
prosecutor asked for, except In the
case of Naumoff, for whom the prose-
cutor asked for a sentence of three
years and four months.
There Is no probability OF a new
trial. Countess Tarnowska was In a
serious condition today, following a
trial OF more than three months, which
was the most dramatic heard In an
Italian court In many years. Ply
sicians were In constant attendance
upon her at the jail. Elise Perrier,
the countess maid was acquitted.


AS Naumoff, the hapless lover OF
the countess and the man who did the
killing as the tool for the Designing
countess and Prilukoff. another OF her
lovers, passed the countess cell to-
day, she cried out:


"Nikolas will you still shake hands
with me-"


She reached her hands through the
prison bars and Naumof seized them
and kissed them tenderly.


For all the injury you have done
me, still love you" he said with
great emotion.


For Prilukoff the countess no longer
shows the slightest feeling.

Nowadays we are familiar with all
manner and shapes of spoons intended
for divers purposes, but some of the
old-fashioned ones are merely curiosi-
ties. For instance, there is the old
marrow spoon, used by our grand
parents for extracting marrow from
bones. This spoon was made double
one end being employed for small
bones and the other for those OF larger
bore


Another old spoon was that used for
mulberries. This had a perforated
bowl and a spiked and pointed handle,
and was employed in day when null
berries were more commonly eaten than
they are at the present time. With the
perforated bowl a little sugar was
sprnkled on the berry, which was then
conveyed to the mouth on the spiked
end of the handle.


Very few caddie-spoons are seen
these days Tea-caddies of the old
fashioned type have long since gone
their way. and with them disappeared
the caddie-spoon.


The snuff. candle and pap spoons are
others that have long ago gone out
of use.

Long voyages to south Atlantic states
have been the rule with coasting vessels
during the present summer, and passages
of from thirty to forty days. between
ports south Of New York and those in
South Carolina. Georgia and Florids have
become common. The schooner James B.
Drake. Capt. Cummings, has just con-
cluded a voyage of forty-one days from
Baltimore to Portland, with coal. a trip
ordinarily made in two weeks. The Drake
left Baltimore July and passed out Cape
Henry the next day. All the way down
the coast she met head winds and Gains
that stretched out the trip until the crew
of the vessel thought they would never
make port Southerly winds have pre-
vailed along the south Atlantic coast for
the past three months. and is responsible
for the slow time made by the big cargo
carriers.

United States gunboat Princeton, off
Amapala, Honduras, is cleared for
action and it's guns are trained on
the governors residence occupied by
General Jose Valladares, leader of the
revolt against the Davilla govern
ment.


The dispatch received here this morn
ing from Honduras states that Valla-
dares attacked the American consular
agent and threatened to fire on his
residence. When Commander Hayes OF
the Princeton heard of this he sent
word to the revolutionists that If any
foreigner was molested he would fill
the governors palace full of bullets
The dispatch adds that chaos reigns
throughout western Honduras and
foreigners are fleeing to places OF
safety.

trated Queen AleXandras desire to show

band, wearing red jerseys and carrying
silver instruments and banners with
scarfs of crepe, pushed through the
crowd to the palace Enclosure. The big
iron gates were opened and the band
formed a circle under the windows.


First they knelt. while the leader
prayer. and then they sang Nearer. My
God, to Thee" abide With Me-" and
angels Ever Bright and Fair" Finally
they marched out. singing Onward.
Christian Soldiers"


The blinds were closely drawn. but
the attendants say that Queen Alex
andra left her apartments with Prin-
cess Victoria and her ladies' in waiting
and listened to the singing from be-
hind them.

Most picturesque of all the varied
events OF the three days of festival
just closed was the masquerade ball
last night in the Auditorium at Page
and Fell streets, when thousands of
maskers crowded the immense floor

sands Of visitors looked on at the gay
dance.


Long before the electrical parade had

town streets the Auditorium was filled

height at midnight. did not cease un-
til early this morning. For brilIiancy
and beauty of costumes, as well as for
novelty of makeup, the bali surpassed
any big masquerade dance that ever
has been held in San Francisco.

The strict rule of the committee in
charge of the festivities prevented any
but those in costume from going on
the main floor Of the dance han until

but the balconies were filled with on
lockers, who later Joined in the rev.
elry below. Every conceivable kind

fast and furious from early in the
evening


The great hall was profusely deco
rated with the carnival colors of yell
low and green, with national flags and
with varlcolored bunting and greenery.
Colonel Frank w Marston was the
master of ceremonies, and from the
time Of the grand march until the last
dancers We're ready to leave the floor
this morning there was not a hitch in
the long program of dances.


QUEEN MOUNTS HER THRONE


Jllst on the stroke of midnight Queen
Grace, the monarch of the weeks
makebelieve, entered the Auditorium
and swept with her court through the
cheering throng of dancers to her
throne. She led the march which fol-
lowed Immediately after her arrival.
and then reseated herself in the place
of honor TO review the hundreds of
masked couples who passed before her


Queen Grace herself assisted the
committee charged with awarding the
prizes for the handsomest and most
unique costumes, and with her own
hands made the presentations after the
winners had been selected. This was a
task that taxed the, judges to the ut
most, for so many notable costumes
We're worn that it was only by a long
process Of elimination that the win
ners finally were chosen.


After the awarding of prizes the
dancers unmasked. and the gayety of
the early evening was resumed. 1t
was estimated by those in charge that
up TO ] o'clock this morning 10000 per

after that hour thousands more pre-

forgot there was a bullet left in the
chamber, pulled the trigger and shot
his 3-year-old son Howard in the right
side of the abdomen.


Fortunately the shot was a glancing
one, and although 1t was first thought
the bullet had penetrated the body, ex-
animation at the receiving hospital
showed that a four-inch penetration
of the abdominal wall resulted. The
police surgeons state the child will
recover.


Hughes purchased the pistol yester-
day and last night was studying its
mechanism. He had removed the bull
let's from the magazine, not realizing
another remained in the chamber. AS
he was pulling the trigger the child,
attracted by the click of the gun,
playfully toddled toward his father.
The baby was almost opposite when
the bullet in the chamber was dis
charged, penetrating the abdominal
wall, but not the cavity.


Before leaving for the hospital the
father tossed his recently purchased
gun out of the window. vowing never
again."

MUNICH, Bavaria, July 13.-A
sharp earthquake was felt here at 9:45
o'clock this morning. The walls OF
several buildings were cracked.


The wavelike movement continued
for three seconds, thoroughly terrify-
ing the people, who fled from their
homes and remained in the street long
after the disturbance had subsided.
. The shock was also felt in sur
rounding villages, including Garmisch.
A report from Oberammergau says the
shock was noticeable there, but that
little damage was done.


Although no casualties have been re-
ported here investigation develops that
the effect of the disturbance was
greater than was at first thought.


The wallis of several school houses
cracked and the teachers and pupils
ran shrieking into the streets. The
municipal council ordered the school
buildings closed until they could be
thoroughly examined.

VICTORIA, b. c., July 21.-Further
adVices of the little war Japan Is Wag-
ing against the Formosan aborigines
was brought by the Ava Maru yester-
day. The Japanese forces are now
building entrenched lines with block
houses fanklng the Formosans, the TO-
tai length of the lines to date being
S07 miles. Following the recent heavy
fighting with machine guns, the moral
effect of these has induced the surren-
der of large bodies of natives. The
fighting Is mostly in thick forests and
mountain sides, three to fouf thousand
feet above sea level, and there are
difficulties in the way of using arttl-
lery. The japanese are mounting guns
on high hills from which the native
strongholds can be bombarded.


The Japanese forces, in five detach-
ments, resumed fighting July 2 and
drove the natives from their mountain
strongholds with heavy losses. The
Japanese went into action at thirty
yards distance, the natives throwing
themselves on the bayonets. According
to Japanese officers, the head natives
were unaware what bayonets were,
PRISONERS stating that they were sur
prised that they could be placed on
rifles. Japanese losses are scant in the
attack compared with those during the
night encampment, when the natives
creep up. Most of the natives are
armed with inferior weapons, using
bullets of wood tipped with lead.

sa has been comforting with Toxic Off
cials regarding the colony, and has
had a difference with the financial bu-
reau, which sought to revive the sugar
tax. Premier Katsura interfered, and
the governor, who had resigned because
of his difference with the minister of
finance, resumed his post.

east of Hammond, Ind, and the train
was the Erie flyer. Mrs. Montrelle's home
is in Hammond. Physicians who attended
her after the accident expressed the fear
that she would not survive the shock.

reached the city. The posse which had

ever, made his way as dark as that of

ognized a landmark and led the others

That very evening the work began, for

the chairs little Prudence saw that each
wick was covered with thin coat of
for she did not think they looked at all

If her grandmother had not been near

would have cried. wait, my child, and
you shall see that it is as I tell you,"
even closer than before. After the first
dipping of the wicks all around the six
wicks first dipped were ready for a second
trip to the tallow kettle. When they came
Each time that the wicks were dipped
they received a new coat of melted tai
low, until by noon the candles looked
quite like those which were in the gov
ernor's house. In the afternoon little
Prudence shined all Of the pewter candle

would be needed for the pretty white
candles.

greatly increased.

department force be increased to meet
the emergencies that were daily in
creasing.

storm Nevada has experienced in years
at this season started late yesterday
afternoon and is continuing today,
breaking the longest dry period the
state has ever known.

two inches, which exceeds the total for
the FIVE preceding months combined.

defamation, the shock of which was plain
ly felt In this city, ten miles away, a
tremendous charge of nitroglycerin gela-
tin was yesterday exploded against the
armored turret OF the double-turreted
monitor Puritan, the biggest ship of her
class in the world. An hour after, with
less shoek apparently. another charge
was exploded against the armor belt
along the water line of the ship.


The test was highly spectacular. The
explosive was piled against the after tur-
ret and Capt. knight and a companion
took their posts forward. The charge
was touched off by electricity. There was
a stunning report, a tremendous burst Of
flame and smoke, and the great hull of
the heavy monitor rocked and quaked
from the explosion.


As soon as the smoke cleared the navy
ward tugs ran as close as they could get
to the monitor. which had been moored
in the shallow water off Middle Ground,
with only about thirteen inches of water
between her hull and bottom.


Capt. Knight reported that he and his
companion were uninjured by the expio-
sion, and the chickens that had been
brought down were strutting about the
deck as though proud OF the experience.
A pet cat had been confined inside the
turret. and she was unhurt, but not SO
the turret. The heavy eight-inch plates
were completely demolished.

day, the police had arrested two negro
girls. and the latter had admitted the
crime. Fay Allen and Ethel Cole, each
II years of age, were confronted with
the charge of entering the house last
Thursday night, when they broke down
and confessed. The Cole girl denied
taking anything, declaring that she
simply accompanied the Allen girl.
Both were taken to the county Jail, to
be returned here tomorrow and tried
before ]. c. Steele, acting city re-
corder.

she attended the Twenty-first street
school. The police claim they began
stealing as soon as they arrived here.

banks last week. Then, the police say,

sacked the house, taking away with

Fairbanks today.

nary precautions taken last night to
protect Emperor william and Empress
Auguste Victoria when they left the
city at IL o'clock for Berlin We're ex-
planned today when the police an
nounced that letter threatening his
majesty had been received at the royal
palace yesterday.


The letter was signed by a militant
Brussels anarchist and read:


Since no one has had the courage to
blow up the German autocrat I have
decided to throw a bomb


Efforts of the authorities 70 arrest
the writer were fruitless and accord
ingly unusual steps were taken to guard

Five weary negro sailors. who had lost
their way in a small sloop on the At
| lantic. and were twice snatched from
death by a friendly steamship. were
brought to port last night on the British
| freighter Ikalis. It was the Ikalis which

! The rescued men belonged to the sloop

| had TO go where currents and chance
| took them. Their usual custom had been


to sail by land bearings, as the groups
of small islands among which they

this sort of navigation.

When the fog cleared and the sun


shone hot upon the Sunlight the five
men realized that they were literally and
| fguratively at sea. They knew that the


sun rose in the east and went down In

which direction the land lay. They
counted the sunrise twelve times, and


that was about all they could recall to
show how many days they had been
adrift The Ikalis picked them up on


July %, and after the men came out of


their seni-conscious condition. they es-


timated that they we're thirteen days


adrift.


| The negro traders are all British sub

the British ensign on the Sunlight S


foremast When hunger and fear un-
nerved them Jerrold Frank, the master
and owner of the sloop, flew the inverted

to wait for some helping hand to come

Ikalis came within hailing distance he
|


the black men huddled together in the


stern. Three lay under the shade of

ting posture, waved an arm feebly.
| something wrong on that packet"
said Captain Turner to his chief officer.
Better lower bot quick and get over

Within three minutes the chief officer
and four men went alongside the Sun

! With considerable difficulty the boat 9
| crew pulled the negroes into their boat
and took them over to the Ikalis. Slim
ulants were administered to the suffer-


ers, and after partaking of some food

Sugar and Vinegar as Food.


They mentioned having shipped much

! ing of the fog. Their provisions were
| ruined and the only thing eatable that

| a small case of vinegar. lashed near the


cabin. The men had kept alive by soak

| The negroes remained aboard the

When the men were safe on the deck

fully tried out in Germany. where they
have been varied into open-air summer
schools and forest schools. In no place
where they have been tried have they
been abandoned. In most places they
are being extended. Thus far the schools
have included only the physically weak
and the mentally backward. With plenty
of fresh air and sanitary surroundings.
these weak and defective children have
beer able to accomplish more than nor
NAL children in the ordinary schools. In
some cases progress has been exceptional
~ rapid. While the minds develop as
they never developed before. the bodies
grow strong and children are given a
chance in life.

SEATTLE, March 14.--Charles X.
Hamilton, sore and stiff as a result of
his mishap Saturday afternoon, when
his Curtiss biplane turned turtle and
threw him into a muddy field, made
two short flights at the Meadows this
afternoon.


On the first flight the steering ap-
paratus was improperly adjusted, and
Hamilton narrowly escaped repeating
Saturdays unpleasant performance.
The biplane was slow in rising and
after he had circled the track once at
a height of 200 feet he started to
descend. The machine came down
rapidly, and for moment it appeared
to be driving straight into the pond.
1t barely cleared the water, landing in
a muddy field. Hamilton had some ad-
justments made and prepared for his
second flight


This time the machine rose grace
fully, and the aviator circled the track
two and half times. He was in the
air about five minutes and made a
splendid landing. This second flight
brought forth loud applause.


When a third fight was attempted
the engine baked and the machine
would not move. The crowd, which
numbered more than 5000 persons,
waited two hours while the mechanics
worked with the motor. At last they
got it going, but when Hamilton again
attempted a flight the machine ran
along the ground for 200 yards, but
would not rise into the air.

TRIESTE, Austria, April Is, 1910.
The people of Trieste are proud of their
harbor. which cost thirty millions of
crowns and has all the conveniences
that are required for handling the trade
Of Austria.


Steamships are coming and leaving
every day. About 1900 vessels, includ-
ing 5000 steamers, enter and clear the
harbor annually for all ports Of the
world


Two great steamship companies have
their headquarters here. The Austrian
Lloyd, one of the oldest in the world,
was esta blished in 1885. The Austro-
American Company. a modern organiza-
ton, has thirty-three steamers. aggre-
eating 10000 tons, and four new ones
of 1000 tons building.


Several ships of this line are large
as ten, eleven and twelve thousand tons
displacement. The largest. the flagship OF
the fleet. christeued Martha Washington,
is Il, 800 tons.
|. The Austro-American line connects Tri-
este with New York city. New Orleans
and Savannah. where the ships go every
month for cotton, and Brazil and the
Argentine Republic, where they carry
emigrants.


The Austrian-Lloyd company has more
than a hundred ships, mostly between
twelve hundred and twenty-five hundred
tons, which cruise about the Mediterra-
mean, the Black sea and the Adriatic.
There are monthly sailings for India.
the Straits Settlements, Java and Austria
liza.


Both Companies receive subsidies from
the Austrian government. The Austrian
Lloyd company has its own yards and
machine shops for building and repairing
ships, and now has under construction
four battleships for the government.


In addition to these local companies the
Cunard Steamship Company has line
between Trieste and Fiume, which Is
across the Isthmus Of Istria, at the head
of the other branch Of the Adriatic sea,
and New York, which brings over many
passengers from New York to Naples and
other intermediate ports and carries back
thousands of emigrants.

The ice covering the Potomac above
the Aqueduct bridge, which has remained
undisturbed since the freezing weather
started about three weeks ago, and has
been gradually growing thicker, is from
ten to twelve inches thick and every
night adds something to this thickness.


The uncertainty In the ice situation on
the river is shown from the fact that
the masters of the steamers on the river
Sunday night reported little ice Of con-
sequence except about Fort Washington.
where 1t was particularly heavy. Below
Glymont nothing was found to cause
steamboats, serious Inconvenience.


The officers of the steamer Northumber-
land, which arrived here Tuesday night
from Baltimore and lower river landings.
report having found ice clear down to
Point Lookout, and in the tributaries of
the lower Potomac 1t was quite heavy
The heaviest ice they found was between
the mouth of Mattawoman creek and
Indian Head. Here the steamer stoned
several times and had to back and ram
the gorges. but she finally got through.
AT Fort Washington, where the ice had
previously gorged, nothing but scattered
blocks were found.

playing she might wish.

leisurely pick out his choice from a urz-

the sweet magnolia of the sun-kissed
southland.


John received thirty-six letters in two
days this week.

temple has been rent, the malevolence of

way in which the two bodies are taken
down contrasts keenly with the reverence
and love with which Nicodemus and John,
Joseph of Arimathea and Lazarus wrap
and lower the body of their Master.
These last rites seemed really the end of
the passion story, but there follow, of
course, the resurrection scene and a final
tableau when Christ is seen glorihed in

DUBLIN, May 23-Another scene of
excitement has been witnessed on the
Pollock estate, County Galway The
cattle and sheep which had been
driven off the grazing farms Of Ardagh,
Ballinacurra and Ussy were put back
on the lands by the police and other
employees of Messrs. Payne and Neary
who hold the lands on the Pollock es-
tate from which the sheep were driven.


It was resolved to clear he farms
again, and at the hour fixed nearly
two thousand people and three bands
had gathered on the lands, waiting to
take part in the drive, which was no
hidden mystery from the authorities.
Owing to the fact that the stock had
been put back after the drive of the
previous day. the people resolved not
to deliver them up to the owners the
second time.


Operations commenced at Ballina-
curra, and the sheep and cattle were
driven onto the public road. There
were thirteen police located on the
farms, but with the exception of one
move to stop the crowd driving the
sheep, the police abandoned the idea
of going farther as they were power
less against the enormous crowd of
people present.


The farms cleared contain about 600
acres, and it is stated are held upon the
eleven months system by Messrs.
Payne, Jones and Neary. AS already
stated, the Pollock property has been
sold to the estate commissioners. The
tenants maintain that the holding of
these farms by the graziers prevents
the tenants getting their holdings for
the summer months. Mr.. Payne states
they hold the farms on lease and not
on the eleven months system.


The crowd scattered the cattle and
sheep in all directions but teh stock
was afterward recovered by the police.
Great excitement prevailed in the dis

the Alaska Steamship Company's steamer
Yucatan. which sank in six fathoms of
water off Chicagof Island Wednesday,
after striking an iceberg in Icy strait,
the steamship Georgia arrived last night
None OF the sixty-flve passengers was
injured. All the passengers unite in prais-
ing the officers and crew. The passengers
will leave Monday for Seattle.


1t was learned that the Yucatan officers
supposed they were sailing through slush
ice, and the ship ran into a berg twenty
five feet long and fifteen feet high, which
was hidden from view by a snowstorm.


Cuts Mass of Ice in Two.


Capt. Porter and the pilot, Capt john
son. said that the Yucatan broke the
huge mass Of Ice In two. Swerved from
her course by the collision. the steamer
struck reef and tore a hole in her side.
The ship bounded off into deep water. and
Capt. Porter at once ordered full speed
ahead for Mud bay.


The passengers were rowed ashore. and
all the mail and some of the baggage
taken off before the ship sank. The
landing was made on Goose Island, near
Chicagof Island. The mon built huts
and made tents of sails taken from the
ship. Fires were kept going day and
night, and no one suffered.


Thursday afternoon some of the ten
woman passengers were reWed to Hoonah,
an Indian trading town, where they were
cared for by American traders.


Five sailors are watching the wreck.
Capt. Porter says that If prompt action
is taken the Yucatan can be floated and
repaired


Hope to Raise the Yucatan.

derwriters hope to float the Yucatan and

Carnegie hero medal on record. He is

Mrs. William A. Brewer of Douglass
ton, L. l., the wife of New York silk
merchant, while alone in her home with
her 3-year old daughter. Dorothy.
smelled swoke, and running from her
sewing room on the second floor, found
the wall surrounding the kitchen CHM
ney afire. She ran out to give the
alarm leaving the little girl in the
sewing room, forgetting for the moment
the child's danger.


When Mrs Brewer saw how much
headway the fire had got and realized
her daughters danger she tainted.
Willie Hall, who came along the road
and saw the burning house, ran up to
see what was the matter and found
Mrs Brewer just recovering from her
swoon. The first word the mother said
was about her little daughter, and she
pointed to the room where she had left
the little one.


The gesture was enough for the g.
year-old boy. He ran into the house,
found the stairway ablaze and dashed
through the flames as fast as his legs
could carry him. In the meantime little
Dorothy had become frightened by the
heat and was trying to escape. The
boy found her at the head of the stair
way picked her up and carrid her out
of the house in his arms. After turn
ing her over to her mother he ran
down the road and gave the alarm,
but the fire had such a headway when
the volunteer firemen from Douglaston
and Little Neck arrived that it was
impossible to save the cottage and its
contents. The loss was about $4,000.

Five weeks hence the open season
for wild ducks and shore birds, Eng
lish snipe and valley quail will be
ushered in. During the intervening
time the sportsman has no time to lose
in preparing for a full campaign on

From all accounts the coming duck
season for Los Angeles sportsmen, as

Barbara to San Diego reports have
been received that duck hunting will
be plentiful and, in fact all down the
southern part of the state the indica-
tions are bright for good season.
Rumor had 1t that the ducks were
scarce, but from the reports of the
various game wardens, sportsmen will
have all they desire in capturing the
limit.

eral squads Of ducks have been seen
flying around Balboa, and no doubt
this will be the hunters stronghold

dropped the body and ran. The body
proved to be that of the negro's wife.

to the police station and held for safe
keeping.

death, left the house in the afternoon
and did not return until midnight. The
undertakers were in the house prepar-
ing the body for burial, but Harvey
drove everyone from the house, placed
a cigarette in the dead woman's mouth,
and taking the body in his arms started
out on the street.

racing away with the rope, turned
about and headed directly for the
Sorenson. Passing under the stern of

blow with it's tail and smashed in the
hull.

fire. The next night they were picked
up by a passing vessel. The whale
was afterward found floating, dead.

police expedition arrived during March.

ging supplies on five tohoggans with dog

corded a more prolonged period OF low
temperature. making the trip feat to
be compared with polar expedition

Pherson was thirty-three days. and the
return was made in twenty-four days.

eighty days.

sky every night. It connected at Nc
PhersOn with the police expedition from
Herschel Island and brought 500 letters,
mostly from whalers. missionaries and

Maine. Here the big waves beat

it was not until Helen was taken down

realized what beautiful and many
kinds of trees and flowers there were in
the world.


On her return the rocks and sands

was known to all friends of the family that
Jimmy and Isabella when children at Du-

found her home filled with smoke, and upon
rushing upstairs to the second-story front
bedroom was confronted with the appalling
spectacle of her 6-year-old daughter Margaret
enveloped in flames and screaming in agony.


The sight proved too much for the HORNED
mother who fell in a swoon across the purn-
ing clothing of her child. If 1t had not been
for the fact that Police Sergeant Black OF the
Seventeenth district happened to be passing
at the moment she must have perished with
the unfortunate child, who suceumbed to ter
rible burns few hours later at The Poly"
technc hospital


The sergeant, attracted by the cries OF little
Margaret rushed upstairs in time to beat out
the fire. which had communicated from the
mother and daughter to bed in the room.


When Mrs. Linn was informed that her girl
was dead she said she regretted the oppor-
tune arrival of the officer which had saved
her. and late last night she was In serious
condition from shock and burns.


The tragedy was brought about by new
penny which had been given to Margaret for
retiring early When the little girl had been
nut to bed by her mother the bright penny
rolled on the floor and out of sight After
futile search she went to sleep, but on
awakening yesterday, shortly after O'CLOCK
lust as her mother had gone out to purchase

child ran downstairs and returned with

The United States submarine boats
Grampus and Pike arrived at San
Pedro harbor last evening, en- route
from the Mare Island navy yard to
San Diego. The little boats, each hav-
ing a crew of ten men, left San Fran
cisco bay ten days ago, and in order
to not imperil the lives OF the crews,
the commanders put into San Luis
Oblspo harbor seven days ago and put
to sea again after remaining there for
three days. The boats are propelled
by gasoline engines while on the sur
face and by electric power while un-
Grated by wet storage batteries, which
contain two acids. The boats can
not take to the open sea during q
storm, for as soon as they start to
pitch the acids in the storage bat
teries generate poisonous gas, which
causes death by suffocation. The
boats are so small that they have no
deck, therefore the crew are always
within, and while at sea the matches
are battered down from the inside. AS
soon as the barometers indicate a
storm, the boats are always headed
for harbor, for should they COM
mence pitching the gases would gem
crate and the crews would meet their
death. While nearing San Luis Obispo
a storm came up and the two sub
marines were headed into the harbor


The commanders made three attempts
to proceed on their journey, but could
not do so until the storm had abated.


The supply boats Fortune and Justin
are conveys for the Grampus and Pike.
This is the first trip taken by the two
submarines in the open sea. They Will
leave for San Diego this evening.

NEW YORK. July 3O.-Two days after
leaving Barbados July %, the British
steamer Ikalis, in today from Buenos
Tires. sighted sinking sloop flying sig
mails of distress, which turned out to lie
the little Sunlight, a wandering cargo
carrier between the Islands of Antigua
and Barbados. She lay helpless, with her
master and crew of five fiat on the decks.
There was neither water nor food in
sight.


When the men had been hoisted aboard
the steamer and revived, Capt. J. Frank,
owner of the Sunlight, said that he ran
into a fog a few hours ON of Antigua,
had lost his bearings and for thirteen
days he and his crew had been living on
vinegar and sugar. How long they had
been unconscious before the 1kalis bore
down on them he did not know


AS the fog came on the sloop began
to take water, and the crew worked at
the pumps until exhausted. Distress sig
nails were set after a storm washed their
food and water overheard, and for near
ly two weeks their sole sustenance was
the sugar-saturated vinegar.


Overcome by Exhaustion.


When the storm cleared it was found
that the compass had gone with the
provisions, and the crew pumped and
sailed recklessly, until, one by one, they
were overcome by exertion and starva-
ton. and each in his turn stretched him
silf out on the deck to die. Capt. Frank
was the last man to give in.


When the rescued men had been re-
freshed they insisted on returning to
the Sunlight, which had been kept in
sight. Accordingly they were put aboard
with water and provisions, but while the
Ikalis was bidding them adieu they call
ed for help. The Sunlight was sinking
The Ikalis took them off again, the Sum-
light was abandoned and the shipwreck-
ed men were brought to this port.

Seven hundred poor families of Los
Angeles were yesterday provided with
a good, fashioned Thanksgiving
dinner through the efforts of the
Volunteers of America and the Saliva
tion army.


Seventeen hundred men, most of
them homeless, were given dinners at
the Union Rescue and Methodist mis-
sions.


In all between 450O and 5000 persons,
who otherwise would have had only
meager fare, were provided with DIM
ners worthy the season.


Four hundred big market baskets,
packed to overhowing with seasonal
provisions, were given away by the
Volunteers of America to women who
are doing their best to support faml-
lies of children and whose husbands
either have deserted them, are i'll or
for some other reason are temporarily
out of employment. With each basket
went a ten-pound sack of flour, and
in $50 Of the 400 was a liberal por-
tion of turkey, turkey enough for tiVe
persons. The remaining fifty baskets
contained chicken instead. Other pro-
visions packed in these baskets In
cluded beans, coffee, tea and sugar,
bread, potatoes, beef, canned goods.
celery and apples.


VOLUNTEERS SUPPLY CROWDS


There were more applicants than the
Volunteers could care for, and conse-
quently late comers were turned away
empty handed. The Thanksgiving
street collection made for the purpose
proved insufficient to purchase the
supplies needed and additional money
was appropriated from another fund.


Only women were supplied by the
Volunteers, the men being sent else
where. Chiefly the women were MeXi-
cans, Spanish and Russians. The
distribution was made by ticket, issued
to applicants by officials of the or
ganization after they had questioned
the women and satisfied themselves
that their cases were worthy. One
woman who applied brought with her
family of ten children, the eldest
not more than 10 years old. She was
given two baskets and two sacks of
flour.


The Salvation army made its dis
tribution Wednesday afternoon. Three
hundred baskets were given away,
containing provisions for 1900 persons.
Each basket contained a roast of beef,
vegetables, fruit, tea, coffee, sugar,
celery and bread. The distribution
was in charge of Major and Mrs. Har-
ris and was made at the army bar
racks, 431 South Hill street. Here, too,
the donations were principally to
women.


MEN DINE AT MISSIONS


The men were taken care of at the
Union Rescue mission, las North Main
street, and at the Methodist mission,
255 East Fifth street. At the former
place fully 1000 men were served with
dinner consisting of mulligan stew,
rolls, mince and pumpkin pie and
fruit. The meal was served by women
of the Ladies' Aid society, and each
man was given a flower as a souvenir.
One table was occupied by fifty boys,
each of whom was under 10 years of
age. A continuous song service was
held in the mission auditorium all day,
and in the afternoon Evangelist w. A..
Ward gave a blackboard talk on the
evils of cigarette smoking.
At the Methodist mission 700 meals
were served, 100 to children. Mostly,
however, the dinners were given to
homeless men. Here the menu in
cluded vegetable soup, boiled beef and
beans, sandwiches, celery, pie, cake,
fruit, tea and coffee. No questions
were asked at either mission, all ap-
plioants for a dinner being welcomed
and supplied.

day morning, developing into torren-

east, changed to southwest. and with
renewed fury the cyclonic hastings

and Havana provinces, completing the
destruction wrought by the first storm.

cyclone on account of rumors OF the
approach OF third storm reported to
be forming south OF Jamaica. AT 9
o'clock, last night the rain was still
falling in frequent heavy gusts, but
the wind had abated considerably and
the sea was falling.

amount Of damage. which doubtless
