feet above all former marks. The lower
part of Winnemucca is submerged, the
great bridge spanning the river at that
place Is threatened and the levee Is
now thought to be menaced. Great
property damage has been done, the
principal loser being the Western Pa
cific railroad.


The roadbed of that line is badly
damaged and in one place suddenly
sank into the water with a train Of
loaded cars.


Although the river is falling slightly
this afternoon there Is still great fear
that the levees and bridge at Winnie
mucca will go out. Watchers have
been posted at various points and all
possible effort is being made in prep
aration for still higher water.


Ranches between Winnemucca and
Battle Mountain have suffered much
damage and many head of cattle and
horses are reported to have been
drowned

main line and loop in the northern part

buffet car left the track. Although the
two locomotives were drawing the
train at a fast rate of speed the engi-
neer at the instant he felt his engine

brakes, which brought the train to a

derailed were returned to the yards,

and repaired the track. Traffic was
demoralized for four hours. No one was
injured.

SEATTLE. Dec 17.-The trading
schooner Louise. which was crushed in
the ice of Bering strait. pieces of which
were found near Cape Prince of Wales,
the most westerly point of North
America, sailed from Nome for Siberia
on trading expedition.


Captain Harry Owens, commander
and owner of the boat. had been run
ming small vessels in the far north for
several years, and was familiar with
ice navigation. John w. Kelly, one of
the passengers, had been trading with
the Siberian natives for 25 years, and
Mount Kelly, a noted landmark near
Anadyr. was named for him. He had
made a study of the strange people and
compiled dictionary of their language.


1t is likely that all the men were
drowned. In the winter Bering strait
is not frozen over, but ice drifts south
from the Arctic filing the passage and
always moving. Eskimos make their
way from Siberia to the Diomed islands
and it is possible. but not probable, that
the Louise's men may have reached the
islands over the ice.

San Francisco's prohibition against

ton ended yesterday when the supreme
court upheld the constitutionality of
the ordinance and its validity under
the police powers of the board of su-
pervisors.


The measure forbidding the inter
ment of the dead within the city was
opposed by the cemetery associations,
and the Laurel Hill association brought
suit in the superior court. The city's
right was here upheld and the state
supreme court affirmed the decision.


Assistant City Attorney Jesse Stein
hart has during the last two years had
charge of the case for the municipality,
and a few months ago went to Wash
ington to lay before the court the city's
final contention.

One passenger was killed, brakeman

waukee & st. Paul railroad at Key
stone, twenty-five miles west of here

the St. Paul road and the eastbound
fast train were ordered to pass at Key
stone A freight train on the siding

train from pulling On the switch.

run past the station and was ready to
back on the siding when the overland
limited, going twenty-five miles an
hour. crashed into it. Both engines
were reduced to scrap, and the mail,
baggage and chair cars of the limited
were badly smashed. The engineers
escaped by jumping.


Mrs. Louis Zee of Cleveland, Texas,
was killed. Ralph Morrow, a brake
man, of Marion, Iowa, had his legs
broken and was internally injured.
He cannot live.

Dear Aunt Lauries


We had some very interesting neigh
bors several years ago, while we were
in Colorado. They were a family of
four, a widow and three children. The
eldest, a girl of ten, and two brothers,
aged eight and five


The mother took in washing and
plain sewing. 1t made our hearts ache
to see the little sister take care of
the boys and help mother with the
housework. She would help with the
meals and hang out the wash and get
them ready for ironing.


Dorothy, for that was her name had
more sense and kenw how to work
more than many girl twice as old.
She could not work so much when
school began but I'm sure she dressed
the boys, got breakfast and then some
times if she had time she would Clean
some of the rooms.


At night, when she came home, she
put on her apron and worked until sne
went to bed. People never found out
anything about them for it seemed
as though they never had time to
talk. They never would beg nor take
anything from the charities.


One day there was a great buzzng
and talking in their house and the
neighbers were very curious. The
mother came over to all of the people
that night and told her glad tidings.


Her husband had worked for the
railroad and one day there was an ac-
cident. The newspapers all said that
not one person had been found as they
all had perished. By a miracle her
husband was saved although he lost
his. memory. A few days before he had
received shock and his memory was
restored.


How haoppy they all We're! In week
he had a good position and his wife
remained at home to attend to the
housework. The girl lost her grand
mother look and one never knew
that she could be so jolly and happy.

Readings increase affects all employees
who receive less than 5000 a month.
The Readings advance, however. does
not include those employees whose
wages have been adjusted within the
last ninety days.

three months the Reading has ad-
iusted wages of certain classes OF
trainmen and other employees. In
cluding those the increase announced
today affects about $4,000 employees.

the railroads and the cost of living are
given as reasons for the increase.

SEATTLE, Feb. 26.-With rain fall
ing on the west slope of the Cascade
range and heavy snow slides near the
crest of the range, the northern trans
continental railroads tonight are fac
ing the worst difficulties they have ex-
perienced in the operation of trains
this year.


The rivers in western Washington
are rising rapidly. Reports received
from Everett and other points to the
north say that all streams are rising,
and the same conditions prevail south
of Seattle.


While the railroa Is are preparing to
fight foods their fights with the snow
blockades are not over. The Great
Northern and the Milwaukee lines are
completely blocked No Milwaukee
trains are being sent east from Seattle,
and the Great Northern is routing it's
overland trains via Vancouver, Wash,
and the Spokane, Portland & Seattle
railroad-the North Bank road.


The Northern Pacific, which is the
only transcontinental road that has
been able to operate trains through the
Cascades for nearly a week, suffered
severely from snow slides today. Three
eastbound transcontinental trains are
held in the mountains, but it is ex-
pected they will be released late to-
night. All westbound trains have been
stopped at Ellensburg until the line is
cleared.

ported to the police yesterday that
a suspicious looking man abruptly
entered his offices Sunday afternoon.

supposed to have been made. Clark

quickly regaining his composure, beat

dals

A large proportion goes into the

endangering the friendship between

uary 29 and had narrow escape. The

OAKLAND, June 9.-Accompanied by
Mayor Frank K. Mott of Oakland and

Johnson, candidate for the republican
nomination for governor, continued his
Alameda county campaign today with
addresses at Alvarado, Decoto, Niles
Irvington and Centerville. Both Mott
and Stetson spoke at all the meetings
in support of Johnsons candidacy.


The meeting at CenterviIle, held un-
der the name of the Lincoln Roosevelt
club there, was the most largely at
tended of the day. Two bands met the
speaker and his companions and the
streets were lined with people. The
hall where Johnson spoke was packed
Good crowds, however, listened to the
speaker at the different towns visited.


There is a peculiar thing about this
campaign said Johnson in his Center
vile address. THE peculiar circum-
stance is that the people and not the
corporations have all the chances. This
is the most peculiar political situation
California has known in the last 40
years. Other candidates may talk about
good roads and building UP the coun-
try; about believing in the decalogue
and keeping the ten commandments
but have hut one issue to heed-shall
the Southern Pacific or the people
rule?"


Mayor Mott declared that Johnson
represented his belief that a candidate
should run on good government prin-
ciples, and said that he would for that
reason do all he could to elect him.


Senator Stetson in his speeches said
he knew that Johnson spoke truth, and
recited instances of corporation lobby
lists approaching him in the capitol and
trying to influence his vote.


At Decoto. when Johnson spoke. sew
eral old men from the Masonic home

johnson went two miles over to the

SAN PEDRO, June 1.-THE South
Yacht clubs season of 1910 opened at
noon TODAY with the firing of the gun
which started the fleet of eight boats
on the annual cruising race around
Catalina island for the Whitley trophy.
The start from the end of the break
water was one of the finest ever seen
in Southern California waters An
eight-khot breeze was blowing from
the southwest and gave the yachts
headWay for the maneuVering behlnd
the starting line When the final gun
was fired at 12:15 o'clock the eight rae
ers were away in a bunch.

at the wheel, was first across the line.
The Sweetheart. the schooner which
Commodore Smith has remodeled for
the Honolulu race, was but few sec
onds behind the Seabird. Morgan Ed
wards big sloOp Mah-pe, which won

distance behind the Sweetheart and
the Mischief !, Warren Woods craft,

fifth place at the start, closely fol-
lowed by the Sradow and Old Royal
The Wave, George Gibson's craft, with
George Wallace at the wheel, was last


The Mah-pe soon took the lead and
seemed to draw rapidly away from
the others racers, while the Sweet
heart failed to make good showing
and will probably be given some rad
ical changes before the start of the
race to Honolulu. Until well on their

hold the positions which they had soon
after the start.


The winner of the race should be
back in the harbor not later than to-
morrow noon, as the record for the
course of approximately eighty miles,
as the yachts sail, is 16 hours, made

expect that with ordinary weather the

winds the yawls are expected to have

ligious ceremonies. The Indians also

Merry shouts of laughter with the
gay tinkling of gay sleigh bells, rang
out on the keen November air.


"Three cheers for grandma and her
pumpkin pies!" shouted big brother
Ben, in which p&pa, mamma, Florence
and baby Bobbie Joined. The air rang
again with their shouts, and grandma,
hearin~ the noise, came to the door.
A pretty picture in her gingham apron,
rosy cheeks, a daub of flour on her
nose and pan in her hands in which
she was stirring vigorously.


Papa, jumping quickly out of the
sled, helped mamma and Bobbie out
while Florence helped brother Ben
carry the holly.


''I am so glad you have come, al
though you are rather earlyl" cried
grandma, delightedly, kissing them all.
"And what lovely holly, Ben. Where
did you get it?"


"Oh, that's a secret" said Ben,
winking at Florence, who could hardly
keep from laughing.


"Well, come in out of the cold, for
it will soon be snowing," said grandma,
and everybody danced In to the fire.


"Take off your wraps and make
yourselves comfortable, for dinner will
soon be ready" and grandma went
bustling back to the kitchen.


"Come, everybody" called grandma
a few minutes later from the dining
room. and everybody hurried in.


And what a Thanksgiving dinner
that was! There was turkey, cram
berry sauce, all kinds of pudding,
mashed potatoes, apples, candy and
nuts. The table was decorated with
the holly Ben brought, which made 1T
look like Christmas.


Papa declared he never ate such good
turkey, to which all agreed. Bobbie
and Florence had five helpings of pud-
ding, and 1 don't dare to say how
many Ben had. Then grandma kissed
all goodby and there was 1ingling
of sleigh bells and they were off.


Remember" called back mamma,
''you are to take dinner with us for
Christmas" TO which grandma threw
back a kiss. Your loving niece,

CLEVELAND. July 15.-One man is
dead and two others are badly wounded
as the result Of raid by bandits on
a Lake Shore construction camp near
Olmsted Falls late last night. Charles
Brunner. aged thirty, who was shot
through the abdomen, died today. The
injured men are James Counterwane,
shot through the body. and Thomas
Zurach, shot in the head. 1t is be-
lieved that they will recover.


Sheriff Hirstius and posse covered
the country for miles around the scene
of the shooting. but could find no trace
Of the men who shot up the camp.


Demand Their Money.


Shortly. before midnight FIVE negroes
appeared at one of the shanties used as
sleeping quarters, and awakened the
laborers, demanding their pay, which
they received yesterday.


The first man handed over $33, the sole
booty Of the robbers. Three other men
answered they had no money and the
robbers opened fire.


There was a rush from the shacks.
Many of the workmen had revolvers. but
as the bandits ran as soon as they fired
upon their victims, they were out OF sight
before the men in camp had an oppor-
tunity to return the fire.


Exchange Shots With Detective.


Lake Shore detectives believe the five
negroes are the same men with whom De-
tective H. b. Bridenbach had a pistol
fight near Shawville yesterday afternoon.
Bridenbach saw the colored men on a
freight train and ordered them of. The
negroes opened fire on the detective and
many shots were exchanged on the fast
moving train.


The negroes finally jumped Off near
shawville, only six miles from tine con-
struction camp.

Following a wild ride behind a run
away horse for nine blocks down the
long Van Ness avenue hill south from
California street, pretty Miss Elizabeth
Whooten of 1908 Van Ness avenue and
Edward Mullin, proprietor of the Suisun
hotel at Suisun, were hurled 15 feet yes
terday afternoon with terrific force,
when their buggy collided with d hy-
drant at Golden Gate avenue. Both
received severe injuries, Mullin being
hurt internally and sustaining a frac-
ture of the arm.


The occupants of the runabout struck
the pavement within few feet of
each other Both were unconscious
when horrified spectators went to their
assistance.


Miss Whooten lay with the side of
her head badly gashed and bleeding
freely. She did not recover conscious
ness for more than an hour after
the accident. There were ugly lacera-
tions on the right side that may perma-
nently disfgure her face.


STRIKES STAIRWAY


Mullin struck jutting stairway in
his fall. Bleeding from many cuts and
bruises he was hurried to the central
emergency hospital, where Doctor Till
man attended him. He was bruised
and lacerated about the body and head
in addition to his other injuries.


The young couple had just left the
home of Miss Whooten and were on
their way to Golden Gate park when
the horse took fright at the sudden
opening of parasol by Miss Whooten.


Mullin, an expert horseman, tried TO
control the frightened horse, but the
animal started to kick. At this point
the parasol was carried from the hands
of Miss Whooten by the wind and the
horse, frightened to madness, ran wildly
down the hill. Three times the run
about Swerved to the sides of the ave-
nue., dangerously near trees and poles
and careened first on one pair of wheels
and then on the other.


GIRL TAKES LINES


Hundreds witnessed the runaway and
many sought to stop it. Near Golden
Gate avenue, when the strain of tug
ging on the lines began to tell on
Mullin, Miss Whooten reached for the
lines and turned the horse into the
sidewalk where the collision with the
hydrant occurred. The occupants shot
from their seats through the air to the
sidewalk.


Miss Whooten was removed to her
home and Mullin was taken to the
Mount Zion hospital Miss Whooten
is suffering from severe shock to her
nerves.

RICHMOND, Va, June 13.-Allen b.
Paul. treasurer of the Pine Street Baptist
Church, shot and instantly killed his wife
and within FIVE minutes blew out his
brains yesterday.


The shooting followed an all-night quar-
rel. Mrs. Paul was killed in defending
her eight-year-old son, Leslie. The father,
who had retired shortly before the deed
was committed, entered the boys room
soon after. armed. His wife, who had
been watching him, rushed In just as he
pulled the trigger. the bullet taking ef-
feet in her left arm and penetrating her
lung.


Crying for the lad to run for his life.
the mother fell to the floor, and stanolng
over her body, Paul fired another bullet
into her left breast, resulting in death a
few minutes later. The son escaped ana
gave the alarm to neighbors, VINO 1ound
that Paul had cheated justice by taking
his own life.


Quarreled All Night.


According to the boys story, his parents
had quarreled all night long. and the
youngster. frightened beyond measure,
and fearful that something awful was
going to happen, had lain awake in his
room with all MS CLOTHES vi. INC Stoi Ia
broke suddenly, for, as the boy tells it,
his mother arose at o'clock and went
down stairs When she returned her
husband was still in bed. Then she went
to Leslie's room, and after attempting to
quiet his fears. started to go to oeo
again. She had not been In her own
room more than a minute before Paul
pushed his way into the lads room and
attempted to shoot. 1t was here that the
mothers Intervention cost her ner life.


Leslie was q stepson. Paul had married
his mother only nine months ago. Their
marital existence had been unhappy.
Twice before he had attempted suicide.
once by taking gas and another time by
shooting. On the first attempt he was dis
covered after the gas had overcome him
and the second time his nerve failed him.
Paul left a note to his father, stating
that he intended to kill young Leslie, his
wife and himself. He had made the
threat several times.

DOVER, n. j., June 13.-With the ter
rible force of its speed Of sixty miles an
hour Lackawanna eastbound train
raked itself along the side of a de-
rallied box car about a mile east of the
Mount Arlington station early last even
ing. Yet by freak Of fate nobody was
injured severely among the dozens VINO
were imperiled


Jutting out from the westbound track
directly in the path of the eastbounu
flyer, the box car stove in the side Of the
locomotive and ripped along the edges
of eight Pullman cars and day coach.
smashing windows, tearing of steps and
giving the passengers a most terrifying
experience.


Men and women were tossed from their
seats by a sudden application of the
brakes. A few were cut by flying glass
and splinters. But not even William
Nichols. engineer of the express train.
was badly huft; though his engine cab
was wrecked.


Goodness Saved His Life.


Nichols experience was hair-raising
one His iron nerve saved his life. When
he stopped his train passengers who piled
out were amazed at the story he told.


Peering ahead through the rain and
mist Nichols said, he had deserted only
a few hundred yards ahead. in the path
of the train, the object that he after
ward learned was the derailed box car.
He applied the emergency brakes. swung
back out of his cab and straddled the
boiler OF the locomotive, holding fast
to the bell standard. With an extra effort
he swung to the opposite side OF the
locomotive and was clinging to the side
when the crash came.


Locomotive Still Fit for Work.


Nichols climbed back into the wrecked
cab after the train had swept past the
box car. Then he stopped the train. 1t
was delayed about half hour. but the
locomotive was not crippled and Nichols
brought the train into the Hoboken ter
minal half hour behind the scheduled
time. 7:15 o'clock. Passengers. forgetting
their recent terror, were enthusiastic in
praise of the engineer


The box car was freighted with shoes.
Enough footwear to serve a regiment Of
tramps was strewn along the tracks.

Dear Aunt Laurie:


Behind a huge clump of trees a large
house stood upon a hill. Perhaps you
would not call it house if you had
seen it. 1t had once been house, or
rather a beautiful mansion.


The walls were grown with ivy like
those of the old castles described by
Sir Walter Scott. The roof was decay
ing and partly fallen in. The doors
were some of them rotted and some
were still standing. On the inner side
of those doors still standing We're sew
eral strong iron rods.


The gardens about the house were
once very beautiful. There were old
marble statues at the gateway. The
fountain was there, but the weeds grew
in its rocky bottom.


The inside of the house was also very
beautiful. The walls were hung with
rich tapestries woven with gold and
silver threads. There also were beau
tiful paintings and rich marble statues.


The upper story had never been
finished. The house was built by rich
old man who had lived many years ago.


This old man, whose name was Sir
Walter Carben, had lived in England
most of his life, which had been ro-
mantle one.


Sir Walter Carben had been very
daring youth, and against his fathers
will had married young American
woman, who afterward died, leaving
little daughter.


Sir Walter began to build this beau
tiful mansion and put within it every
thing he thought his daughter would
like While making trip to England
there came a storm and the ship sunk.
All members of the party were lost.


AS there were no heirs to the man
sion it was never finished. Perhaps
Soma dow soma unknown DerSOn may
appear and claim ownership. | really
hope someone fixes it up as it was and
makes it beautiful.

emperor's train for an hour today on the
return TO Cologne was abandoned be-
cause of tempestuous weather.


The German airship fleet. consisting OF
three cruisers, arrived here about 4
o'clock yesterday afternoon, landing
being made in a field outside the city.
AS soon as the squadron was sighted
Emperor William entered an automobile
and started for the landing place, which
he reached before the airships descended


Lieut.. Gen. Baron Moritz Won Lyncker,
inspector general of the Transportation
Of troops. and two officers of the general
staff Of the army. made the aerial trip
from Cologne. The emperor remained on
the landing grounds for two hours care
fully examining the aerial craft and con-
versing with the officers and engineers.


Averages 90 Miles an Hour.


The fleet averaged twenty-five miles an
hour on the trip. Before descending the
three airships executed a series Of pic
turesque maneuvers above the town. de-
lighting the kaiser and his companions.
They then approached the landing place,
keeping in line.


The trio reascended and started on
their return at O'Clock. The northwest
wind, which had helped them on their

freight steamer Santurce. which was in
collision with the north-bound tank
steamer Lgonier of Cape Cod last night,
arrived here at dawn today with a twelve
foot hole in her starboard side and her
after compartment full Of water


No one was injured in the accident
Half the crew of the Santurce. however,
jumped on the Lgonier. The collision

O'Clock. in the midst OF dense fog.


The Santurce had discharged a heavy
for New York. The Lgonier, with sev-
eral hundred thousand gallons Of oil

Santurce's side.

panic-str1cken and leaped over the bow

drew apart. Ten minutes after the colli-

out of hearing Of each other.


The Ligonier IL equipped with wire
less. Capt. Gates Immediately notified

and stated that he would remain In the

Edith three times and then fired a
bullet into his own head All four bull
lets were detected and the two pa
tients rasted easily last night at the
central emergency hospital with excel
lent chances to recover.


Mrs Cordes and her II year old
daughter Anna had just finished their
midday meal, when the husband
walked in, apparently intoxicated. Ac-
cording to the girl he shouted "Hullo"
in a loud voice and then pulled his re-
volver and fired.


The first bullet hit the woman in the
left breast, struck the fourth rib and
followed it beneath the skin across the
chest. The second shot entered just
below the eye, tearing down through
the cheek and passing through the
mouth The third bullet struck in the
back of the head, glanced upward on
the skull and emerged two inches
above where it struck.


The girl dashed into the lot, calling
for help. Mrs Cordes followed, run
ming to the bottom of the hill. where
she sat waiting for the ambulance,
which arrived half an hour later. AS
his wife was going out the gate Cordes
went into the kitchen and shot him
self in the head. The bullet glanced
off the skull and emerged about an
inch above where it entered. Cordes
was not found by the police for half
an hour or more after Mrs. Cordes had
been taken to the hospital.


The two bought their little story
and a half home just after the fire.
They had four children, Fred, aged
16; August, aged IA; Charles, aged 6.
and Anna Marie, aged II. Cordes is 40
years old and has been doing odd jobs
about the city. The two eldest sons
helped materially in supporting the
family and the wife added to the in
come by nursing.


According to Mrs. F. A. Teasland,
who lives next door, Cordes has been
intoxicated almost continually for five
or six weeks. During the last two
weeks Mrs. Cordes and the children
slept with Mrs. Teasland three times,
fearing to stay in the same house with
Cordes. Last Sunday night, said Mrs.
Teasland, Cordes put his wife out of
the house and told her not to come
back.

Captain William Griffith master of
the British ship Alexander Black.
which was wrecked January in the
breakers at Kahului, arrived here yes
terday on the liner China, accompanied
by two of his officers and nine mem
bers of the crew The ship was a total
loss and only the good judgment of the
skipper saved all hands from a watery
grave.


The Alexander Black with cargo of
inter from Chile for Kahului, arrived
off the Hawaiian port the afternoon of
January 4. The weather was fine and
clear and the sea smooth. The ship
entered the bay and set signal for a
pilot to guide the vessel TO safe
anchorage.


Suddenly there came a change in the
weather in the shape of a heavy squall
from the northwest. The wind was
accompanied by rain, thunder and
lightning. The sky darkened until 1T
was impossible to see more than a
ships length away. Sail was reduced,
but the storm was too fierce and the
space too restricted to allow the ship
TO work out of the bay.


In spite of all efforts the ship was
swept toward the beach When the
roar of the breakers struck his ear
Captain Griffith gave his order to aban-
don the ship. The crew got away in
two boats and they were barely clear
of the ship when it went with a crash
into the breakers, where the sea made
short work of the Alexander Black.


Captain Griffith found an opening in
the reef and through this the small
boats made their way. Nearing the
beach they encountered another line of
breakers shallow. but dangerous.
About this time two men on horseback
appeared on the beach and by sigus
showed the shipwrecked party where
to land.


Except the clothes they wore when
all hands lost everything.
The ship disappeared altogether jan
uary 10. The British consul at this
port Will hold an investigation of the
wreck and will make provision for
sending the crew home. With Captain
Griffth on the China were Chief Officer
John II. Jenkins, Second officer Robert
Slower and Sherwood Forest, an APP
prentice.

New York. Oct ARTHUR Irwin, the
Hlghlanders' scout. who is a close stu
dent OF baseball politics, says the time is
not far distant when the major leagues
will play series among themselves. He
predicts that after two Western and
Eastern trips have been made in each
league and each club has played fourteen
games with every other club in the same
circuit, the two seasons will end and the
two leagues viii come together in a
championship series, each American
League club playing eight games with
each National League club. This ar
rangement. which has been strongly ad-
vocated by Garry Hermann and other
progT essive club owners, Irwin says,
would renew the interest In the sport
and would enable fans in all the major
league cities to witness games With all
the clubs


Take New York, for instance" said
Irwin to-day. The Giants would play
seven games at home with all the Ma
tional League clubs, and along about the
middle of August they would begin play
ing all the American League teams, four
with each at the Polo grounds. In that
way there would be plenty of new base
ball for the public and increased gate
receipts for the club owners. The records
of games won and lost in each league
could be combined. and the finish would
afford many interesting situations. As
1t is now, in many of the cities public
interest is at low ebb after the LIST of
September, because the fans grow tired
or the same old faces"

SAN ANSELMO, June 19.-Huddled
about a campfire, sleepy. cold and badly
frightened, seven young women of San
Francisco, who are camping near here,
were forced to remain awake most OF
last night because gipsies stole all
their bedclothes while they were alb
sent at banquet and dance. From
shortly after midnight until breakfast
time they braved the chilly night air,
walking up and down at intervals to
keep the numbness from their cramped
limbs. In the party, besides Mrs. t.
Ellis. the chaperon, were. Miss Edna
Johnson, Miss Hazel Morrison, Miss
Ada Johnson, Miss Anita Sparna. Miss
Ruth Morrison, Miss Eva Morrison and
Miss Myrtle Bishop.


The young women moved into their
camp yesterday afternoon. On their
return, just after midnight, they en-
tered the camp singing and laughing
with their chaperon, who had accom-
panied them.


Miss Eva Johnson and her sister.
Ruth, were in the lead. AS the two
girls entered the circle of tents they
were startled at the sight of woman,
dressed in the gaudy rags of a gypsy.
stealing away in the moonlight with
large bundle in her arms. The girls
screamed and retreated to their COM
panions. A hurried consultation was
held, which resulted in Mrs. Ellis and
her charges venturing on an investiga- :
ton.


One by one the tents were entered
and each was found TO be bare of bed
clothes. Sheets. pillows. blankets and
quilts had all disappeared.


Their trunks were still at the rail
road depot, and aside from the few
articles of clothing which they had
brought in their suit cases there was
practically nothing in camp with which
they could cover their thin ball dresses


AS the nearest neighbor was a con-
siderable distance away they decided to
remain where they were.


The gipsies have not been found
They were caught stealing at San Ra-
fael yesterday and run out of town
after being fined.

afternoon from the Thames for Cardiff.

Antarctic will then be continued.

Evans, second in command, say that

officers and scientists to the number of

The young subaltern, detecting faint futtering

the helpless bird, warming 1t against his own body,
and, since to him Milan Mittu owed his life, his wise
little heart babe him repay with gratitude and the
penitude of his gifts


They formed a bond of comradeship, these two,
the and the parrot, and when the young subal-
term on the expiration of his furlough returned to
his regiment in India Milan Mttu journeyed with him


The Wise One thus the gray parrot was known in
those days to his winged brothers and this man of
comprehension learned there to chatter in the man
tongue; to whistle J1nSng DarTack tunes and repeat

Also the gray parrot learned to perch in compan-
ionable silence upon the high chair back when pic
lures formed in the curling smoke spirals from the
mans pipe and he drifted into vague reverie.


AS brother with brother they lived, Milan Mittu
sharing in the events of the days routine with equa
BILE philosophy. At night he assisted gravely at the
card table, drawing corks with gusto, and shriekng
approval when the man held the winning hand.


Then had come the desoatng plague With it the
regiment fell heir to the Wise One; but it was
rade, scarcely yelling his contempt for these man
folk who were too stupid to understand the ways of
the little feathered brothers And since he would not
i'ay the butfoon for them, they left him UNDECIDED
perch grouchlly in his window nook. Even his name
they forgot Milan Mittu they called him now after
the fashion of all parrots in this hated land, and
above all else he hated that name.


With the passing of time Milan Mittu's evil mood
settled to dignhed reserve. Converse he vol
unteered. He met it with naughty stare,
tempt uousy cooking his head one side but he no
longer vented his resentment with beak and claw
upon the unintentionally intrusive.


EVENTUALLY as the first cloud drifted away
- there came to the regiment commander,
headed Elise. And with them to Milan Mittu
the great love that flames in parrots heart.
and then for all time.

station at San Pablo was robbed last
night, about 500 being taken from the
till.


George Sloan, the agent, left the
station to go to his dinner about 8
o'clock in the evening. He returned to
the station about $50 o'clock. and one

At Marash, neighboring city, is
prosperous college for women, started in
1882. with preparatory departments at
Adana,s HAHN and Aintab, all f1ourishing
and popular, particularly since the new
regime has made it possible for Turkish
families to send their girls to school At
first it was difficult to persuade even
Protestant parents to educate their
daughters. 1t was contrary to custom,
but now that an educational 'boom" has
been started these schools are over
whelmed with applications from young
women they cannot accommodate. Their
educational standards are about the same
as those of the average finishing school
for young women in the United States,
and the same text books are used.


The college at Marash is on the Mount
Holyoke plan. There has been another
college for women on the Mount Holyoke
plan at Bitlis for more than forty years.
where two noble women, the Ely sisters
have been training wives and mothers for
the passing and the coming generations
Their usefulness cannot be even esti-
mated.


There is school for girls at Smyrna.
founded in 1881, with two hundred and
fifty students, and another at Adabazar.
eighty miles from Constantinople, with
about one hundred students.

PHOENIX, Ariz., May 13.-Sheriff
Carl Hayden and posse arrived at
Phoenix today with the Maricopa train
robbers in custody. The latter are
brothers, Oscar and Ernest Woodson,
recently from Oklahoma City and mere
youths Their flight from the railroad
and attempt to reach Mexico was made
without knowledge of desert conditions
and but for their arrest they probably
would have perished.


Ernest, the younger, emerged from
an arroyo in which they were hidden
near the Vikol mine when Hayden's
automobile appeared. He demanded
water and was told that he was under
arrest. The youth was so famished
that he paid no heed, only appealing
for water again and again and drink
ing almost a gallon. His brother, with
show of resistance, was languidly
taking his rifle from the saddle scab-
bard under cover of scant mesquite,
but desisted upon command


Both men were "tenderfeet" and too
weak after their so mile desert ride to
make a fight.


Hayden was forced TO abandon his
automobile on account of a breakdown
and the party rode into Casas Grandes
on farm wagon, continuing thence to
Phoenix.


The two young bandits were veri-
table walking arsenals when captured.
They carried a rifle, four revolvers and
two bowie knives. They will be tried
for train robbery under the federal
instead of the territorial statutes.
Their preliminary hearing before the
United States commissioner is set for
Monday. There is doubt that Woodson
is their right name. They declined to-
night to tell where their parents live

CHICAGO, Sept. 19.-William Jones,
negro, was partially identified this
evening as the slayer of Charles d.
Hitler, who was shot in defending his
daughters from an intruder who en-
tered through their bedroom window.


Hitler was chief local freight clerk
of the Rock Island railroad. He was
aroused early this morning by the
screams of his daughter Florence,
aged 12, and Clarice, is, who slept to-
gether. Hitler rushed to the bed
room and grappled with the man. They
rolled down the stairs locked in each
others arms. Then the intruder began
firing, three bullets entering the rail-
road mans body. His grasp relaxed
and the murderer fled. The police were
notified at once and soon arrested
Jones as he, was boarding a car.

During a four-hour Sweating" the
negro succeeded in concealing a bullet
wound in his hand, but blood from the
injury at length trickled down his
wrist and dropped upon the floor An
examination convinced the police that
the wound was fresh and they believe
that while Jones was graphing with
Heller and had his arm around Killers
back, a bullet from the negro's re-
volver passed through the white mans
body and entered Jones hand.


Florence Hitler told the police she
was awakened by feeling a rough
beard against her face. She knew the

worn by her fathers assailant.

The two-Story brick stable Of the Ar
lington Brewing Company at Rosslyn,
Va, was wrecked and the botting pant
badly damaged by fire last night The
fire occasioned a loss. il is believed. OF
about $1,000


Two weeks ago the stable OF tho Ross
lyn Packing Company, adjoining the
brewery property. was Quilted by FIRE.

could the cause he determined


Carl Croen, watchman in the employ
of the brewing company. discovered the
blaze while making his rounds through

distress signal was conveyed across tho
river by the steam whistle at the plant
and the fire department was notified by
telephone. An alarm was sounded from
box IA, calling engine companies ].
anu and truck L to 35th and NJ streets.

Under the rules of the fire department

ceed at once across the river, the other
companies awaiting orders. Only slight
delay was caused. however and the three
companies assisted in lighting the flames.



and directed the iiremen. The flames
were stubborn. Ii was nearly midnight
when the blaze was out.


When Watchman Croen discovered the
fire his first thought was for the thirty
eight horses in the building. They had
returned from the city after days
work and were in their stalls Tor the
night.


The watchman obtained assistance and
the rescue was prosecuted wi h such
haste that all the horses were saved
They were turned loose as they Wee
taken from the stable. Some difnculty
was experienced in getting them together
again.


Members of the fire department worked
hard to save the big buildings near the
stable. The flames managed to reach the
bottling plant, however, and damaged the
floor and roof, although the machinery In

1t is certain that the lire started on

ness and ether property were kept

oats and other feed were there.


Several Hours Hard Work.


The fire had gained considerable head

building. The roof had been attacked

floor. All the horses had been removed.

effect upon the flames It was only
after several hours hard work that the
firemen were able to control the blaze.


Only the four walls OF the stable were
left standing. The roof was entirely
destroyed Considerable damage was
done the bottling establishment.


The fire will not cause any interruption
to business.

terday afternoon the muddy water laden

gait.


Tugs and steamboats, felt it's power

This morning the current was. if any

The flood was racing down river at a

an hour.

NEW YORK, June 22.-At least four
persons were fatally injured and a doz-
en- others seriously hurt early today
when two crowded cars of a scenic rail
way on the bowery at Coney Island
jumped the track and dropped sixty
feet to the ground.


The cars of the big switchback had
filled and hauled up the incline and
the party, laughing and shouting,
plunged down the first incline. Up the
next incline the cars shot to the high
level of the scenic road and began to
dive down at a mile a minute pace.


Something went wrong with the
mechanism and the rear car jumped
the track rounding the turn jerking
the forward car with it. Ten of the
occupants were hurled from the cars
and went crashing down among the
scenery, falling to the ground, where
they lay unconscious. Six went down
with the first car and were pinned
fast beneath the wreckage., These
last We're the ones most seriously in
jured Five of them, Misses Minnie
Cobalt, Tessie Ericsson and Rose Will
son, all young girls, Richard RAIDER
maeher and Manuel De Colo, are resi-
dents Of Brooklyn. The sixth is Harry
Fletcher, twenty years old, of Los
Angeles.


Fletcher's injuries are reported to be
injury to the brain and the breaking
of four ribs.

which supply water for irrigating the

more sugar than formerly was

DENVER, Nov. 17.-With one wing
tip Of his machine crumpled like piece
of paper, Ralph Johnstone, the bril-
liant young aviator, holder of the
worlds altitude record, dropped like
plummet from height of 500 feet into
the inclosure at Overland park avia-
ton field and was instantly killed.


When the spectators crowded about
the inclosure reached him, his body lay
beneath the engine of the biplane. with
the white planes that had failed him in
his time of need wrapped about it like
a shroud. Nearly every bone in his
body was broken.


He had gambled with death once too
often. But he played the game to the
end, fighting coolly and grimly to the
last second to regain control of his
broken machine.


Fresh from his triumphs at Belmont
park, where he had broken the worlds
record for altitude with fight of 9714
feet, tombstone attempted to give the
thousands of spectators who stood with
craned necks to watch him an extra
thrill with his mast daring feat, the
spiral glide which had made the Wright
aviators famous. The spectators got
their thrill, but it cost Johnstone his
life.


The fatal fight was the second john
stone had made this afternoon. In the
first flight, when he was in the air
with Hoxsey and Brookins, he had
gone through his usual program of dips
and glides, with his machine apparent
ly under perfect control.


Then Johnstone rose again, and after
few circuits of the course to gain
height. headed toward the foothills.


WING TIP BREAKS


Still ascending, he swept back in
big circle. and as he reached the north
end of the inclosure he started his
spiral glide. He was then at an alti-
tude of about 800 feet. With his planes
tilted at an angle of almost 80 degrees
he swooped down in narrow circle,
the aeroplane seeming to turn almost
in it's own length. AS he started the
second circle the middle spur which
braces the left side OF the lower plane
gave way and the wing tips OF both
upper and lower planes folded up as
though they had been hinged. For a
second Johnstone attempted to right
the machine by warping the other wing
tip. Then the Mortified spectators saw
the plane SWerve like wounded bird
and plunge straight toward the earth.
Johnstone was thrown from his seat
as the nose of the plane swung down
ward. He caught on one side of the
wire stays between the planes and
grasped one of the wooden braces of
the upper planes with both hands. Then
working with hands and feet he fought
by main strength to warp the planes
so that their surface might catch the
air and check his descent.


For q second it seemed to the white
faced spectators almost under him
that he might succeed, for the football
helmet he wore blew off and fell much
more rapidly than the plane.


LOSES BRAVE FIGHT


The hope was only momentary,
however, for when about 500 feet from
the ground the machine turned COM
pletely over, and the spectators fled
wildly as the broken plane with the
tense-faced boy still fighting grimly in
it's mesh of wires and stays plunged
among them with a thud that could
be heard over the big field.


Scarcely had he hit the ground when
sensation mad brutes, both men and
women, swarmed over the wreckage
lighting with one another for SOU
venirs of the terrible occasion.


One of the broken stays had thrust
it's Jagged end almost through John
stones body. Before doctors or police
could reach the scene one man had
torn this splinter from the crushed
and mangled body and ran gleefully
away, carrying his horrible trophy
with the aviator's blood still dripping
from its end. Frantic the crowd tore
away the canvass from over his body
and fought for the very gloves that
had protected Johnstone's hands from
cold


DEATH INSTANTANEOUS

possible. Physicians declare death

wheels.

though trying to right herself.

divers to locate the Inflated submarine
entombed in which are three officers
and twenty-seven men.

because, in the opinion of experts,
either the naphtha reservoirs of the
Pluviose burst or the craft was so
badly damaged that she filed.

type Her length was 160 feet and her
displacement 39S tons.

triumphing.


The mayors proposal to build houses

forward and fell dead OF the back stoop.

neighbors TO the house. and Dr. Reid. of
Seabright. was summoned by telephone.
On his arrival he pronounced Truax dead.
Mrs. TruaA d!de a few hours later. Both
Truax and his wife were about forty-fve
years old.

Nairn, Ont. Jan. 23-The icebound
Spanish River to-day began to give up its
dead The first class car, one of the four
of the Canadian Pacific passenger train
which took the plunge down the embank-
ment on Friday afternoon, was raised
above the surface Of the river this after
noon


With one end suspended by heavy cables
from the bridge above and the other end
resting on the bank, workmen crept into
the wrecked interior and brought out sew
eral bodies. The forward part of the
coach WAS badly demolished from contact
with the ice and the river bottom. and ii

river.

known of twenty-five in addition to four
unidentified women and children whose

coach to-day. Besides these twenty-nine, IL

second class car.

Bridge late on Saturday. The ice directly
under the bridge was broken to-day and
diver was sent down. He located both the
first class car and the tourist car, which
disappeared from view on Saturday. Oper-
ating the big cranes from the bridge proved

ASBURY PARK, N. j., Nov. 13.-The
body of little Marie Smith, aged 10,
who had been missing since last
Wednesday, was found at dusk today
in the woods near her home.


Her mother, divining how the search
had ended, rushed from the house and
took in the full horror of the scene.
Half fainting, half in convulsions, she
was carried into the house, and there
is fear she will die.


Chance discovered the body, as
chance had hidden it. The wind had
strewn fallen leaves until their color
so matched the brown of the child's
dress and her brown hair that, as she
lay face downward, she was nearly in
distinguishable from her shroud.


Searchers had often passed within
twenty feet of the spot in full day.
light in the last three days, and it was
only a random glance that discovered
the mutilated body.


Thomas Williams, known in the
neighborhood as "Black Diamond" a
negro woodchopper, employed by the
girls aunt, has been missing since the
day on which Marie disappeared A
warrant was issued for him tonight,
and an alarm for his capture sent
broadcast through the county and
state. His ak was found near the
body.


The child was small for her years
and not strong, but seems to have
fought desperately with her assailant.
The broken sticks and trampled ground
around indicate that, as do her in
juries. The blue ribbon she wore in
her hair had been tied tight about her
throat. She also had been beaten on
the forehead with some blunt instru-
ment. The leaves under her face were
matted with her blood


In her struggles she had been

Frank, owner of the Sunlight said

How long they had been unconscious

the provisions, and the crew pumped

starvation, and each in his turn

Southampton, May 24.-Twenty-four
persons lost their lives as a result of a
collision to-day between the steamer
Skerryvore and the German bark j. c..
Vinnen. in the English Channel. The
Skerryvore sank. Only two Of the
steamers crew were rescued, one of
whom died short time later. The bark
arrived here.


The collision occurred about 1 o'clock
this morning off Hastings. The night
was clear.


According to the account given by the
officers of the Vinnen. the Skerryvore
suddenly crossed the bark's bows. The
Vinnen struck her abaft the n1ainmast
The Skerryvore's boilers exploded and
she sank in a few minutes


Boats were lowered from the Vinnen
and a search was made of the waters
where the steamer went down Two
men were found, but one died The sole
survivor says that the crew numbered
twenty-five men. He and most of the
others were in their hunks at the time
of the collision The crash awoke him.
but the vessel sank before boats could
be cut away. He clung to the wreck
age and became unconscious


The Skerryvore had a cargo of iron
ore. The Vinnen's bows were badly
damaged

Dear Aunt Laurie:


One day little May was baking cakes
with her mother.


MAY l bake a ginger bread man?"
she said.


Her mother consented, so she baked
a very nice one She did not eat him
that night.


AS the clock struck II she was awak-
ened Some one was calling her. At
first she thought it was her mother,
but soon she saw that on her pillow
was the same ginger bread man she
baked


"Come with me-" he said, "and 1 will
bring you back safe


The window flew open and they all
flew away. Soon she arrived at Gin
gertown. The gates were guarded by
two fat ginger bread men who bowed
very low as they entered. They went
into a palace which was made of gin
ger bread. There was table set. The
plates, cups, saucers, knives, forks and
spoons were made of ginger bread.
Soon the guests came. They were all
ginger bread men, but they wore beau
tiful costumes.


The king sat in the big chair with
May on his right and the queen on his
left. The supper was delicious and
May was sorry to leave for home.


When she awoke her mother was
shaking her and asking if she was go
ing to sleep all day.


Your loving niece,


MARGARET ELLIOTT,

The Circulation team of The Evening
Star Duckpin League took two games
from the Ads Thursday, the last even
ing Of the season, tying the latter team
for first place, and won the roll-off
game by ten pins. It being anybody's
game until the last ball on each side
had been rolled. Incidentally, Circula-
ton rolled 548 in the last game OF the
regular set thereby taking the prize
for high game. and came within three
pins of making high set also.


The contest in The Star league this
season has been interesting through
out, as no one team at any time had
commanding lead in the race. nearly
every team being at the top at some time
during the year. The Ads have done
the steadiest work. however, although
they lost out in the final set. For thir-
teen weeks they took two games out OF
three in each set lost two in the four
teenth week and then for four weeks
more took the odd game. Circulation,
however. developed the habit or taxing
the entire set every now and then, haV-
ing ten such performances to its credit
out of twenty-five sets rolled, and this
together with the uphill fight of Thurs
day. was sufficient to land the cham
pionship.


The Omegas took third prize. being
but five games behind the leaders. This
team would probably have made bet
ter showing had all its members been
regular in attendance.


The Pleas were fourth-four games
behind-and the Antiques and Alphas
tied for the cellar position. The latter
team was very weak at the start of the
season, but has been winning pretty
regularly for some weeks. Its members
deserve credit for sticking gamely after
being almost hopelessly distanced In
the first few weeks.

dicates. is made up Of men from the
distribution department Of The Star,

VICTORIA, B. c., May 7.-While
y Commander Sakuma and his four


teen men were dying under the
sea on the drowned submarine No.
during the Japanese naval maneuvers
off Kure April Is the commander wrote
a letter to the emperor begging for
giveness for the loss of the vessel and
commencing his officers and men.


The letter was found after the sub
marine had been raised. Portions of
the letter were brought to Victoria to-
day on the steamer Aymeric.


The submarine was Of the newest
type and was engaged near Hiroshima
bay, carrying out it's part in the
maneuvers, being submerged 1900 yards
east of it's parent ship.


Two hours passed without notice Of
the submarines failure to rise, and the
usual naval signals being unanswered
a boat was lowered and efforts made to
locate the submarine. Seven destroyers
were ordered to the scene and a search
made.


The submarine was located April 16
and next day it was refloated and
towed to Kure. After the craft was
docked an examination revealed the
bodies Of the commander and crew and
also the record of the commander tell
ing what happened from the time the
vessel sunk.


COMMANDER PRAISES MEN


Much of the message was not pub
lished, but it is stated that Lieut..
Sakuma expressed sorrow to the en-
peror for the loss of his vessel and
brother officers and crew, whom he
praised for their heroisn and calm wait
for death. He requested the emperor
to succor their families.


The last writing was made an hour
and twenty minutes after the boat was
submerged and conveyed messages of
farewell to the minister of the navy
and friends, stating that breathing had
become so difficult that further writing
was impossible.


The letter said one of the crew had
tried to close the valve of the ventila-
tlon pipe. but the chain had broken.
He tried to close the valve with his
hand, but was too late.


Water began to enter by the rear
part of the boat, which fell 20 degrees
The dynamo was submerged and all
the lights went out, bad gas accumu-
lating almost simultaneously and max
ing breathing difficult.


The crew drove the current of water
from the main tank and tried to get
rid of it by hand pumps. They were
drenched as they worked and also
chilled.


The message ended with statements
that all were ready for death, realiz-
ing no more could be done, and they
hoped for forgiveness for the loss of
the vessel.


The submarine was being tested on a
gasoline, semi-submerged voyage.

THE Chinese woman is generally regarded as


i the meekest creature living: but it has been
scarcely two generations since Chinese women
fought CALAMITY against the imperial forces and
the soldiers of England, France, and the
United States.


Sometime prior to 1850 Chinese literary
authority read a number of Christian tracts
and became convinced that he was chosen to
uproot idolatry in China. He formed a society
known as the God Worshipers. and assumed
the title of Heavenly Prince. The society grew
amazingly and his followers declared that he
was the Son of God, and worshped him accord
ingly. Polygamy was a feature of the God
Worshipers' religion, and the founder himself
had thirty wives.


In 1850 the society came into collision with
the imperial authorities. the state religion in
to the support of the Heavenly Prince and for
sometime the rebellion was a great success,
some of the richest provinces of China being laid
waste. In 1853 half million women from vari-
Gus parts of the country were formed by the God
Worshipers into brigades Of thirteen thousand
EACH under female officers. OF these. ten
thousand were picked women. carefully drilled.
The remainder formed sappers' and miners
corps. digging moats making earthworks, erect
ing batteries, and the like.


For ten years the rebels fought with varying
success and throughout the war the brigades
of women exhibited splendid courage: but in
1864 the rebellion was finally put down, the
founder making his last stand in Marking, which
place his remaining followers, including the dec
mated brigade of women warriors, defended
CALAMITY. Finally, however it fell under the
combined attack of the imperial forces, the
English, the French, and the Americans. The
leader persisted by his hand in the blazing ruins
of the palace he had occupied for eleven years.

"Since no one has had the courage to
blow up the German autocrat, l have
decided to throw bomb"

the writer were fruitless and accord
ingly unusual steps were taken to
guard against any untoward incident.


All of the windows of the houses
overlooking the streets through which
the royal party passed brom the pal
ace to the railway station were or
dered closed temporarily and the sta
ton itself was packed with troops.

distance was closely guarded.

Mrs. Marie Bloberger, widow living
at 721 Santee street, was in Justice
Summerfleld's court yesterday charged
by J, L. Starr, a dairy inspector, with
falling to provide for her two minor
children. Mrs. Bloberger was arrested
Tuesday and remained in the county
Jail all night. She vas released
Wednesday morning by Justice Sum
merfield when he heard her story, but
when she reached her place of employ
ment she was told the story of her
arrest had preceded her and she was
discharged. The discharge meant the
loss of a position paying 81 a week.


When Mrs. Bloberger entered the
court room about the noon hour yester-
day she carried q small parcel. Sitting
In a. corner of the empty chamber she
opened the parcel, disclosing two
crackers. 1t was her MONDAY meal,
and she ate it, not as a defense of her
position nor to arouse sentiment, but
because she was hungry.


Mrs Bloberger was without an at
torney because she was without money.
The proceedings were beyond her COM
prehension, and she could not under
stand why she was arrested for failing
to provide for her children when she
had barely enough to support herself.
The children, she said, had been taken
by a charitable organization receiving
state assistance, and were well cared
for. How her arrest and the loss of
her wages would benefit them was
puzzling.


The preliminary examination was
continued by Justice Summerfield I'M





cused was alone and there were q
number of persons present to testify
for the prosecution, the latter was not
ready to proceed. Justice Summerfield
again ordered the woman's release on
her own recognizance, and she left the
court room for her home, still wonder
ing over the peculiarities of justice.

Der of cases it was impossible to get

camp began today. A special plot of
ground was set aside on the opposite
side of the hill from the mouth of the
slope and men were engaged all day
digging graves while the mourners
carried their loved ones and laid them
to rest.


The rescuers have now reached the
lowest part of the stope and have been
working their way back examining
headings on the other side. Eight or
ten bodies were found in one group.


About midnight three bodies were
found lying close together with every
indication that they had not been
killed by the explosion, but had died
of suffocation.

coat and wrapped it around his head
as if to keep out the gas. Another
was lying face downward with his arms
covering his face. Another was holding
cloth over his face.

S LONDON, July 10.-When Theodore
Roosevelt was here he had two inter
views with King George.


The first conversation was formal and
ceremonial. The second, it is said now,
was arranged especially so that the
former president could have a heart to
heart talk with the king. 1t took place
at luncheon to which King George
had invited Roosevelt. Except Queen
Mary. nobody of consequence was at
the luncheon, and the king and Roose-
welt could and did talk with perfect
freedom and frankness. Mrs. Roosevelt
joined the little party some time after
luncheon.


The Call correspondent learns on au-
thority that at this second meeting
Roosevelt explained TO King George his
views on world politics, especially with
reference to Anglo-German relations
and Anglo-American relations and in
direct connection with the latter sub
ject on Anglo-Irish relations.
DANGER AHEAD


Then the question of an Anglo
American arbitration treaty was dis
cltssed. Roosevelt frankly told the
king that as long as Americans of
Irish birth or parentage remain un-
conciliated by the English there will be
no chance that the United States SEN
ate will ratify such treaty. Further
more Roosevelt insisted that the dan
ger to Anglo American relations from
the same cause would be. very grave
should a crisis arise under circum-
stances in which ordinary American
sentiment would favor England.


King George regretfully admitted
the truth of 'Roosevelt's representations.
At this point the conversation between
King George and the former president
naturally turned to home rule for Ire
land Roosevelt advocated granting
home rule as essential to cementing
not only the British empire but Anglo
American sentiment.


It is certain that before this inter
view with the king Roosevelt had OBJ
tained the opinions not only of the
Irish leaders with whom he has been
long familiar. but OF Irishmen who are
not connected with the home rule
movement, like Sir Horace Plunkett,
who explained perfectly that home rule
should be tried under certain condi-
tions.


Besides, Clifford Pinchot, formerly
United States forester, and Roosevelt S
friend, made it his business during his
two protracted visits to Ireland this
year to gather information for Roose-
welt from the Irish unionists. whom he
met at Sir Horace Plunkett's home.
where he was a guest and other
sources.


HOME RULE INEVITABLE


The effect of this information was
that Roosevelt and Pinchot realized
that home rule is inevitable and that
there is no serious opposition to 1t by
a coterie of Ulster Orangemen. They
learned, too, that the tory feeling
against home rule except among Irish
unionists and their family connections
in England, has died out, practically,
and that at the last two general elec-
tions the old anti-Irish cry was found
wholly ineffective for electioneering
purposes


King George sympathized with Roose-
velt's arguments.


Subsequently his majesty called to
him not only Premier Asquith. but
Lloyd-George, chancellor of the ex-
chequer, and Arthur Balfour, formerly
premier and now leader OF the oppo-
sition in the house of commons. with
all of whom he discussed the views
Roosevelt had laid before him. The
queen strongly supported the king In
his demand that the leaders of both
English parties put their heads together
and try to solve the Irish problem.

CHICAGO. ILL.,, March 25.-Eight thou
sand painters and decorators in Chicago
are preparing for a strike April 1. whei,
their present agreement with the con-
tractors expires. The local unions af-
filiated with Martin b. Madden's District
Council have repudiated the agreement
which their officers signed with the en-
,ployers, and will join the '.revolutionists''
in the strike for an increase of cents
an hour In wages.


Several months ago three of the larg-
est local unions of painters rebelled
against the dictation OF Madden and with
drew their delegates from the Painters
District Council. An appeal was taken
to the painters International convention
and the rebellious locals were ordered
back. When they refused their char
ters were revoked. The rebels pro-
cured an injunction restraining the other
locals from interfering with them, and
an internal fight has been in progress
two months.


The officers of the unions which re-
manned loyal to Madden and his council
made an agreement with the employers
for two years at the present scale of 90
cents an hour.


When the rank and file of the unions
discovered that they had been bound for
another two years at the old wages they
charged their officers with bad faith,
and they have since gone over to the Sc
ceding faction.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 22.-Loom-
ing out Of dense fog near the light
ship off Point Reyes, her course laid
seaward across the path of the coast
wise steamers, the tramp steamer
Selja, bound for San Francisco from
Hongkong, was rammed and sunk by
the steamer Beaver this afternoon.


Although the big vessel filed with
water and .was lost to sight within
fifteen minutes after the collision, the
only fatalities were the death of two
Chinese members of the crew.


Captain Olaf Lie, his wife and two
children, the six other officers and the
thirty-five members of the crew, were
rescued by the crew of the Beaver.


The Beaver had just cleared this port
and was northbound for Columbia river
points. The passenger vessel was pro-
ceeding under a slow bell, her Whls-
tie sounding at intervals of one min
ute. Suddenly, not more than two
ship lengths away, the Selja appeared
off the starboard bow The Beaver S
engines were quickly reversed, and
from her deck the passengers could
see the other vessel come to a stop.
The collision could not be averted,
however, and the Beaver ploWed
her way into the port side of the Selja,
just forward of amidship. There was
no confusion on either vessel.


Three boats, with Mrs. Lie and the
children in the first one, were lowered
over the side of the sinking ship. One
boat was battered against the side and
demolished, it's occupants being thrown
into the water, two of them being lost.


Under the direction of Capt. William
Kidston, two boats left the Beaver and
took the remainder of the Selja's crew
in safety from her deck a few minutes
before the vessel disappeared beneath
the surface.


Capt Lie remained with his ship
until the last, scrambling over the side
and into the water after the boats had
left, and being rescued along with Chief
Engineer Ronbeck Eggen, who had
fallen overheard.


The Beaver, her bow plates smashed
and leaking slightly, put back to this
port arriving at o'clock tonight.


The Selja was owned by the Port
land-Asiatic Steamship company. She
carried a cargo of general merchandise
consigned to local Chinese and Jap
anese merchants, valued at more than
500 900. The Beaver plies between
Portland, San Francisco and Los An
geleS.

BERLIN. May IA sham fight, in
which 10000 German soldiers of all
arms took part occupied the atten-
ton of Colonel Roosevelt and Emperor
William for several hours this morning.


After the battle on the field of Doe
beritz the troops paraded before the
former president and the emperor, who
were standing side by side some 20
PAGES in front of the gorgeous staff.
They saluted the colors of the vari-
Gus commands. the emperor touching
his helmet and Colonel Roosevelt lift
ing his sombrero


HONORED, SAYS KAISER


Speaking partly in English and part
ly in German, the emperor, turning to
Colonel Roosevelt. said: My friend
Roosevelt, you are the first civilian
who has reviewed our soldiers,' and
then TO the German officers: we are
honOred in having here the distin-
guished colonel of the Rough Riders"


The former president was five hours
in the saddle, having been furnished
superb mount by the emperor. During
the battle. which covered a field 20
miles square, Roosevelt spent much
time talking with the emperor. They
drew apart from the others and at
times were exceedingly vehement in
their gestures. Roosevelt wore dingy
khaki uniform. while the emperor and
his generals in uniforms of blue with
gold helmets made a striking contrast.


The maneuvers were witnessed also
by a party which included Empress
Auguste Victoria, Crown Prince Fred
erick William. Crown Princess Cecilie,
Princess Victoria Louise, Prince Adel-
bert Kermit Roosevelt and Henry
White, former American ambassador to
France.


The engagement opened with an ar
tiIIery duel. followed by a sharp col
lision along the whole front between
the cavalry and infantry. The thou
sand cavalry participated.


The day was bright and sunny and
the effect was most pleasing from
Muehlenberg hill, from which Roose-
welt, the emperor, the umpires and Off
GERS of the general staff watched the
finale.


Parting saIutations were then ex-
changed and the imperial party left in
automobiles for Potsdam, while Roose-
welt, Kermit and White returned to
this city.

quite able to deliver his lecture tomor-
row before the university. Doctor
Fraenkel. who has been treating the
former presidents throat. said that in
all probability he would permit his
patient to carry out his plans.

embassy tonight to the Roosevelts.

nounced at strike headquarters that

about by the New Jersey strikers, who

mn. They had rejected the trims last

City and President Towne of the New
York merchants association cleared
way for agreement this afternoon.

day night to accept the companies
offer conditional upon similar action
being taken by the men across the
river The agreement provides that

lence during the strike

panies and their employees does not

pathy with the express company en-
ployes and later presented demands of

brotherhood of teamsterS declared to-
night that the fight of the chauffeurs

She reached q stretch Of woods and be-

PASADENA, Aug. 91.--Drinking to
the fullest of the beauties and grand
eur of Southern California, 107 of the
worlds greatest star gazers yesterday
made the pilgrimage to the summit
of Mt. Wilson, where are located the
wonderful telescopes and Astronomical
instruments of the Carnegie solar OBJ
setvatory.


The trip up the long, winding trail
started in the early morning while the
dew was on the grass and the air was
filled with the songs of many birds.
Some of the astronomers made the as
cent by the observatory road or wagon
train, via Eaton's canyon. In this lot

reporters, drivers and guides. At Sny-
ders camp, about half way up the
mountain side, where the old nursery

the halt was made for luncheon. There
were eleven wagons in the trains and
each had its own lunch basket which
was filled with good things to eat
direct from the larder of the Hotel
Maryland.


The other contingent made their way
via Sierra Madre and the old foot
trail. At the end of the car line the
mountain climbers were met with sad
die horses, mules and burros. There

about twenty of the astronomers pre-

stated they We're mountain climbers

This party lunched at the Orchard

SCIENTISTS DINE AT HOTEL


The advance guard began arriving

o'clock. From that time until sun
down, tired although bouyant and
happy scientists came struggling into
camp ready for hearty dinner which
was waiting.


Contrary to expectations, instead of
sitting down to rest after the long
journey, the visitors had no sooner
reached sight of the great tower tele-
scope, piercing the air over 100 feet
above the tallest tree, than they made
grand rush for this marvel of the
age which has been planned and built
under the personal direction of DR..
George Ellery Hale, director of the
observatory


Just at sunset, while the famous star
gazers were being thrilled by the gor-
geous glow of the departing sun,
which today will be the subject of

summit until this morning, but when

gers. While two of them kept the VIC

down the aisle.

work one of them entered the motor
mans compartment and ran the car to
Edmonds. small station north OF
Georgetown, where the men got off and
entered the Northern Pacific freight
yards.


1t is thought they boarded a south
bound train which left shortly after.

saloonkeepers and bartenders, who were
on their way home after their night s

OAKLAND, Nov. 8.-Numerous bur
glaries in downtown stores have been
traced to a boy robber band composed
of four schoolbodys, led by an Indian
named Frank Marshall, 80 years old.
The four Juvenile members of the gang
were arrested this afternoon when de-
tectives raided their rendezvous in a
shack back of the Pacific States tele-
phone company building in Franklin
street.


The boys were reported, missing from
their homes two weeks ago. When
captured this evening. the four boys
were cooking over an open Are. The
recently served time in the city Jail for
petty larceny.

Mountford, IA years. Doyle was the
leader when Marshall was away, and

ing cups and trophies. The trophies

deserted shack in the vacant lot back

took for sleeping quarters, cooking out
side. The view from Franklin street
is obscured by big brick wall of the
telephone building. From other streets
the inclosure could not be seen. The
shack is within a stones throw of the
poStoffice

through their. having made slugs to tap
nickel in the slot machines. They We're
looting candy boxes, telephone ma

means. The police, seeking the mis-
creants, found that the slug users were

Matthew does not mention any names
or number of persons. but as perfected
tradition requires both names and num-

forthcoming The number was fixed at
three. for symbolical reasons: First. to
represent the trinity Cor SO says Hilary
of Aries: second, to represent the three
branches OF the human race descended
from Noah through his sons Shem. Ham
and Japhet, and third, to represent the
three gifts, gold. franklncense and myrrh.


Bede in his De Collect gives the names
Of Melchoir, Gaspar and Balthasar in
the order named. He also describes
their dress, which is probably taken from
an early painting. He also says that
the first two brought gold. while the last
named wise man brought the myrrh,
leaving out of account the frankincense
But other names had been in use long
before Bede wrote. Among these earlier
names were Rithiscara, Melchoir and
Gathaspar; Magalath. Pangalath and
Saracen; Appellius. Amerius and Damas-
Gus, and scores Of others. Gaspar, Mel
choir and Balthasar are the now COM
monty accepted names, which have long
been In use as charms against epilepsy,
while the three wise men under the
names given are the patron saints Of
travellers.

winter sometimes lost her temper

MANCHESTER, Sept. 9.-About 200
unemployed invaded and took posses
sion of ST. Martins church here and
remained encamped in it all one night.


Their leaders said. after their evic-
ton, that the seizure was designed to
call public attention to the fact that
the labor exchanges did not meet the
wants of homeless and workleSS men,
and that nothing was done for them.


Amid the dust and dirt of four years
desertion, for the building has been
closed that time, the men slept and
rested, and in the early morning, after
the passing of a raging thunderstorm,
the interior presented strange spec
tacle.


Two hundred men, hungry and worn
out, sat or lounged about, and Pendle-
bury, their leader, vigorously ha-
rangued them from the chancel steps,
urging them to resistance against the
forces of order till some attention was
paid to their. needs.


With brooms borrowed from cottages
around, the tenants began to put
their house in order. and they quickly
made a place a bit cleaner and more
comfortable.


They did not, however. enjoy the
fruits of their labor, for barely was 1t
finished when they were challenged by
the police, who ordered the men to
leave the building.


There was a momentary show of re-
sistance, and then Pendlebury led the
men out, being satisfied that the au-
thority of the trustees had been given
for their eviction.


The mems leader now states that the
occupation of other buildings Of the
kind is contemplated. and that these
tactics will be supplemented by a mass
meeting called on the scene of former
unemployed riots.

hundred. but it is possible that this will
be exceeded

tago from San Jose and other points, are
now engaged in the work of rescue, and
even to-day several living persons were
TAKEN from under the piles of stone and
timbers- where dwelling houses once
stood


The number of sick and injured can
not be counted, many of them having
been removed to adjoining towns and
villages, and since the disaster scores
have died from their injuries.


Dr. Bocanegra, the Guatemalan repre-
sentative to the Central American Court
of Justice. was demented when removed
from the ruins the day following the
earthquake. but ne is now recovering

slightly injured. The body of his wife
who was killed, has been embalmed, pre-
paratory to being sent 20 Guatemala.


Paraiso village OF two thousand per-
sons about eighteen miles east of San
jose, also suffered severely from the
earth shocks, reports reaching here indi-
eating that nearly a hundred persons
were killed.


Large assures have opened in Cartago
province. which have given additional
cause for alarm. Ten thousand persons
have been rendered homeless, and the
severe rains and lack of food and drink
ing water are responsible for much suf-
fering 1t has been found Impossible TO
provide shelter for the people. who are
hIddled together in a pitiable condition

ton Of Ricardo Jiminez as President OF

SAN BERNARDINO, July 21.-
George Hamer and Roy L. Davis ar
rived here today after terrible ex-
perience crossing the desert and noun
tains. For 12 hours they were without
water, the mercury standing at 13O


The hot blasts of wind blowing from
Death valley added to their sufferings.
The men started from Furnace creek
Monday, driving a covered wagon.
They figured on making certain water
holes on the way, but in the night
camped during the morning hours in
the very heart of a desolate waste
being compelled to stop in order to
doctor a sick horse.


At o'clock that morning they con-
sumed their last drop of water and
started for the mountains, having re-
gained their position on the desert,
The heat and the illness of one horse
made progress slow, and it was not
until o'clock that night that they
finally reached a waterhole.


The two horses were ready to drop.
Their tongues were hanging from their
mouths, their eyes were sunken and
it was with difficulty the men could
restrain the animals from plunging
into the water hole Both men also
suffered, and were barely able to water
the horses. This duty performed and
their own thirst being quenched, the
men threw themselves down on the
open desert and slept.


The mountain climb proved a try
ing one, the heat waves ascending to
the summit, and relief was not eX-
perienced until they had crossed Cajon
pass and were half way down the
west side of the mountains.

building had ample warning and sought
places of safety before the water reached
the structure.


The flood and ice gorge was the in
direct cause of a small-siZed strike among
about 200 railroad section hands this
afternoon. These men were landed about
mile and a half from the town from
trains sent out from Baltimore and Will
mington for the purpose of clearing the
tracks. The men walked TO town along
side the huge ice blockade.


When the men realized the dangerous
work they We're about to tackle they
placed their shovels upon their shoulders
and marched back to the trains, refusing
pointblank to work.

From the London Chronicle


OF bills introduced. read and passed In
the shortest possible time, one recalls
the bill suspending the habeas corpus act
in Ireland in 1866, which passed through
both houses and received the royal assent
before the midnight of the day which had
seen its birth. Similar hustling methods
distinguished the explosives bill of 1855,
which followed the scare cause by the at
tempt To injure a Whitehall building The
bill was steered through both houses in
one evening and received the royal as
sent the following morning.


Bills for general pardon. or acts of
grace. as they are generally called, prob
ably hold the record for rapid progress
through parliament. For they originate
with the crown, and are simply read once
In each house. all the members being UNI
covered after which they receive the
royal assent. Neither house has the
power to amend them in any way. An
act of indemnity. too. protecting any one
against the consequences of breach OF
the law. although subject to the ordinar,
procedure, is usually passed through all
its stages in single sitting, was done
for instance. in 1850. when a bill was
passed indemnifying a noble lord who
had voted without taking the oath.

landed safely and the fire was extin-
guished with $2500 damage, but there
was great alarm in the city and on the
harbor until all details were known.
Everybody remembered how u little
more than six years ago the Slocum
caught fire in the East river when
crowded with 1900 pleasure seekers,
mostly women and children, and was
burned to the waters edge, with 93S

Today, as then, the fire started in the

wooden superstructure. There was no
panic The women were badly fright
ened, but the crew had no trouble in

urging the abolition of the United States
