The terrible wreck near Benson, Ariz.,
furnishes another argument against the
continued use of wooden cars for pas
sengers on railroad trains. A steel bag
gage car was uninjured, but the mail
car was splintered and partly telescoped,
while the chair car and tourist sleepers
were badly smashed.


1t is time for Congress to take positive
action on this matter. A law should be
enacted at the present session requiring
all interstate railroads within seven years
to scrap all their wooden passenger cars
and substitute steel cars, changing at
least one-seventh of their entire equip
ment every year. beginning with the pas
sage of the law.


1t ia a national shame that the rail-
roads are permitted to carry coal and
coke in safer cars than they furnish for
human beings.


Steel cars have been proved practical;
they are not unduly expensive, and they
are exceedingly durable. There is no
reason why the forced substitution should
be longer delayed.

Teresa Carreno, the only pianist in
the Philharmonic course this year,
made her recital appearance at Simp-
son auditorium last night. She was
greeted by one of the most representa-
tive musical audiences that has assem-
bled under that roof this year. and
her work throughout the interesting
program was keenly sympathetic and
in that best mood which an artist can
only attain when cognizant of under
standing and appreciative listeners.


Madame Carreno in selecting her
program conferred two great kind
nesses upon her audience First, she
chose works which were entirely un-
hac<neyed, and many of them almost
new here, and she also made up pro-
gram with gratifyingly intelligent
selections. She was not content, as
are many pianists of her brilliant tech
nidue. to play a few scintillant piano
smashing numbers, but found instead
selections which permit the exhibition
of supreme manual skill and also or
a magnificent mentality.


This selection of new numbers for
the program is more more important
than it appears to the casual concert
goer, for last year practically every
one who played during the winter in
cluded the moonlight Sonata" upon
the program, and only the most daring
pianist omitted the rendition of Liszt
Rhapsodie.


Last night we had neither Of these,
but had instead the beautiful MacDoW-
ell (Celtic) Sonata, which has all the
novelty of newness, although it was
Dlayed here recently at the concert of
the American Music society. There
are many beautiful movements in this
work, and while the treatment of the
themes is essentially modern, 1t never
theless embodies some beautiful mel
odies and phrases which are rarely
sensuous. These passages became
glowing and warm under the magic
touch Of the artist, who imbues every
one with a richness which rivals the
cello, so deep her touch and so reso-
nant her tonal power.


The Chopin sonata, op. 5S, was her
opening number, and was warmly
greeted especial interest centering on
the almost reverential manner in
which she interpreted the slow move
ment in the second part.


One might exhaust all the adjectives
suggestive Of limpidity when describ-
ing the playing OF Beethoven's G
major Rondo, and yet fail to give
an adequate idea of the beautiful sim
plicity with which this charming eX-
ample of early composition was rem
dered.


The Schubert-Liszt arrangement of
the King" and three other Liszt
numbers concluded the announced pro-
gram, to which We're added the artists
own composition "Valse Teresita," 3"
and the "Valse Souvenir de Wen"


Madame Carreno will play the Grieg
Concerto at the Symphony concert
Friday afternoon.

Back went Miss Katy. On went Miss
Greenie. Through field and field hop
ped the proud grasshopper. Often did
she hear herself admired. That was her
only happiness. If she was so beauti-
full among the green, how much finer
she would look out in the brown road.
She knew too well the dangers of the
roads, for her mother had told her
that there only brown grasshoppers
were safe. But oh, to be admired! Just
one song would she sing out in the
dust. She began. Sure enough, she had
been heard, for from all around came
flutterings in the grass.


She saw the field creatures look at
her in admiration. Yes, she would
sing once more, to see how many
would praise her. Down the road came
the proudest creature. she had ever
seen. His high head was in the air
and his straight long legs were step
ping proudly toward her. How quiet
he was. Such bliss to be sought after
by one so proud! on he came as if to
whisper his praises, but alas, the Tur-
key Gobbler must have gotten too
close, for poor, proud Miss Greenie
was soon struggling in his bill and the
song was stopped short.

Once upon a time there was a Miss
Greenie Grasshopper, who got her name
from the beautiful silken gown she
wore She was very vain, because
the other grasshopers and wood bugs
thought her beautiful. But none of
them liked her, for she seemed always
to be trying to attract attention just
to show her beauty.


Never was there a party nor merry
dance that she did not try to dance
the longest and sing the highest. Even
her warmest friends had tired of her.
Now, Greenie Grasshopper's mother
was very sensible creature who
prieved over her daughters unladylike
ways. Often did she talk to her about
her proud actions and try to teach her
good manners. But no use. Her kind
ness was not appreciated. The other
grasshoppers would have nothing to
do with the disagreeable neigEbor. No
one but Miss Katy Did, her cousin,
would even go hopping with her. But
one day even she became hurt at the
way in which her pretty cousin acted

Washington. Jan. 4.-The President and
Mrs. Taft held their first state reception

and in every detail it was a brilliant affair.
So many changes had been scheduled for
the large receptions this winter that the
several hundred visitors were on the out
look from the time they entered the east
door. and from that time on agreeable sur
prises awaited them.


For many years the line of those invited
reached through the lower corridor up
through the front hallway into the state
dining room and on through the Red Room
into the East Room. where the visitors dis
persed. Tonight the entrance was directly
into the East Room from the lower cor
ridor through the Green Room and on
through the Blue Room. where. almost be-
fore the guests were aware. they were
presented to the President Mrs Taft and
the wives OF the Cabinet members.


Mrs Taft received with the President
and Cabinet women until the guests of
honor. the diplomats, had passed down the
line. She then retired to the other side OF
the room. where Miss Helen Taft. Miss
Elizabeth Parsons and few friends en-
gagged her attention Later on Mrs Taft

impromptu reception.


In the state dining room a table was laid

nations and pink shaded candles. with ferns

tractive spectacle. Ranged along the table
were salads. sandwiches. confections and

HAMPSTEAD. L. L.. March 1O.-Ons
man was burned to death and five others
were injured. one perhaps fatally. when
fire destroyed the Nassau county poor
house early this morning. The injured
persons were taken to the county hospital
at Mineola.


Most of the thirty-seven inmates OF the
poorhouse were old. many invalids and
some bedridden. All were asleep when
the fire, which is supposed to have started
in the kitchen. began to crackle and send
forth volumes of smoke. Supt. Benjamin
Sprasue and his three assistants were
also asleep when the alarm was given
Already the old building was reeking with
smoke and soon the inmates were in
panic.


Hall Congested by Panic.


Those who could get to their feet made
rush for the stairs, and presently the
hallway was congested with screaming
men and women.


The house burned like finder. The con-
gestion in the hall was relieved by drag
ring men and women to the open, but the
stairs were soon blazing. and then came
cries of terror from the windows. Ihere
was no time to get to all those hemmed
in by the fire. and many leaped from the
second story to the ground


One old chap landed on his feet. but
broke his leg, and then he plunged for
ward and injured himself internally.


Abandoned by Rescuers.


When the fire was out the f1remen went
through the building, and on the third
floor found the body of an old man. This
man was known only as "Old Nick" He
was on the third floor when the fire started,
and some of the other inmates tried to
help him down stairs, but were compelled
to leave him owing to the ~ense smoke
and flames.


The cause of the fire is unknown. 1t
may have started from some fat boiling
over in the kitchen.

With business-like precision that
smaeked of West Point training. the Dis
trict National Guard was bundled off to
Gettysburg in four comfortably crowed
trains yesterday morning. Hundreds OF
young soldiers in khaki and regulation
equipment thronged the vestibules and
cheered from car windows as the first train
pulled out the Baltimore and Ohio freight
station at o'clock. Three more train
loads left within fifteen minutes


Brig Gen. Harries' eyes glistened with
pride as the First and Second regiments
with their ranks complete swung into
the big station. shortly after o'clock.
In the hours that followed there was not
a moment OF confusion. Even the young
est officers refused to lose their leads
for an instant, and promptly at the ap-
pointed time the starting signal was given
to the railroad people.


The trains were not allowed to become
crowded. There were three seats for
every two men, with plenty of room for
equipment. On the first train were the
horses and guns OF the field artillery and
the apparatus of signal corps including
wireless equipment for the field.


Tents, grub wagons" ammunition. and
mess outfits were slowed away in the
most approved military way without a
hitch. and the men were marched TO their
respective cars Just as smoothly The
First Battalion OF colored troops carried
out their part of the general orders with
precision.


By the time the second and third trains
were ready to leave, the station platforms
were crowded with mothers. sisters. and
sweethearts. Though there were no tears.
the ones left behind made up for it with
enthusiasm, and never did wartime
regiment get more applause.


The usual hurry and hustle that char
aeterizs such departures was absolutely
lacking. Every one knew Just what to do.
and every one did it, with the result that
there was not a blunder to mar the first
chapter OF the maneuvers. Regulars
couldn't have done it better.


The guardsmen went away Just as they
would If they had been going to war. The
officers Jared just as did the men. and
they will have to work just as hard get
ting into camp at Gettsburg as the boys
who went to Cuba did. The luxuries that
used to go TO camp with National Guard
regiments were conspicuously absent.


But is was a cheerful Ieave-taking, and
officers and men alike were ready to
welcome the hardsfips that are coming.
Every man who went was examined by a
doctor and pronounced physically perfect.

MASSILLON. Ohio March GA
story unique in the history Of Ohio

murder the police have laid against
Catherine ManZ, a child 16 years old.
She is accused of poisoning her sister
Elizabeth, three years her senior, with
strychnine Her motive is said to
have been jealousy of her sister s
wardrobe, more brilliant than her own.


Not guilty" was the plea entered by
the girl when arraigned before Mayor
Remley today. The warrant charges
murder in the first degree.


After a night in the Massilon Jail the
girl underwent today two hours eX-
animation. throughout which she
calmly chewed gum and affirmed her
innocence She reiterated her original
story of a mysterious man for whom
she had purchased strychnine and who
had given her two capsules, which she
says she believed contained quinine.
Her hearing will be deferred until the
Cleveland chemist makes his report.


The girl was arrested yesterday in
Akron. where she had applied for
work under the name of Ethel Morgan.
Brought here to Jail, she faced her ac-
cusers calmly and told them unemo-
tionally that her sister was dead be-
fore she left the house.


The most damaging evidence against
the girl is the admitted fact that she
purchased strychnine at a local drug
store shortly before her sisters death,
and also bought a small quantity of
chloroform. The girl claims she bought
the strychnine for a man, whose name
she has refused to divulge. The chlO-
roform she says she bought for clean
ing purposes,


The mother of the girls has been
dead for fifteen years, and. according
to GATHERINGS father, she has grown
up headstrong and absolutely beyond
his control.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. S.-Fifteen
thousand men and women marched in
the labor union parade tonight. This
parade, which had been postponed from
the first week in October because of the
explosion which wrecked the Los Ange-
les Times office. had caused the city
authorities considerable uneasiness, but
that this was unfounded was evident
tonight when not an act of violence
marred the demonstration.


Although efforts have been made to
connect organized labor with the de-
struction of the Times, this feature
was ignored by the marchers, and in
perfect order, and without even hoot
or jeer. the thousands paraded through
the business streets and out to Fiesta
park, where speeches were made
Prominent in the parade were the
metal workers, whose strike precipi-
tated the bitter labor troubles of the
last few months. Leading the line OF
march were the iron workers, and
bringing up the rear was the division
of the allied printing trades, led by the
typographical union.


The park, which is nearly a mile
from the downtown district. was com
fortably filed before the last of the
parade had passed the starting. point OF
the leaders. Union officials declare the
parade was the greatest union demon
stration that has ever been made in
Los Angeles.

A French scientist, Doctor Perrier,
has been investigating the question
whether criminals have longer arms
than the more law abiding members of
the community-that is to say, to what
extent, If any, they approach in length
of arm the negro and anthropoid ape
types. The results obtained are inter-
estine, because they indicate just the
opposite to what might have been ex-
pected


Doctor Perrier premises that in
Europe normally proportioned man
can stretch with arms extended about
2M inches more than his height, says
the London Globe Out of S56 prisoners
of the Mines prison who were examined
he found IL per cent could not stretch
their own height. e., had arms much
shorter than usual; In per cent the
measurements were the same and in
SO per cent the arm stretch exceeded
the height by from one to two inches.
or, in other words, their arms were also
slightly shorter than the normal.


Distinguishing next between the diff
ferent classes of crime some curious re-
suits are noted For instance, vagrants
who were put to the test were found to
have very short arms. Murderers had
arms of slightly short or normal length.
Those convicted of theft and moral
crimes approached more nearly to the
normal standard, while coiners, on the
contrary, were mostly remarkable for
very short arms.


Other results obtained are equally
entertaining, especially the fact which
the learned investigator had discov-
cred, that married criminals have more
normal proportions than the single
rogue. It suggests possibly that the
single man is born criminal while
the married man has been forced into
crime through circumstances, of which
his marriage may be one.

text:
Would you like to hear about the
good fairy who lives in the sky?


Her name is Beautiful, and at nights
she sleeps on the bosom of some soft,
white cloud.


Now, in the daytime this little fairy
is constantly at work. and all of the
time she is creating something more
beautiful and lovely for the people who
live down here on the great earth.


Each night. when the tired sun sinks
to rest behind the western hills, she
takes her magic brush, and. flying to
the western part of the sky. paints
beautiful bands of soft. trembling
colors of purple. red and gold fire along
the horizon line.


Then she stands off a short ways and
admires her pretty work. From a. dis
tance she blows ever so gently, and
10! the wonderful colors undergo a
marvellous change. The red , slowly
fades to a most delicate pink, the gold
to the palest yellow, while the purple
sifts away into restful gray.


All the time the little fairy is singing
a quaint little night song-much the
same as your mamma sings to you at
bedtime-and the great sun, getting
sleepier and sleepier sinks lower and
lower. until finally 1t dips altogether
out of sight


The sky fairy then blows a bit
harder, and the fire colors become like
a fountain mist in the afterlight. Then
they fade-fade away into that Won
derfuI soft gray


Good night, dear sum-" she mur-
murs, and she turns and floats lightly
away through the dusk of the coming
night.


AS she travels along she pauses at
the door of each little star in the
heavens and calls softly: "Come out;
come out" And then from each little
sky house there appears a silver star
which flashes out a good evening to
you little folk down here on the earth.
Jupiter, Venus and Saturn all are
there, and together the millions of
stars wave their tiny night lanterns
to each other in a salute Of greeting.
The little sky fairy laughs happily,
and. turning to the east, she calls
softly, ALREADY, dear moon, already"


And somewhere-it seems right from
the heart of that long stretch of east
ern hills-there pokes into view the
good natured face of the jolly moon.


Away to some big cloud flies the good
fairy, where soon she falls asleep just
for all the world like you do.-Colum-
bus News.

VIENNA, Sept. 3.-The continual
national disputes between Germans
and Czechs have led to unfortunate eX-
cesses in Vienna. Four hundred Czechs
arrived here from Prague the other
day with the object, of visiting the field
sports exhibition. The Germans, how
ever, regarded this visit as a provoca-
ton and considerable agitation against
the coming of the Czechs was carried
on by the Germans.


On their arrival the visitors pro-
ceeded to the Czech club house, where
a crowd of several hundred people had
assembled, and commenced demon
strating on the appearance of the
strangers. One of the Czechs was so
maltreated that the police intervened,
upon which the crowd attacked the
officers, throwing beer tankards and
rotten eggs at them and using their
sticks as weapons. Several policemen
were injured, one officer very seriously.


The demonstrators were finally dis
persed with great trouble and the
Czechs were again able to venture on
the streets.

With brilliant vocalism, definite, con-
vincing pianism, and a well trained,
well balanced group of instrumental
lists, the Women's Symphony orchestra
played its first concert of the season
at the Auditorium last night.


The house was well filled, and the
ambitious group of women received
due appreciation for the earnest eff
forts they have made along musical
lines and for the splendid strength they
have achieved. They show good vol
ume for their numerical strength, and
the tonality of the instruments. es-
peclally of the strings was notably
good. There was noticeable once or
twice in the work last night some
lack of unity, which is no doubt due
entirely to the lack of public appear
ances of the orchestra. 1t is evident
from many causes that more playing
in public would have beneficial enliv-
ening and strengthening effect, and
would serve to familiarize Los An
geles music lovers with the decidedly
creditable work which these players
do. The program last night opened
with the sparkling and familiar over
ture to Tampa, in which the players
were at their best. The Beethoven
Symphony in major proved a more
difficult number for the instruments,
but the strings with their cantabile
helped over some of the thin places in
the reeds. The fantasie on themes
from Grieg was an interesting and
gratifying selection. The beautiful
"Ballet of the Hours" from Giorconda
and Wagner's "Albumblatt" concluded
the program for the evening, and each
was we'll selected to display to most
advantageous manner the many ad-
mirable qualities of the orchestra.


Paloma Schramm was the piano
soloist, playing the Beethoven con-
certo on e fiat, with these three num-
bers, Allegro, Adagio un POGO motto
and the Rondo, each with studious
reading. and abundant technical abil-
ity. The restraint which sometimes
follows this young players effort to
exercise classical severity, was less
marked last night than in some of her
previous experiences, and the orches-
trail accompaniment seemed to affect
both soloists with a most desirable
spirit and we've.


Miss Blanche Ruby sang the I'll
tania aria" from Mignon with an aban-
don and brilliance quite beyond her
usual excellent manner and was ac-
corded the honor Of an encore, return
ing to the stage repeatedly to bow
and accept the great bouquets ana
baskets of flowers which were rendered
her.


Mr.. Hamilton, who directed the SYM
phony was obliged to return and bow
his appreciation for applauses both
for himself and the orchestra several
times during the evening.

NEW YORK, April 1.-Two Italians
fought duel early today in New York
street not far from the East Side water
front. One of them was killed by shot
fired straight through his head. His ad-
versary escaped, leaving no clue to his
identity.


The strange battle was seen, so far as
can be learned, by only one witness, an
automobilist, who was on his way to his
uptown home. Though two blocks away
he saw the two men step out from hall
way, measure of a certain number of
PAGES, and then turn quickly, revolvers in
hand. There were three shots and one of
the combatants fell. The other, throwing
down his weapon, dashed back into the
hallway and made his escape


The automobilist called policeman. but
the latter found nothing but the corpse
and the two revolvers. The dead man
has not been identified.

tache of the American embassy, and a
representative from the American con-
sulate.


American boats surrounded the
steamer, which, after stopping sud-
denly, crashed into and sunk a tug.

rescued and the incident caused great
excitement.


Mrs. and Miss Roosevelt were landed
and went to the Hotel Excelsior, where
they met many friends. They may
take passage Wednesday for Egypt.

NEW YORK, July 4.-The news that
johnson had won from Jeffries at
Reno, New, flashed through the con-
gested streets and squares of Manhat-
tan, and wherever it ran trouble fol-
lowed it. Great crowds packed the
open spaces in front of the bulletin
boards. cheering and groaning for their
favorite The blacks were exultant
and good natured, and the whites were
surly and disappointed. From the mo-
ment the decisive words, Johnson
wins" went upon the bulletin boards
until midnight there were seventeen
calls for police and ambulances, and
in almost as many parts OF the town.


Four negroes were arrested and eight
whites. Five negroes, but no whites,
were taken to hospitals.


There was a fresh outburst in the
BLACK and Tan" belt and on san
Juan hill"


Late tonight, after seeming quiet had
been settled over the seething streets,
a gang of ruffians set fire to negro
tenement house, threw stones at win
dows whenever a frightened face ap-
peared and tried to keep the tenants
inside by blocking the exits. An alarm
was turned in so quickly, however, and
the response of the police and of the
fire department was so prompt that the
gang was scattered and the fire put
out before much damage had been
done.


In the better hammered negro quarter
Lob of white men rushed out of a
saloon, shouting, Lets lynch the first
niger we see."


Presently came convenient trolley
car with negro riding on front seat.
The crowd stormed the car, pulled the
negro into the street and beat and
kicked him. He was rescued by the
police. Three of his assailants were
arrested.


Farther down town two detachments
of the "allied hounds of hell' and the
pearl button gang" accosted peace
able negro who was buying a paper.


"What do you think of the hght?"
demanded the toughs.


81 am neutral" answered the negro


Lets kill the coon," said the gang
of men and rushed for him. The negro
drew a wicked looking stiletto and held
them off until the police came. He
and three of his assailants were
locked up.

RENO, New, July 4.-Jack Johnson
removed the last cloud upon his title
as heavyweight champion of the world
this afternoon when he stopped Jim
Jeffries in the fifteenth round of a
slow and disappointing battle that was
scheduled over the forty-ive-round
route.


Technically, Johnson does not get
credit for a Knockout, although JEFF
fries was out and could not have
arisen in time to avoid the fatal count
by Timekeeper Harting, who had
tolled eight when Sam Berger, Jeffries'
manager, jumped into the ring, COM
mitting an intentional foul that ended
the fight, and assisted jeff to his feet.
At this foul Harting ceased counting
and Referee Tex Rickard declared
Johnson the winner.


Although Johnson had been leading
in every round and friends of Jeffries
had ceased roofing and had become
sullenly quiet after the sixth round,
realizing that the big fellow was
beaten unless he could make winning
rally and era the fight with one
punch, the end came suddenly and un-
expectedly. At the beginning of the
fifteenth round Johnson crossed sharp
ly with right hook to the jaw that
Jared jeff and forced him to clinch.
breaking away III d HSulIul tOIhCA
Johnson slammed hard left to the
wind and uppercut fiercely with his
right, staggering JEFF, and followed it
with left smash to the jaw as he was
tottering.


FALLS IIAIPLY


jeff fell sideways to the floor, his
arms falling Imply over the ropes.
Friends and seconds at the ringside
half raised and pushed him to his feet,
the big fellow staggering weakly as
he rose.


johnson rushed in with a hard right
swing to the jaw and jeff went
through the ropes, falling to sitting
position with all his body outside the
ring except his legs. He was again
assisted and called on to arise. Ref
cree Rickard forced Johnson to step
back several feet.


Jeff came UP gamely, but was prac-
tically out and was unable to make
any effective defense. Johnson rushed
at him as he staggered to the north
side of the ring and swung another
vicious right to the jaw. JEFF went
down a third time, almost falling out
of the ring. Only his legs remained
In the inclosure, while his body hung
over the lower rope.


He struggled to get UP again, but was
all in and could not rise, and Time
keeper Harting began to call off the
seconds in a loud voice. Manager
Berger and Jim Corbett yelled to
Referee Rickard to stop the fight right
there, but he did not act and both
jumped into the ring, committing an
intentional foul to save Jeff the further
humiliation of being counted out. They
picked him up and assisted him to
his corner, where he leaned weakly
against the ropes and seemed to sink
to the floor when he was helped to his
chair.


JEFF HEARTBROKEN


AS he sat down he leaned over and
seemed heartbroken over his deteau,
and did not assume an upright posi-
tion until he had been given restora-
tives He presented pittable spec
tacles. Both lips were swollen and
puffed out, blood gushing from his
mouth and nose. His right eye was
closed tightly and was discolored. His
left eye was nearly closed. His left
cheek was slightly cut as was his
forehead.


AS soon as the fans realized the
fight was at an end and their once
unbeatable gladiator had made the
once-too- often battle, they surged to
the ringside and climbed into the ring,
shutting off all air and almost suffo-
eating the big fellow. Jim Corbett,
John L. Sullivan, Sam Berger and
others ordered the crowds away, but
no heed was given these orders, and
finally police and state rangers jumped
into the ring and charged the crowd,
throwing them bodily from the ring.
Some showed resistance and were
promptly turned upside down in their
flight through space from the ring to
the floor of the pavilion. The ring was
cleared in about two minutes, ana
Jeffries was able to leave for his
dressing room


Jeffries was whirled away to his
training camp at Moana Springs in an
automobile and made little effort to
talk about his first and last losing

The big crowd seemed dazed and did

long after Jeffries had left, remaining

through the area covered by the prin-

lodged from bush to bush in front Of

from none of the machans could the

shot. Next morning the tiger, a mag
nifcent specimen, was found dead. 1t

fortune.

OSSIN1NG. N. Y, October 7.-Six con.

Sing Sing prison early today.


After beating one keeper into in
sensibility and binding and gagging an
other guard. they removed an iron bar
from window and lowered themselves
to the ground by blanket cut into
strips. One of the convicts, a West
Indian negro, returned to the prison
after an hours liberty, and gave the
alarm.


The ringleader of the escaped con.
victs is William Green, a desperate
character. serving a long term for high
way robbery. The four other convicts
are Robert Boylan of Queens county.
Walter Branigan of Mount Kisco, Israel
Blum and Joseph White of New York.


Keeper Sent for on Ruse.


Shortly after midnight word was sent
to Keeper Drum, in charge of the
chapel dormitory in the administration
building, where the convicts were con-
hned. that prisoner was ill.


Green set upon Drum and beat him
repeatedly with a hammer. until he
to Drums aid, but was quickly bound
and gagged.


Then the convicts locked the dormitory
door and fled to the toilet room.


An iron bar, evidently filed through
some time before. was quickly removed
The men lowered themselves to the
ground and fled.


Escaped Man Returns.


Meanwhile, one of the convicts cut the
telephone wire connecting the dormitory
with the warden's Office. The escape
would not have been known until g
o'clock had not the negro convict re-
turned to the prison and told the wardens
what had happened.


The alarm whistle was sounded. War
den Frost hurried to the dormitory. where
Drum was found still unconscious. One
Of the convicts had taken $40 from
Foley's pocket.


Almost the entire force Of keepers was
sent out in pursuit Of the convicts. In
stead Of going to work as usual this
morning the 1,716 convicts were locked
in their cells.


The two keepers had charge OF 195
convicts. Warden Frost was surprised
that more prisoners did not seize the op-
portunity to escape.


All the conv1cts were serving terms for
larceny.

Cairo, April THE Egyptian Gazette
reports a savage assault on an Irish
priest named Mullan and four American
students by Arab boatmen at Haifa, on
the Bay of Alden. The Arabs were row
ing the visitors to a steamship at night.
and demanded treble fare When this
was refused, they attacked the visitors
with knives and a fierce fight followed,
in which the boatmen were worsted.


They continued rowing, but the noise
of the fight had attracted other boatmen
who rowed alongside the visitors boat
and battered the travellers with their
oars. Another struggle ensued.. and the
visitors were overcome. Their pockets
were rifed and their baggage stolen.
The first crew took them to the steamer.
hastily landed them on the gangway. and
then decamped in the darkness. The
travellers were exhausted They had
numerous but not serious wounds The
British and American consuls are inves-
tigating.

wise the muscles are coated and lose

irritation to the nerves produces swell
ing and Inflammation of the flesh.

afternoon.

float her until her cargo has been jet
tisoned.

can communicate with the owners. The
passengers still on board and the crew
are well.

for wrecks, and came upon the Louisiana

Canary Islands and Teneriffe, with gen.
eral cargo and SAT passengers. When
within fifty miles of Havana, Monday,
and in the teeth of the hurricane, the
captain lost control of his ship. which at
5 o'clock that afternoon was driven hard
upon Sombrero reef.


The cutter found that those on board
were not suffering and. after taking on as
many Of the passengers as the cutter
could accommodate, sailed for Key West
Pending her return to the wreck those on
board will be cared for comfortably.


Schooner a Total Loss.

knights Key, reports the American
four-masted schooner Edward T. Stotes-
bury total loss on Pigeon Key. One
man was washed overheard and drowned.
Three others were brought to the marine
hospital here. The schooner, Capt Burke
commanding, was bound from Tampa to
Baltimore with 2 load of phosphate.


The schooner Serafins has been towed
into port. The Spanish schooner Marta
from Havana, has been dismasted and
abandoned.

DOVER, England. April S.-The emf
grants who were transferred to the
steamer Kanawha from the British
steamer Cairnrona after fire broke out
on the Cairnrona yesterday became SO
unruly this morning that the captain OF
the Kanawha was obliged to ask for
naval assistance


A detachment Of armed marines was
sent aboard the vessel to restore order


The fire on board the Cairnrona was
extinguished today and the steamer pro-
ceeded for London.


Explosion Kills Child.


The Cairnrona sailed Wednesday from
London for Portland, Me. She carried
800 passengers for the most part emf
grants. and general cargo.


a number Of women with children In
their arms were sitting on a hatch, when
suddenly violent explosion hurled them
to all parts of the deck.


Some of them were shockingly injured.
One child was killed. The hatch was
blown to fragments.


A terrible panic ensued, the emigrants.
mostly Russians running up and down,
screaming and wringing their hands.
Another explosion occurred in the engine





The Kanawha and Upland steamed up
quickly and the captain decided to trans
fer all the passengers. This was ac-
complished speedily, but was accompa-
MED by scandalous scenes.


Scores of the men tried to rush the
boats. Many of them fought with the
women, tearing and dragging them aside
and even trampling them under foot.


Frantic Men Knocked Down.
The crew battled valiantly against the
panic-stricken emigrants using fist and
feet and any weapon they could find.
Not few frantic men were felled before
the hysterical. fainting women and chill
dren could be gotten into the boats.


In the stampede four persons fell or
were pushed into the sea and were res
cued with difficulty.


The Kanawha and Upland reached Dow
er with the rescued passengers late In the
afternoon and the scenes at the landing
were piteous. Exhausted by cold and ex-
posure, many half-famished and others
suffering from injuries.


Admiral Prince Louis of Battenberg and
the princess, with the British naval Of
ficers, lent assistance. The naval surgeons
attended the wounded. Many of them

pital

The Christmas rush is at its height.


Streets are thronsed. stores crowded.


markets packed Mails are congested,
express deliveries are behind time.
Buyers are overrushed and sellers
overworked. Lame feet are epidemic.
Grouches are prevalent.


And. as with the Christmas rush, all
the inevitable signs of the season are
here. Children are seraphic, angelic.
incapable of offense The bowl of ginger
cookies stands on the pantry shelf.
The janitor is polite. The ash man


runs to schedule. The garbage col
lector picks up scattered scraps that
have blown from the can.
Mother has headache. Father has


dug and is digging. There is a smell
of evergreen in the air.


Peace With Christmas Eve.


The grand climax of the preliminaries
comes tomorrow night. After that
| there'll be peace for the weary for two
blessed days.


And during that incorporating the


doctrine and practicing the customs of
the Yuletide, happy with family and
friends, joyous in giving and receiving,
warmed by inward spirit and outward
sign-the weariness of the flesh and the
petty annOyances and Vexations of these
last few days before Christmas will be
entirely forgotten, and everybody, old
and young, will be in accord with the


sentiment and atmosphere of the holi-
day season.


But today the grand rush is on. The
downtown streets and stores were not
alone in furnishing evidence of the fact.
The human express service in these last
hours is taxed to it's uttermost. Many a
weary mother and some disguised fathers
may be seen loaded down with bundles
on the way for more. or dragging weary


limbs toward home. that the youngsters


may not be disappointed.


The ten-cent stores and the big depart
ment stores furnish examples of the


rush that would make the old-time


football field feel sorry. The nice things


and the pretty things in the stores are


disappearing from the shelves and coun-


tiers and finding their way into the


homes. into the mails and into the eX-


press offices. Big business by the buy


ers this year ought to make many happy


hearts somewhere.

against prices today.

points not showing in the primary market

buyers out of the market and induce others to
unload. Cash demand has been slim specu-
lators and consumers holding off pending de-
velopments Weather fine over the corn belt

casted.

not large. Commission house demand slim.

priced provisions has counted against senti-
ment today, holders selling and new buyers

SAN BERNARDINO, Feb. 27.-Face
to face with a mad dog, huge blue
Dane, George Barker and Philips
Newman Friday battled for their lives
at their camp in the San Bernardlno
mountains.


For several days the men noticed
the dog about their camp, but though
its actions were peculiar there was
no suspicion that rabies were develop
ing. Friday Barker found the animal
crouching in the woodshed. The mad
dened beast leaped upon him, knocking
him to the ground. Newman, who was
close by, rushed to his partners as
sistance and the two men then battled
with the animal. With clubs they
finally beat the dog to death, but not
before they both had narrow escapes
from being bitten.


The fight lasted only short time,
but the beast sprang at Barker after
he had regained his feet and sank its
teeth into his clothing.


1t is thought that the animal either
contracted the rabies from coyotes or
was bitten by the mad dog near Beau
mont which later made its way into
Redlands.
